weeks.title: Signed quantities and constant-acceleration motion in one dimension
weeks.objective: Choose an origin and a positive direction, compute displacement, velocity and acceleration as signed quantities, and solve constant-acceleration problems, including free fall.

connection.before: Solving linear and quadratic equations, rearranging formulas and computing with signed numbers.
connection.after: Week 2 represents the same motion with position, velocity and acceleration graphs and compares measurements made in different reference frames.

days: Set up a coordinate axis with an origin and a stated positive direction; sort quantities into scalars and vectors.
Compute distance, displacement, average speed and average velocity for trips with several legs.
Define average acceleration and use the signs of velocity and acceleration to decide whether an object speeds up or slows down; read a motion diagram.
Use the constant-acceleration relations, choosing the one that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor need.
Apply the relations to free fall with a = −9.8 m/s^2 (up positive); mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: Physics describes motion relative to a coordinate system: an origin, an axis and a positive direction. A scalar, such as a time of 12 s or a distance of 30 m, has only a size. A vector, such as displacement, velocity or acceleration, has a size and a direction. Along a single axis the direction is carried by a sign, so a velocity of −4.0 m/s means 4.0 m/s in the negative direction. The choice of positive direction is yours, but you must state it and keep it for the whole problem.

Displacement is the change in position, Δx = x_f − x_i, and it ignores the path; distance adds the length of every leg. Average velocity is Δx/Δt and average speed is distance/Δt. Instantaneous velocity is the velocity over a very short interval, and speed is its magnitude. Average acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time, a = Δv/Δt, measured in m/s^2. An object speeds up when its velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows down when the signs are opposite, so a negative acceleration does not by itself mean slowing down.

When the acceleration is constant, four relations connect the initial velocity v_0, the final velocity v, the acceleration a, the time interval t and the displacement Δx: v = v_0 + at; Δx = v_0t + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx; and Δx = (1/2)(v_0 + v)t. Each relation leaves out one of the five quantities. List what you know and what you want, notice which quantity is neither, and pick the relation that omits it. If the acceleration changes partway through, split the motion into stages and carry the final velocity of one stage forward as the initial velocity of the next.

Near Earth's surface, with air resistance neglected, every freely falling object has an acceleration of 9.8 m/s^2 downward, whether it is rising, falling or momentarily at rest at the top of its path. With up as positive, a = −9.8 m/s^2 throughout the flight. Common errors are setting the acceleration to zero at the top, where only the velocity is zero; writing +9.8 m/s^2 after choosing up as positive; using one relation across stages with different accelerations; and reporting a distance when a signed displacement is asked for.

figures.alt: Number line labeled x in meters from −10 to 20 with three marked points: A at −6, C at 2 and B at 14.
Motion diagram: six dots along a dashed line, one every 0.20 s, starting at the left labeled t = 0. The gaps between dots shrink from left to right. An arrow marks +x pointing right.
Velocity–time graph with t from 0 to 8 s and v from −8 to 20 m/s. A straight line falls from 18 m/s at t = 0 to −6 m/s at t = 8 s.
A horizontal axis pointing in the +x direction with the origin O marked, an initial position x_i and a final position x_f to its right, and an arrow from x_i to x_f labeled Δx = x_f − x_i.
figures.caption: Displacement on a coordinate axis

examples.prompt: An elevator starts 12 m above the lobby floor, goes down to a parking level 6.0 m below the lobby floor, then rises to 3.0 m above the lobby floor. The whole trip takes 30 s. Take up as positive with the origin at the lobby floor. Find the distance traveled, the displacement, the average speed and the average velocity.
examples.answer: Distance 27 m; displacement −9.0 m (9.0 m down); average speed 0.90 m/s; average velocity −0.30 m/s (0.30 m/s downward).
steps: Positions: y_i = +12 m, the lowest point is −6.0 m, and y_f = +3.0 m.
Distance adds leg lengths: 18 m down plus 9.0 m up = 27 m. Displacement uses only the endpoints: Δy = 3.0 m − 12 m = −9.0 m.
Average speed = 27 m / 30 s = 0.90 m/s; average velocity = −9.0 m / 30 s = −0.30 m/s, so it points down.

examples.prompt: A sprinter accelerates uniformly from rest to 9.0 m/s in 2.5 s and then runs at that constant velocity. Take the running direction as positive. Find (a) the acceleration, (b) the distance covered in the first 2.5 s and (c) the total time to run 60 m.
steps: (b) The velocity is not needed as an unknown, so use Δx = (1/2)(v_0 + v)t = (1/2)(0 + 9.0 m/s)(2.5 s) = 11.25 m ≈ 11 m.
(c) The remaining 60 m − 11.25 m = 48.75 m is run at 9.0 m/s, taking 48.75 m / 9.0 m/s ≈ 5.42 s; total ≈ 2.5 s + 5.42 s ≈ 7.9 s.

examples.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 14 m/s from a balcony 6.0 m above the ground and later lands on the ground. Take up as positive with the origin at the release point, and neglect air resistance. Find the time in the air and the speed just before landing.
examples.answer: About 3.2 s in the air; it lands at about 18 m/s (17.7 m/s) moving downward.
steps: Knowns: v_0 = +14 m/s, a = −9.8 m/s^2, Δy = −6.0 m (the ground is below the release point).

worksheets.title: Signed quantities and the definitions
worksheets.directions: State your positive direction before computing. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Which list contains only vector quantities?
items.answer: (B) Velocity, acceleration, displacement
steps: A vector has a direction as well as a size.
Velocity, acceleration and displacement each have a direction; distance, speed, time and mass do not.
items.skill: Classify scalars and vectors

items.prompt: A delivery robot moves along a straight hallway shown on the number line. It starts at A, drives to B, then backs up to C. Take the direction of increasing x as positive. Find the distance the robot travels and its displacement.
items.answer: Distance 32 m; displacement +8.0 m
steps: Legs: A (−6 m) to B (14 m) is 20 m; B to C (2 m) is 12 m; distance = 20 m + 12 m = 32 m.
Displacement = x_C − x_A = 2 m − (−6 m) = +8.0 m.
items.skill: Read positions to find distance and displacement

items.prompt: The motion diagram shows a puck sliding in the +x direction, with one dot every 0.20 s. Which statement describes the puck's velocity and acceleration during the motion shown?
items.answer: (C) Velocity positive; acceleration negative
steps: The puck moves in +x, so its velocity is positive.
Equal time intervals cover shrinking distances, so the puck slows down; slowing down with positive velocity means the acceleration is negative.
items.skill: Interpret a motion diagram

items.prompt: A motorcycle moving at 6.0 m/s in the positive direction accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m/s^2 for 4.0 s. Find its final velocity and its displacement during the 4.0 s.
items.answer: Final velocity +16 m/s; displacement +44 m
items.skill: Apply constant-acceleration relations

items.prompt: A ball is released from rest above a river and takes 1.8 s to reach the water. Neglecting air resistance, how far does it fall, and how fast is it moving just before it reaches the water?
items.answer: It falls about 16 m (15.9 m) and reaches about 18 m/s (17.6 m/s).
steps: Take down as positive: v_0 = 0, a = 9.8 m/s^2, t = 1.8 s.
items.skill: Model free fall from rest

items.prompt: A car traveling at 22 m/s brakes with constant acceleration and stops in 55 m. Take the direction of motion as positive. (a) Find the acceleration. (b) Find the stopping time. Name the relation you chose for each part and explain why it fits.

rubric.criterion: Chooses v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx for (a) because the time is unknown, with v = 0.
a = −4.4 m/s^2 with a negative sign (accept −4.3 to −4.5 m/s^2).
t = 5.0 s (accept 4.9–5.1 s) from v = v_0 + at or Δx = (1/2)(v_0 + v)t.

steps: (b) Now a is known: t = (v − v_0)/a = (0 − 22)/(−4.4) = 5.0 s. Check: average velocity 11 m/s × 5.0 s = 55 m.
items.skill: Choose a relation by the missing variable

worksheets.title: Choosing a constant-acceleration relation
worksheets.directions: List knowns and the unknown before choosing a relation. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and state your positive direction.

items.prompt: A skateboarder rolls down a ramp, speeding up uniformly from 1.5 m/s to 7.5 m/s in 3.0 s. Find the acceleration and the distance covered along the ramp.
items.answer: a = 2.0 m/s^2; distance 14 m (13.5 m)
steps: a = (7.5 m/s − 1.5 m/s)/3.0 s = 2.0 m/s^2 down the ramp.
items.skill: Use average velocity for constant acceleration

items.prompt: The graph shows the velocity of a cart launched up a long ramp, with up the ramp as positive. (a) Find the cart's acceleration. (b) At what time is the cart momentarily at rest? (c) Is the cart speeding up or slowing down at t = 7.0 s? Explain using signs.
items.answer: (a) −3.0 m/s^2; (b) t = 6.0 s; (c) speeding up: at 7.0 s the velocity is −3.0 m/s and the acceleration is −3.0 m/s^2, the same sign.
steps: (b) v = 0 where the line crosses the time axis: 18 − 3.0t = 0 gives t = 6.0 s.
(c) After 6.0 s the velocity is negative (the cart rolls back down) while the acceleration stays negative, so the speed increases.
items.skill: Connect velocity readings to the sign rule

items.prompt: A rocket sled starts from rest and reaches 120 m/s after traveling 400 m along a straight track with constant acceleration. Find its acceleration and the time this takes.
steps: Time is unknown, so v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx: a = (120)^2/(2 × 400) = 18 m/s^2.
items.skill: Solve for acceleration without time

items.prompt: A ball thrown straight up reaches a maximum height 7.2 m above its release point. Neglecting air resistance, find its launch speed and the time it takes to reach the top.
items.answer: Launch speed ≈ 12 m/s (11.9 m/s); time to the top ≈ 1.2 s
items.skill: Use the top of a vertical throw

items.prompt: An elevator starts from rest and accelerates upward at 1.2 m/s^2 for 2.5 s, moves at constant velocity for 8.0 s, then slows uniformly to rest in 2.0 s. Find its total displacement.
items.answer: About 31 m upward (30.75 m)
items.skill: Chain stages of motion

items.prompt: A student claims that a ball thrown straight up has zero acceleration at the top of its path because it is momentarily at rest there. (a) Evaluate the claim. (b) Support your answer by finding the ball's velocity 0.50 s before and 0.50 s after it reaches the top, and the average acceleration over that 1.0 s interval. Take up as positive.

rubric.criterion: States that the claim is incorrect: the acceleration is 9.8 m/s^2 downward at the top, as everywhere in the flight.
Explains that zero velocity at an instant does not mean zero acceleration; the velocity is changing from positive to negative there.
Finds +4.9 m/s before and −4.9 m/s after the top.
Computes the average acceleration (−4.9 − 4.9)/1.0 = −9.8 m/s^2 and connects it to the claim.

items.answer: (a) The claim is wrong. (b) The velocity is +4.9 m/s 0.50 s before the top and −4.9 m/s 0.50 s after, so the average acceleration is −9.8 m/s^2, not zero.
steps: At the top v = 0. With a = −9.8 m/s^2, 0.50 s earlier v = 0 − (−9.8)(0.50) = +4.9 m/s and 0.50 s later v = −4.9 m/s.
Average acceleration = Δv/Δt = (−4.9 − 4.9)/1.0 = −9.8 m/s^2: the velocity is still changing at the top, so the acceleration is not zero.
items.skill: Separate zero velocity from zero acceleration

worksheets.title: Multi-step motion and reasoning
worksheets.directions: Show the relation you use before substituting. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Car P starts from rest at x = 0 and accelerates at 2.0 m/s^2 in the +x direction. At the same instant car Q passes x = 0 moving at a constant +12 m/s. When and where does car P catch car Q, and how fast is P moving then?
items.answer: At t = 12 s and x = 144 m (about 1.4 × 10^2 m); P is moving at 24 m/s.
steps: Positions: x_P = (1/2)(2.0)t^2 = t^2 and x_Q = 12t.
Set equal: t^2 = 12t, so t = 12 s (t = 0 is the start); x = 12 × 12 = 144 m.
items.skill: Solve a catch-up problem

items.prompt: A stone is thrown straight down at 5.0 m/s from the top of a cliff 40 m high. Taking down as positive and neglecting air resistance, find the stone's speed when it reaches the bottom and how long the fall takes.
items.answer: About 28 m/s (28.4 m/s); about 2.4 s
items.skill: Free fall with an initial velocity

items.prompt: Ball X is released from rest at height h. Ball Y is released from rest at height 4h. Neglecting air resistance, how does Y's fall time t_Y compare with X's fall time t_X?
items.answer: (D) t_Y = 2t_X
steps: From rest, h = (1/2)gt^2, so t = √(2h/g) and t is proportional to √(h).
Multiplying h by 4 multiplies t by √(4) = 2.
items.skill: Reason proportionally from a relation

items.prompt: A cyclist riding at 8.0 m/s sees a hazard. Her reaction time is 0.60 s, during which she keeps riding at 8.0 m/s; she then brakes at a constant 5.0 m/s^2 until she stops. Find her total stopping distance.
items.answer: About 11 m (11.2 m)
steps: Reaction distance = (8.0 m/s)(0.60 s) = 4.8 m.
Braking distance from v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx: 0 = 64 − 2(5.0)Δx, so Δx = 6.4 m.
items.skill: Combine constant-velocity and braking stages

items.prompt:
A cart's velocity is recorded every 0.50 s:
| t (s) | 0 | 0.50 | 1.00 | 1.50 | 2.00 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v (m/s) | 0.40 | 0.85 | 1.30 | 1.75 | 2.20 |
Is the acceleration constant? Find the acceleration and the cart's displacement from t = 0 to t = 2.00 s.
items.answer: Yes; a = 0.90 m/s^2; displacement 2.6 m
steps: Each 0.50 s interval adds 0.45 m/s, so the acceleration is constant: a = 0.45/0.50 = 0.90 m/s^2.
items.skill: Test data for constant acceleration

items.prompt: Two identical balls are released at the same instant from the same height. Ball 1 is released from rest; ball 2 is thrown straight down at 3.0 m/s. Neglect air resistance. (a) Without calculating, compare the balls' accelerations and explain whether the vertical gap between them grows, shrinks or stays the same while both are falling. (b) Find the gap after 1.5 s.

rubric.criterion: States that both balls have the same acceleration, g downward.
Reasons that the difference in their velocities therefore stays 3.0 m/s.
Concludes that the gap grows at a steady rate (linearly in time).
Writes the positions (or their difference) with Δy_2 − Δy_1 = (3.0 m/s)t.
Gap = 4.5 m after 1.5 s (accept 4.4–4.6 m).

items.answer: (a) Same acceleration, so the velocity difference stays 3.0 m/s and the gap grows steadily. (b) 4.5 m.
steps: Both balls accelerate at 9.8 m/s^2 downward, so each gains speed at the same rate and ball 2 stays 3.0 m/s faster.
Down positive: Δy_1 = 4.9t^2 and Δy_2 = 3.0t + 4.9t^2, so the gap is 3.0t, which grows linearly.
items.skill: Translate between a qualitative claim and equations

weeks.title: Motion graphs and relative velocity
weeks.objective: Translate among written descriptions and position–time, velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs using slope and area, and find the velocity of an object as measured in different reference frames.

connection.before: Week 1's signed definitions of displacement, velocity and acceleration and the constant-acceleration relations.
connection.after: Week 3 treats motion in a plane as two one-dimensional motions along perpendicular axes, starting with vector components and projectiles.

days: Read position–time graphs: slope as velocity, a horizontal tangent as a turning point, curvature as the sign of the acceleration.
Read velocity–time graphs: slope as acceleration and signed area as displacement; locate reversals.
Build acceleration–time graphs, use their area as change in velocity, and convert among all three graphs and words.
Reference frames in one dimension: subscript notation and adding relative velocities.
Relative velocity in two perpendicular directions (boats and aircraft); mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: On a position–time graph the slope at any instant is the velocity. A straight line means constant velocity; a steeper line means a greater speed, and a line sloping down means motion in the negative direction. A curved graph means the velocity is changing: if the curve bends upward (concave up) the slope is increasing and the acceleration is positive; if it bends downward the acceleration is negative. Where the graph has a horizontal tangent the object is momentarily at rest, often at a turning point. Where two objects' graphs cross, the objects are at the same position at the same time.

On a velocity–time graph the slope is the acceleration and the signed area between the graph and the time axis is the displacement. Area above the axis counts as positive displacement and area below as negative; the distance is the sum of the areas without signs. Where the graph crosses the time axis the object reverses direction, even though its acceleration may not change at all. On an acceleration–time graph the area is the change in velocity, not the velocity itself, so you also need a starting velocity.

To translate a velocity graph into a position graph, work interval by interval: positive velocity means the position increases, a larger velocity means a steeper position graph, and zero velocity means a flat spot. To check, compute the area under the velocity graph up to a few key times and plot those positions. A common error is to read a velocity graph as a picture of the path: the highest point on a velocity graph marks the greatest velocity, not the greatest position, and a line sloping down on a velocity graph does not mean the object moves downward.

Every velocity is measured relative to some reference frame. Write v_AB for the velocity of A relative to B; then v_AC = v_AB + v_BC, so the inner subscripts chain together. In one dimension these are signed numbers: a passenger walking backward at 1.2 m/s in a train moving forward at 20 m/s has v_PG = −1.2 + 20 = +18.8 m/s relative to the ground. When the velocities are perpendicular, add them as vectors with the Pythagorean theorem and find the direction with the inverse tangent. Two observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other measure different velocities but the same acceleration. Check every relative-velocity answer by imagining what each observer actually sees.

figures.alt: Position–time graph of a walker with t from 0 to 10 s and x from −6 to 10 m. Straight segments join (0, 0), (4, 8), (6, 8) and (10, −4).
Velocity–time graph of a cart with t from 0 to 8 s and v from −8 to 6 m/s. The graph is horizontal at 4 m/s from t = 0 to t = 3 s, then a straight line falls to −6 m/s at t = 8 s.
Acceleration–time graph: a = 0 from t = 0 to t = 3 s, then a = −2 m/s^2 from t = 3 s to t = 8 s.
figures.caption: Key: acceleration of the cart

figures.alt: Position–time graph: a straight line from (0, 0) to (3, 12), then a curve bending down to a peak at (5, 16) with a horizontal tangent, then falling to (8, 7).
figures.caption: Key: position of the cart

figures.alt: Top view of a river between a near bank and a far bank separated by width w. The current v_WG points along the banks to the right. A boat at the near bank has velocity v_BW relative to the water pointing straight across toward the far bank.
figures.caption: Boat crossing a river

examples.prompt: Use the walker's position–time graph. Find the walker's velocity in each interval (0–4 s, 4–6 s, 6–10 s), the average velocity from t = 0 to t = 10 s, and the total distance walked. Take +x as positive.
examples.answer: +2.0 m/s, 0, −3.0 m/s; average velocity −0.40 m/s; distance 20 m
steps: Average velocity uses the endpoints: (−4 m − 0)/10 s = −0.40 m/s.
Distance adds the leg lengths: 8 m out, 0 m standing, 12 m back = 20 m.

examples.prompt: A moving walkway carries passengers east at 1.2 m/s relative to the floor. A traveler walks at 1.5 m/s relative to the walkway. Take east as positive. Find the traveler's velocity relative to the floor (a) when walking east and (b) when walking west on the walkway.
steps: Write v_TF = v_TW + v_WF, with v_WF = +1.2 m/s.
(b) v_TW = −1.5 m/s, so v_TF = −1.5 + 1.2 = −0.30 m/s: the traveler drifts slowly west relative to the floor.

examples.prompt: A small airplane points due north with an airspeed of 60 m/s while the wind blows toward the east at 15 m/s. Find the airplane's speed relative to the ground and the direction of its ground velocity.
examples.answer: About 62 m/s, directed 14° east of north
steps: v_PG = v_PA + v_AG: 60 m/s north plus 15 m/s east, which are perpendicular.
Direction: tan θ = 15/60, so θ ≈ 14° east of north.

worksheets.title: Reading motion graphs
worksheets.directions: Use slopes and areas from the graphs. State the positive direction. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: According to the walker's position–time graph, during which interval does the walker move in the negative direction?
choices: The walker never moves in the negative direction
items.answer: (B) From 6 to 10 s
steps: Motion in the negative direction means a negative slope on the position–time graph.
Only the segment from 6 s to 10 s slopes down.
items.skill: Read direction from slope

items.prompt: Using the cart's velocity–time graph, find the cart's acceleration from t = 3 s to t = 8 s and the time at which the cart reverses direction.
items.answer: a = −2.0 m/s^2; it reverses at t = 5.0 s
steps: The velocity passes through zero where 4 − 2.0(t − 3) = 0, at t = 5.0 s; the sign of v changes there.
items.skill: Read acceleration and reversal from a velocity graph

items.prompt: Using the cart's velocity–time graph, find the cart's displacement from t = 0 to t = 5 s and from t = 5 s to t = 8 s.
items.answer: +16 m from 0 to 5 s; −9.0 m from 5 s to 8 s
steps: 0 to 5 s: rectangle (4 m/s)(3 s) = 12 m plus triangle (1/2)(2 s)(4 m/s) = 4 m, total +16 m.
5 s to 8 s: triangle below the axis, (1/2)(3 s)(−6 m/s) = −9.0 m.
items.skill: Find signed displacement as area

items.prompt: An object's position–time graph is a straight line with a negative slope. Which describes its velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs?
choices: Velocity: a line sloping down; acceleration: a horizontal line below the axis
Velocity: zero; acceleration: a horizontal line below the axis
Velocity: a horizontal line above the axis; acceleration: zero
Velocity: a horizontal line below the axis; acceleration: zero
items.answer: (D) Velocity: a horizontal line below the axis; acceleration: zero
steps: A straight position graph has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant; a negative slope makes that constant negative.
Constant velocity means zero acceleration.
items.skill: Translate a position graph into velocity and acceleration graphs

items.prompt: A scooter moving at +2.0 m/s has an acceleration of +1.5 m/s^2 for 4.0 s and then an acceleration of −0.50 m/s^2 for the next 6.0 s. Use the area under its acceleration–time graph to find its velocity at t = 4.0 s and at t = 10 s.
items.skill: Use area under an acceleration graph

items.prompt: Sketch the acceleration–time graph for the cart whose velocity is shown, from t = 0 to t = 8 s. Label the values, and explain what happens to the acceleration at t = 5 s, when the cart reverses.

rubric.criterion: Shows a = 0 from t = 0 to t = 3 s.
Shows a constant a = −2.0 m/s^2 from t = 3 s to t = 8 s (accept −1.9 to −2.1).
States that the acceleration does not change at t = 5 s: only the velocity changes sign.

items.answer: a = 0 from 0 to 3 s and a = −2.0 m/s^2 from 3 to 8 s; nothing happens to the acceleration at t = 5 s.
steps: Slope of the velocity graph: 0 on the flat segment, then (−6 − 4)/5 = −2.0 m/s^2 on the sloped segment.
The sloped segment is one straight line through t = 5 s, so the acceleration stays −2.0 m/s^2 while the velocity passes through zero.
items.skill: Translate a velocity graph into an acceleration graph

worksheets.title: Translating among representations
worksheets.directions: Show how you use slope or area. State the positive direction. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt:
A cyclist starts from rest at x = 0. Her positions are:
| t (s) | 0 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 6.0 | 8.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x (m) | 0 | 4.0 | 16 | 36 | 64 |
Show that the data fit constant acceleration from rest and find the acceleration.
items.answer: x/t^2 = 1.0 m/s^2 for every row, so x = (1/2)at^2 with a = 2.0 m/s^2.
steps: From rest with constant acceleration, x = (1/2)at^2, so x/t^2 should be the same for every row.
items.skill: Test a table against a motion model

items.prompt: Sketch the position–time graph for the cart whose velocity is shown, from t = 0 to t = 8 s, taking x = 0 at t = 0. Label the positions at t = 3 s, 5 s and 8 s.

rubric.criterion: Straight rising segment from (0, 0) to 12 m at t = 3 s.
Curve that bends downward and has a horizontal tangent at its maximum at t = 5 s.
Curve falls after t = 5 s to 7 m at t = 8 s.
Labeled positions 12 m, 16 m and 7 m (accept ±1 m), found from areas.

items.answer: x rises linearly to 12 m at 3 s, curves to a maximum of 16 m at 5 s and falls to 7 m at 8 s.
steps: Areas under the velocity graph: 0–3 s gives 12 m; 3–5 s adds 4 m (x = 16 m); 5–8 s subtracts 9 m (x = 7 m).
Constant velocity gives a straight segment; constant negative acceleration gives a downward-bending curve, flat where v = 0 at 5 s.
items.skill: Translate a velocity graph into a position graph

items.prompt: A velocity–time graph starts at −5.0 m/s at t = 0 and rises in a straight line to 0 at t = 2.5 s. Which description matches the motion?
choices: Moving in the negative direction and slowing to a stop
Moving in the negative direction and speeding up
Moving in the positive direction and slowing to a stop
Moving in the positive direction and speeding up
items.answer: (A) Moving in the negative direction and slowing to a stop
steps: The velocity is negative throughout, so the motion is in the negative direction.
The magnitude of the velocity shrinks from 5.0 m/s to 0, so the object slows to a stop.
items.skill: Translate a velocity graph into words

items.prompt: A train's velocity–time graph has three straight pieces: from 0 to 20 m/s in 40 s, constant at 20 m/s for the next 100 s, then down to 0 in the last 30 s. Find the total distance traveled and the average velocity for the trip.
items.answer: Distance 2700 m (2.7 km); average velocity about 16 m/s (15.9 m/s)
steps: Average velocity = 2700 m / 170 s ≈ 15.9 m/s.
items.skill: Find displacement from a piecewise velocity graph

items.prompt: Two runners on a straight path have positions x_A = 3.0t and x_B = 40 − 5.0t (x in meters, t in seconds). When and where do they pass each other, and what is runner A's velocity relative to runner B?
items.answer: At t = 5.0 s and x = 15 m; v_AB = +8.0 m/s
items.skill: Connect crossing graphs to relative velocity

items.prompt: An object's position–time graph is a curve that is concave up and has a negative slope at t = 2 s. At t = 2 s, the object is
choices: moving in the positive direction and speeding up
moving in the negative direction and slowing down
moving in the negative direction and speeding up
items.answer: (C) moving in the negative direction and slowing down
steps: A negative slope means negative velocity; concave up means positive acceleration.
Velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, so the object slows down.
items.skill: Infer motion from slope and curvature

worksheets.title: Relative motion
worksheets.directions: Name each velocity with subscripts (v_AB is A relative to B) before adding. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures; give directions as angles from a named reference.

items.prompt: A passenger walks toward the back of a train at 1.4 m/s relative to the train while the train moves forward at 18 m/s relative to the ground. Take forward as positive. Find the passenger's velocity relative to the ground and relative to a car driving forward alongside the train at 25 m/s.
items.answer: +16.6 m/s (about 17 m/s) relative to the ground; −8.4 m/s relative to the car
steps: v_PC = v_PG − v_CG = 16.6 − 25 = −8.4 m/s: the driver sees the passenger moving backward.
items.skill: Chain relative velocities in one dimension

items.prompt: A boat points straight across a river 120 m wide, moving at 4.0 m/s relative to the water, while the current flows at 3.0 m/s parallel to the banks, as in the figure. Find (a) the boat's speed relative to the ground, (b) the time to cross and (c) how far downstream it lands.
items.answer: (a) 5.0 m/s; (b) 30 s; (c) 90 m downstream
steps: (a) Perpendicular velocities: √(4.0^2 + 3.0^2) = 5.0 m/s.
(b) Only the across component moves the boat toward the far bank: t = 120 m / 4.0 m/s = 30 s.
(c) Downstream drift = (3.0 m/s)(30 s) = 90 m.
items.skill: Resolve a crossing into independent directions

items.prompt: A boat that moves at 4.0 m/s relative to the water must cross a river 120 m wide flowing at 3.0 m/s and land directly opposite its starting point. At what angle upstream from the straight-across direction must it point, and how long does the crossing take?
items.answer: About 49° upstream from straight across; about 45 s
steps: The upstream component must cancel the current: 4.0 sin θ = 3.0, so θ = arcsin(0.75) ≈ 48.6° ≈ 49°.
items.skill: Choose a heading to cancel a current

items.prompt: Rain falls vertically at 8.0 m/s relative to the ground. A car drives through it at 6.0 m/s. What is the speed of the raindrops relative to the car?
steps: v_RC = v_RG − v_CG: 8.0 m/s down combined with 6.0 m/s backward (opposite the car's motion).
The components are perpendicular: √(8.0^2 + 6.0^2) = 10 m/s.
items.skill: Combine perpendicular relative velocities

items.prompt: Two cars approach each other on a straight road: one moves east at 24 m/s and the other west at 16 m/s. They are 1.0 km apart. Use the reference frame of the eastbound car to find how long it takes them to meet.
steps: In the eastbound car's frame the other car approaches at 16 + 24 = 40 m/s.
items.skill: Use a moving frame to simplify

items.prompt: A rider on a cart moving at a constant +3.0 m/s (to the right) tosses a ball straight up, relative to herself, at 5.0 m/s. Neglect air resistance. (a) Describe the ball's path as seen by the rider and as seen by a person standing on the ground. (b) Find the ball's velocity relative to the ground just after release. (c) Does the ball land back in the rider's hand? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Rider sees the ball move straight up and straight back down.
Ground observer sees a parabola-shaped arc moving to the right.
Ground velocity about 5.8 m/s at about 59° above the +x direction (accept 5.7–5.9 m/s and 58°–60°).
Yes: the ball keeps the cart's 3.0 m/s horizontal velocity, so it stays above the hand and lands in it.

items.answer: (a) Rider: straight up and down; ground: an arc to the right. (b) About 5.8 m/s at 59° above horizontal, to the right. (c) Yes, because ball and rider share the same horizontal velocity.
steps: Ground velocity = 3.0 m/s right + 5.0 m/s up: magnitude √(9 + 25) ≈ 5.83 m/s, angle arctan(5.0/3.0) ≈ 59°.
No horizontal force acts on the ball, so its horizontal velocity stays 3.0 m/s, the same as the rider's; it lands back in her hand.
items.skill: Compare descriptions in two reference frames

weeks.title: Vectors and projectile motion in two dimensions
weeks.objective: Resolve and add vectors by components, treat horizontal and vertical motion of a projectile as independent motions that share one time, and analyze supplied motion data by linearizing a graph.

connection.before: Week 2's perpendicular relative velocities and week 1's constant-acceleration relations and free fall.
connection.after: Unit 2 explains why velocities change, starting in week 4 with systems, centers of mass and free-body diagrams.

days: Resolve vectors into components, add vectors by components, and recover magnitude and direction.
Horizontal launches: constant horizontal velocity, free-fall vertical motion, and the shared time of flight.
Angled launches on level and unlevel ground: launch components, time to the top, maximum height and range.
Paper investigation: linearize supplied ramp data, find an acceleration from a slope, and discuss uncertainty and design.
Unit 1 review and the Unit 1 test.
explanation: A vector in a plane can be replaced by two perpendicular components. For a vector of magnitude A at angle θ measured from the +x axis, A_x = A cos θ and A_y = A sin θ, with signs that show direction. To add vectors, add their x components and their y components separately; the resultant has magnitude √(R_x^2 + R_y^2) and direction given by tan θ = R_y/R_x, checked against the quadrant of the components.

Once a projectile leaves the launcher and air resistance is negligible, the only force on it is gravity, which acts vertically. So a_x = 0 and a_y = −9.8 m/s^2 (up positive): the horizontal velocity stays constant while the vertical motion is exactly the free fall of week 1. The two motions are independent but share the same clock. At the top of the path the vertical velocity is zero and the velocity is horizontal, not zero. The figure shows a constant horizontal arrow and a vertical arrow that shrinks, vanishes at the top and then grows downward.

Method: write the x and y givens in separate lists. Find the time from the direction that has enough information, usually the vertical one, then use it in the other direction. On level ground the path is symmetric, so the time up equals the time down and the landing speed equals the launch speed. Common errors are using the launch speed as the horizontal velocity, setting the velocity (rather than its vertical component) to zero at the top, giving the horizontal motion an acceleration, and forgetting the launch height when the landing point is lower.

Experiments often test a model by making its graph a straight line. If a cart starts from rest with constant acceleration, d = (1/2)at^2, so a graph of d against t is curved but a graph of d against t^2 is a straight line through the origin with slope a/2. The slope carries units (here m/s^2), the intercept tests the model (a large intercept signals a systematic error such as a late start of the clock), and scatter about the line shows random uncertainty. College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

figures.alt: A launch velocity vector v_0 at 30° above a horizontal ground line, with its dashed horizontal component v_{0x} and dashed vertical component v_{0y}.

Graph of a ball's height y against horizontal position x, with x from 0 to 26 m and y from 0 to 6 m: a symmetric arc starting at the origin, peaking at the labeled point (12, 4.9) and landing at the labeled point (24, 0).
Blank grid of 12 by 9 squares for plotting, with heavier lines along the left and bottom edges.
Graph of d in meters against t^2 in s^2 with six plotted points lying close to a straight line through the origin; the best-fit line is labeled slope ≈ 0.42 m/s^2.
figures.caption: Key: linearized ramp data

figures.alt: A stone at the top edge of a cliff 20 m high is launched with velocity v_0 at 35° above the horizontal; flat ground lies below and beyond the cliff.
figures.caption: Launch from a cliff

figures.alt: A dashed projectile path over x and y axes. At five points along it a horizontal arrow v_x of the same length is drawn, and a vertical arrow v_y points up and shrinks on the way up, vanishes at the top (labeled v_y = 0), then points down and grows on the way down.
figures.caption: Velocity components along a projectile path

examples.prompt: A hiker walks 3.0 km at 40° north of east, then 2.0 km due north. Find the magnitude and direction of her total displacement.
examples.answer: About 4.6 km at about 60° north of east
steps: First leg: x = 3.0 cos 40° ≈ 2.30 km, y = 3.0 sin 40° ≈ 1.93 km. Second leg: x = 0, y = 2.0 km.
Sum: R_x ≈ 2.30 km, R_y ≈ 3.93 km.
Magnitude √(2.30^2 + 3.93^2) ≈ 4.55 km ≈ 4.6 km; direction arctan(3.93/2.30) ≈ 60° north of east.

examples.prompt: A marble rolls off a horizontal counter 1.2 m high and lands 0.75 m from the base of the counter. Neglecting air resistance, find the marble's speed as it leaves the counter.
examples.answer: About 1.5 m/s
steps: Horizontal: the launch velocity is horizontal and constant, so v_x = 0.75 m / 0.495 s.
v_x ≈ 1.5 m/s, which is the launch speed because the vertical launch component is zero.

examples.prompt: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 40° above the horizontal on level ground. Neglecting air resistance, find the time to reach maximum height, the maximum height and the range.
examples.answer: About 1.3 s to the top; maximum height about 8.4 m; range about 40 m
steps: Components: v_0x = 20 cos 40° ≈ 15.3 m/s and v_0y = 20 sin 40° ≈ 12.9 m/s.
Level ground is symmetric, so the flight lasts 2 × 1.31 ≈ 2.62 s and the range is 15.3 × 2.62 ≈ 40 m.

passages.title: Investigation data: a cart rolling down a ramp
passages.text:
A student releases a cart from rest at the top of a straight ramp 4.5 m long and films it beside a meter tape with a phone camera. Reading the video frame by frame, she records the distance d the cart has rolled at several times t after release.
| t (s) | 0.50 | 1.00 | 1.50 | 2.00 | 2.50 | 3.00 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| d (m) | 0.11 | 0.41 | 0.96 | 1.66 | 2.64 | 3.76 |
passages.attribution: Original data set written for Liminal.

worksheets.title: Components and horizontal launches
worksheets.directions: Neglect air resistance and use g = 9.8 m/s^2. State axes and positive directions. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A displacement of 25 m points 37° above the +x axis. Find its x and y components.
items.answer: x component ≈ 20 m; y component ≈ 15 m
items.skill: Resolve a vector into components

items.prompt: A robot moves 12 m east, then 9.0 m north, then 4.0 m west. Find the magnitude and direction of its total displacement.
items.answer: About 12 m at about 48° north of east
steps: R_x = 12 − 4.0 = 8.0 m east; R_y = 9.0 m north.
Magnitude √(8.0^2 + 9.0^2) ≈ 12.0 m; direction arctan(9.0/8.0) ≈ 48° north of east.
items.skill: Add vectors by components

items.prompt: A ball rolls off a horizontal table 0.80 m high at 2.5 m/s. How far from the base of the table does it land?
steps: Fall time: 0.80 = 4.9t^2, so t ≈ 0.404 s.
Horizontal distance = 2.5 m/s × 0.404 s ≈ 1.0 m.
items.skill: Link horizontal and vertical motion by time

items.prompt: A package is released from a drone flying horizontally at 12 m/s, 45 m above level ground. Find the time to reach the ground, the horizontal distance it travels, and its speed just before landing.
items.answer: About 3.0 s; about 36 m; about 32 m/s
steps: Vertical: 45 = 4.9t^2, so t ≈ 3.03 s. Horizontal: x = 12 × 3.03 ≈ 36 m.
At landing v_x = 12 m/s and v_y = 9.8 × 3.03 ≈ 29.7 m/s, so speed = √(12^2 + 29.7^2) ≈ 32 m/s.
items.skill: Analyze a horizontal launch fully

items.prompt: At the same instant, one ball rolls off a horizontal shelf at 3.0 m/s and an identical ball is released from rest at the same height beside it. Neglecting air resistance, which statement is correct?
choices: The rolling ball lands first, because it moves faster
They land at the same time, because their vertical motions are identical
The released ball lands first, because its path is shorter
It depends on the masses of the balls
items.answer: (B) They land at the same time, because their vertical motions are identical
steps: Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g.
The horizontal velocity of the rolling ball does not affect its vertical motion, so both fall the same height in the same time.
items.skill: Use independence of perpendicular motions

items.prompt: A soccer ball is kicked from level ground at 18 m/s at 30° above the horizontal, as in the figure. (a) Find v_0x and v_0y. (b) Find the ball's speed at the highest point of its path. (c) Find the total time the ball is in the air.

rubric.criterion: v_0x ≈ 15.6 m/s and v_0y = 9.0 m/s (accept ±0.1).
Speed at the top equals v_0x ≈ 15.6 m/s because the vertical component is zero there.
Time in the air ≈ 1.8 s from 2v_0y/g (accept 1.8–1.9 s).

steps: At the top only the horizontal component remains: 15.6 m/s.
Level ground: total time = 2v_0y/g = 18/9.8 ≈ 1.84 s.
items.skill: Use components at key points of a path

worksheets.title: Angled launches
worksheets.directions: Neglect air resistance and use g = 9.8 m/s^2; take up as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A ball is launched from level ground at 22 m/s at 50° above the horizontal. Find its time of flight and its range.
items.answer: About 3.4 s; about 49 m
steps: Time of flight = 2v_0y/g ≈ 3.44 s; range = 14.1 × 3.44 ≈ 49 m.
items.skill: Find time of flight and range

items.prompt: At the highest point of a projectile's path (with air resistance negligible), which statement is correct?
items.answer: (D) Velocity horizontal; acceleration 9.8 m/s^2 downward
steps: At the top v_y = 0 but v_x is unchanged, so the velocity is horizontal.
Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is still g downward.
items.skill: Describe velocity and acceleration at the top

items.prompt: The graph shows the path of a ball launched from the ground, with the highest point and the landing point labeled. Using the graph, find the time of flight, the horizontal velocity, and the launch speed and angle.
items.answer: Time of flight 2.0 s; v_x = 12 m/s; launch speed about 15 m/s (15.5 m/s) at about 39° above the horizontal
steps: From the maximum height 4.9 m: v_0y = √(2 × 9.8 × 4.9) = 9.8 m/s, so the time up is 1.0 s and the flight lasts 2.0 s.
items.skill: Translate a trajectory graph into launch conditions

items.prompt: A stone is thrown from the top of the cliff in the figure at 15 m/s, 35° above the horizontal, and lands on the level ground below, 20 m beneath the launch point. Find how long the stone is in the air and how far from the base of the cliff it lands.
items.answer: About 3.1 s; about 38 m
steps: Vertical: −20 = 8.60t − 4.9t^2, so 4.9t^2 − 8.60t − 20 = 0 and the positive root is t ≈ 3.08 s.
Horizontal: x = 12.3 × 3.08 ≈ 38 m.
items.skill: Solve a launch that lands below its start

items.prompt: Two projectiles are launched from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and one at 60° above the horizontal. Which statement is correct?
choices: The 30° launch has the longer range and the longer flight time
The ranges are equal, and the 60° launch stays in the air longer
The 60° launch has twice the range
The flight times are equal, but the ranges differ
items.answer: (B) The ranges are equal, and the 60° launch stays in the air longer
steps: Range = 2v^2 sin θ cos θ/g, and sin 30° cos 30° = sin 60° cos 60°, so the ranges match.
Flight time = 2v sin θ/g is larger for the larger vertical component, the 60° launch.
items.skill: Compare launches with proportional reasoning

items.prompt: A player releases a basketball 2.0 m above the floor at 7.2 m/s, 55° above the horizontal. The rim is 3.05 m above the floor and 4.2 m away horizontally. When the ball has traveled 4.2 m horizontally, is it above or below the rim, and by how much? Is it rising or falling then?

rubric.criterion: Finds v_x ≈ 4.13 m/s and the time to cover 4.2 m, t ≈ 1.02 s.
Writes y = 2.0 + v_0y t − 4.9t^2 with v_0y ≈ 5.90 m/s.
Finds y ≈ 2.93 m (accept 2.92–2.94 m).
Concludes the ball is about 0.12 m below the rim (accept 0.11–0.13 m) and falling, since v_y = 5.90 − 9.8t < 0.

items.answer: Below the rim by about 0.12 m (the ball is at about 2.93 m), and it is falling.
steps: v_y = 5.90 − 9.8(1.02) ≈ −4.1 m/s, so the ball is falling.
items.skill: Evaluate a projectile at a given horizontal position

worksheets.title: Investigation: acceleration from ramp data
worksheets.directions: Use the ramp data set for every item. Show your work on graphs and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

items.prompt: Using the ramp data, explain why a graph of d against t is curved if the acceleration is constant, and name the quantity to plot on the horizontal axis so that the graph is a straight line through the origin.

rubric.criterion: States that d = (1/2)at^2 from rest, so d depends on the square of t and d against t is a parabola.
Plots d against t^2, giving a straight line through the origin with slope a/2.

items.answer: From rest, d = (1/2)at^2, which is quadratic in t, so d against t curves upward. Plot d against t^2: the graph is a straight line through the origin with slope a/2.
steps: Starting from rest with constant a, the model is d = (1/2)at^2.
Let X = t^2; then d = (a/2)X, a line through the origin with slope a/2.
items.skill: Choose variables that linearize a model

items.prompt: Using the ramp data, add a row of t^2 values to the table. Then plot d against t^2 on the grid, choosing and labeling scales, and draw a single best-fit straight line.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled with quantities and units, scales that use most of the grid, and all six points plotted correctly.
One straight best-fit line passing close to the origin with points scattered on both sides.

items.answer: t^2 (s^2): 0.25, 1.00, 2.25, 4.00, 6.25, 9.00. The plotted points lie close to a straight line through the origin.
steps: Plot d on the vertical axis against t^2 and draw one line that balances the points; the key shows a fitted line through the origin.
items.skill: Plot linearized data with a best-fit line

items.prompt: Using your best-fit line for the ramp data, find the slope of the d-against-t^2 graph, with units, and use it to find the cart's acceleration.
items.answer: Slope ≈ 0.42 m/s^2 (accept 0.40–0.44 m/s^2); acceleration a = 2 × slope ≈ 0.84 m/s^2 (accept 0.80–0.88 m/s^2).
steps: Read two well-separated points on the line, not data points, e.g. (0, 0) and (9.0 s^2, 3.77 m): slope ≈ 3.77/9.0 ≈ 0.42 m/s^2.
items.skill: Interpret the slope of a linearized graph

items.prompt: Suppose the student had given the cart a small push at the top instead of releasing it from rest, and timed from the push. How would the graph of d against t^2 differ from a straight line through the origin?
choices: It would still be straight through the origin, with a larger slope
It would be a horizontal line
It would be straight but with a negative intercept
It would bend, because d would include a term proportional to t
items.answer: (D) It would bend, because d would include a term proportional to t
steps: With an initial speed, d = v_0t + (1/2)at^2.
The v_0t term is proportional to √(t^2), not to t^2, so the points no longer lie on a straight line.
items.skill: Anticipate how a changed procedure changes a graph

items.prompt: Use the acceleration you found from the ramp data to estimate how long the cart takes to roll the full 4.5 m length of the ramp from rest.
items.answer: About 3.3 s (accept 3.2–3.4 s for accelerations of 0.80–0.88 m/s^2)
items.skill: Use a fitted parameter to estimate a time

items.prompt: For the ramp data, identify one source of uncertainty in the time readings, explain how it would affect the slope you found, and describe one change to the procedure that would reduce it.

rubric.criterion: Names a plausible source, such as the release not falling exactly on a video frame or the frame rate limiting time resolution.
Explains the effect: for example, if every time reading is too large by the same amount, the t^2 values are too large and the slope (and a) comes out too small.
Describes a specific improvement, such as a higher frame rate, an electronic release that starts the clock, photogates, or repeated trials averaged.

items.answer: Example: the release may happen between frames, so every t is slightly too large; then each t^2 is too large and the fitted slope, and the acceleration, are too small. Filming at a higher frame rate or triggering timing with the release reduces this.
steps: A constant timing offset shifts every t by the same amount, which bends the d against t^2 graph and lowers the fitted slope when the offset is positive.
Better time resolution or a synchronized start removes most of that offset.
items.skill: Analyze uncertainty and its effect on a result

items.prompt: Using the same ramp, video setup and meter tape, design a procedure to test whether the cart's acceleration down the ramp depends on the cart's mass. Name the independent, dependent and controlled variables and describe how you would analyze the results.

rubric.criterion: Independent variable: cart mass (add known masses); dependent variable: acceleration found from a d against t^2 slope for each mass.
Controls: same ramp angle, same release point, release from rest, same track surface and camera position.
Analysis: compare accelerations (or graph a against mass) and judge whether any differences exceed the scatter between repeated trials.

items.answer: Vary the cart's mass with added known masses; for each mass record d and t from video, plot d against t^2 and take a = 2 × slope; keep the ramp angle, release point, surface and camera fixed; compare the accelerations against their trial-to-trial scatter.
steps: The model being tested gives the same acceleration for every mass if friction is negligible.
Repeat trials at each mass to estimate scatter, then decide whether any trend is larger than that scatter.
items.skill: Design an experiment with controlled variables

weeks.title: Systems, center of mass and free-body diagrams
weeks.objective: Choose a system and sort forces into internal and external, locate the center of mass of a set of objects, and draw free-body diagrams that show every force on an object together with the object exerting it.

connection.before: Unit 1's vectors, components and acceleration as the rate of change of velocity.
connection.after: Week 5 pairs every force with its Newton's third-law partner and uses Newton's first law to find unknown forces when the net force is zero.

days: Define a system and its surroundings; sort forces as internal or external and explain why only external forces change the motion of the center of mass.
Locate the center of mass of point masses on a line and in a plane; use symmetry for uniform objects.
Name the forces of mechanics (gravitational, normal, tension, friction, applied, spring) and the object that exerts each one.
Draw free-body diagrams: arrows starting on the object, lengths in reasonable proportion, angles marked, no velocity or 'ma' arrows.
Find net force by components from a free-body diagram, including forces at angles and tilted axes; mixed practice.
explanation: A system is whatever object or group of objects you choose to study; everything else is the surroundings. A force between two parts of the system is internal, and internal forces come in pairs that cancel when you add up the forces on the whole system. Only external forces, exerted by the surroundings, can change the velocity of the system's center of mass. Choosing a good system is a strategy: treat two blocks pushed together as one system to find their common acceleration, then treat one block alone to find the contact force between them.

The center of mass of point masses on a line is the mass-weighted average position, x_cm = (m_1x_1 + m_2x_2 + …)/(m_1 + m_2 + …), and the same formula gives y_cm in a plane. It lies closer to the larger masses. For a uniform symmetric object it is at the geometric center, which need not be inside the material (think of a ring). When only the translational motion of a system matters, the system can be modeled as a single object with all its mass at the center of mass.

A force is a push or pull from an interaction between two objects, measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s^2). The gravitational force of Earth on an object near the surface has magnitude mg and points down. Contact forces include the normal force, perpendicular to the surface of contact; tension, along a rope or string and pulling away from the object; and friction, parallel to the surface and opposing sliding or the tendency to slide. A free-body diagram shows one object (or system) as a dot or box with an arrow for every force on it, each starting at the object and labeled with the type of force; subscripts can name the object exerting it, as in F_{table on book}.

To find the net force, choose axes, resolve each force into components and add the components; tilting the axes along a surface or along the acceleration often removes extra work. Common errors are assuming the normal force always equals mg (it does not when another force has a vertical component or the surface is tilted), including forces exerted by the object on something else, and adding a 'force of motion' in the direction an object moves; a moving object needs no force to keep moving.

figures.alt: A light rod 1.0 m long holding three small masses: 2.0 kg at the left end, 1.0 kg at 0.40 m from the left end, and 3.0 kg at the right end. Dimension lines mark 0.40 m and 1.0 m from the left end.
A crate on a horizontal floor pulled by a rope attached to its right side, angled 30° above the horizontal. An arrow labeled motion points to the right.
Key: free-body diagram for the crate. From a dot: F_N up, F_g down (longer than F_N), F_T up and to the right at 30° above horizontal, and f_k to the left.
figures.caption: Key: forces on the crate

figures.alt: Two blocks side by side on a horizontal floor: a larger block A on the left touching a smaller block B on its right. A push arrow acts on the left face of A.
Key: free-body diagram for block B: F_N up, F_g down of equal length, and F_{AB} to the right.
figures.caption: Key: forces on block B

figures.alt: Coordinate grid with x and y in meters. Point masses: 2.0 kg at (0, 0), 2.0 kg at (4, 0) and 4.0 kg at (2, 3).
Free-body diagram of a book drawn as a box: F_N up, F_g down, F_H to the right and f_s to the left, with equal and opposite pairs of arrows.
figures.caption: A free-body diagram for a book pushed sideways but not sliding

examples.prompt: A 4.0 kg ball is at x = 0 and a 1.0 kg ball is at x = 3.0 m. Find the center of mass of the pair. If the 1.0 kg ball is moved to x = 5.0 m, how far does the center of mass move?
examples.answer: x_cm = 0.60 m; it moves 0.40 m in the +x direction, to 1.0 m.
steps: After the move: x_cm = (1.0 × 5.0)/5.0 = 1.0 m.
Shift = 1.0 m − 0.60 m = 0.40 m: moving 1/5 of the mass by 2.0 m moves the center of mass by 2.0/5 = 0.40 m.

examples.prompt: A 12 kg sled is pulled across level snow by a rope at 25° above the horizontal with a tension of 60 N. Kinetic friction on the sled is 35 N. Describe the free-body diagram, then find the normal force and the net force on the sled.
examples.answer: Normal force about 92 N; net force about 19 N in the direction of the pull's horizontal component.
steps: Free-body diagram: F_g = (12)(9.8) = 117.6 N down, F_N up, F_T = 60 N at 25° above the horizontal, f_k = 35 N opposite the motion.
Vertical forces balance (the sled stays on the snow): F_N = 117.6 − 60 sin 25° ≈ 117.6 − 25.4 ≈ 92 N.
Horizontal: F_net = 60 cos 25° − 35 ≈ 54.4 − 35 ≈ 19 N forward.

examples.prompt: A tow truck pulls a car with a cable. Take the system to be the truck, the cable and the car together. Which force is internal to this system?
choices: The cable's pull on the car
Friction from the road on the truck's tires
Earth's gravitational force on the car
The road's normal force on the car
examples.answer: (A) The cable's pull on the car
steps: A force is internal when both interacting objects are in the system.
The cable and the car are both in the system, so the cable's pull on the car is internal; its third-law partner, the car's pull on the cable, also acts within the system.
The road and Earth are outside the system, so their forces are external.

worksheets.title: Systems and center of mass
worksheets.directions: Measure positions from the stated origin. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Find the center of mass of the three masses on the light rod, measured from the rod's left end.
items.answer: About 0.57 m from the left end
items.skill: Compute a center of mass on a line

items.prompt: A uniform plank 2.0 m long with a mass of 6.0 kg has a 3.0 kg can of paint resting on its right end. How far from the left end is the center of mass of the plank and can?
steps: The plank's mass acts at its center, 1.0 m from the left end.
items.skill: Model a uniform object at its center

items.prompt: Find the coordinates of the center of mass of the three point masses shown.
items.skill: Compute a center of mass in a plane

items.prompt: A person stands in an elevator car that hangs from a cable. Take the system to be the person and the car. Which forces are external to this system?
choices: The cable's tension on the car and Earth's gravitational force on the person and the car
The floor's normal force on the person and the person's push on the floor
Only Earth's gravitational force on the person
The person's weight and the floor's normal force on the person
items.answer: (A) The cable's tension on the car and Earth's gravitational force on the person and the car
steps: External forces come from objects outside the system: the cable and Earth.
The floor–person contact forces act between two parts of the system, so they are internal.
items.skill: Classify forces as internal or external

items.prompt: Earth (mass 5.97 × 10^24 kg) and the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10^22 kg) are 3.84 × 10^8 m apart, center to center. How far from Earth's center is the center of mass of the Earth–Moon system? Is it inside Earth, whose radius is 6.37 × 10^6 m?
items.answer: About 4.67 × 10^6 m from Earth's center, which is inside Earth.
steps: x_cm ≈ 4.67 × 10^6 m, which is less than 6.37 × 10^6 m, so it lies inside Earth.
items.skill: Apply center of mass with large numbers

items.prompt: Two skaters, of masses 60 kg and 40 kg, stand 5.0 m apart on frictionless ice holding the ends of a rope. They pull on the rope until they meet. Where do they meet, measured from the 60 kg skater's starting point? Explain using the center of mass of the two-skater system.

rubric.criterion: States that the rope forces are internal and no horizontal external force acts, so the center of mass stays at rest.
Computes the center of mass 2.0 m from the 60 kg skater (accept 1.9–2.1 m).
Concludes they meet at the center of mass, 2.0 m from the 60 kg skater's starting point.

items.answer: They meet 2.0 m from the 60 kg skater's starting point, at the system's center of mass.
steps: With no horizontal external force, the center of mass, which starts at rest, stays at rest.
x_cm = (60 × 0 + 40 × 5.0)/100 = 2.0 m from the 60 kg skater; they must meet there.
items.skill: Use center-of-mass motion to locate a meeting point

worksheets.title: Drawing free-body diagrams
worksheets.directions: For each diagram, draw a dot for the object, start every arrow at the dot, and label each force with its type. Give numerical answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: The crate in the figure slides to the right across a rough floor while being pulled by the rope. Draw and label the free-body diagram for the crate.

rubric.criterion: Gravitational force down and normal force from the floor up, with the normal force shorter than the weight.
Tension along the rope at 30° above the horizontal, pointing away from the crate.
Kinetic friction to the left, opposite the sliding, and no other forces.

items.answer: Four forces: F_g down, F_N up (smaller than F_g), F_T at 30° above horizontal to the right, and f_k to the left.
steps: Earth, the floor (normal and friction) and the rope are the only objects that touch or pull the crate.
The rope's upward component helps support the crate, so F_N < F_g; friction opposes the sliding to the right.
items.skill: Draw a free-body diagram with an angled force

items.prompt: A book rests on a table while a hand presses straight down on top of it. How does the normal force from the table on the book compare with the book's weight?
choices: It is greater than the weight
It is less than the weight
items.answer: (A) It is greater than the weight
steps: The book is at rest, so the upward normal force balances the weight plus the hand's downward push.
F_N = mg + F_hand, which is greater than mg.
items.skill: Reason about the normal force

items.prompt: Blocks A and B sit side by side on a frictionless floor, and a hand pushes block A to the right, as shown. Draw the free-body diagram for block B, and state whether the hand exerts a force on block B.

rubric.criterion: Gravitational force down and normal force from the floor up.
Contact force from A on B pointing to the right.
States that the hand exerts no force on B because it does not touch B.

items.answer: Block B: F_g down, F_N up and F_{AB} (A on B) to the right. The hand does not touch B, so it exerts no force on it.
steps: Only objects that touch B (the floor, block A) or act at a distance (Earth) exert forces on it.
The push reaches B only through the contact force from A.
items.skill: Identify forces by interacting objects

items.prompt: A 2.5 kg flowerpot hangs at rest from a vertical chain. Describe its free-body diagram and find the tension in the chain.
items.answer: Two forces, F_g down and tension up; tension ≈ 25 N (24.5 N)
steps: The flowerpot is at rest, so the upward tension balances the downward weight.
items.skill: Find tension from a balanced diagram

items.prompt: A hockey puck slides to the right across frictionless, level ice at constant velocity. Which list gives all the forces on the puck?
choices: Weight down, normal force up, and a force to the right
Weight down, normal force up, and a force to the left
Weight down and normal force up only
items.answer: (D) Weight down and normal force up only
steps: Only Earth and the ice interact with the puck; nothing pushes it forward.
With no friction, nothing pushes it backward either, which is why its velocity stays constant.
items.skill: Reject a force of motion

items.prompt: A 30 kg box sits on the floor. A person pulls straight up on it with a 120 N force, but the box stays on the floor. Find the normal force from the floor on the box.
items.answer: About 174 N (1.7 × 10^2 N) upward
steps: The box is at rest: F_N + 120 N − mg = 0.
items.skill: Find the normal force with an extra vertical force

worksheets.title: Net force by components
worksheets.directions: Choose axes and state the positive directions. Resolve every force at an angle. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Two forces act on an object: 45 N along the +x axis and 28 N at 120° measured counterclockwise from the +x axis. Find the magnitude and direction of the net force.
items.answer: About 39 N at about 38° above the +x axis
steps: Components of the 28 N force: x = 28 cos 120° = −14 N, y = 28 sin 120° ≈ 24.2 N.
items.skill: Add forces by components

items.prompt: A 15 kg crate is pushed across a level floor with an 80 N force directed 20° below the horizontal. Kinetic friction on the crate is 50 N. Find the normal force on the crate and the net force on it.
items.answer: Normal force about 174 N; net force about 25 N in the direction of the push's horizontal component
steps: Vertical balance: F_N = mg + 80 sin 20° = 147 + 27.4 ≈ 174 N (the push presses the crate into the floor).
Horizontal: F_net = 80 cos 20° − 50 ≈ 75.2 − 50 ≈ 25 N.
items.skill: Combine a downward-angled push with friction

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg object has four forces on it: 12 N up, 19.6 N down, 8.0 N to the right and 8.0 N to the left. What is the net force on the object?
items.answer: (B) 7.6 N downward
steps: Horizontal forces cancel: 8.0 N − 8.0 N = 0.
Vertical: 12 N − 19.6 N = −7.6 N, so 7.6 N downward.
items.skill: Find net force from a diagram

items.prompt: A 6.0 kg block rests on a frictionless ramp inclined at 25°, held in place by a rope parallel to the ramp. Using axes along and perpendicular to the ramp, find the components of the block's weight, and use them to find the rope tension and the normal force.
items.answer: Along the ramp about 25 N (24.8 N) down the slope; perpendicular about 53 N into the ramp; tension ≈ 25 N, normal force ≈ 53 N
steps: mg = 58.8 N; along the ramp mg sin 25° ≈ 24.8 N, perpendicular mg cos 25° ≈ 53.3 N.
At rest each axis balances: T ≈ 24.8 N up the ramp and F_N ≈ 53.3 N away from the ramp.
items.skill: Use tilted axes

items.prompt: A student draws the free-body diagram of a ball thrown straight up, at a moment while it is still rising, with an upward arrow labeled 'force of the throw' and a downward arrow for its weight. Neglect air resistance. (a) Identify the error. (b) Describe the correct diagram. (c) Explain why the ball keeps moving upward, and what its acceleration is.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the error: once the ball leaves the hand nothing exerts an upward force; every force needs an interacting object.
Correct diagram: only the gravitational force, mg, downward.
Explains that the ball keeps rising because of its upward velocity; a force changes velocity and is not needed to maintain it.
States the acceleration is 9.8 m/s^2 downward, consistent with the single downward force.

items.answer: (a) There is no 'force of the throw' after release. (b) Only the weight, downward. (c) The ball rises because it already has upward velocity; its acceleration is 9.8 m/s^2 downward, so it slows.
steps: The hand exerts a force only while it touches the ball.
With only gravity acting, a = g downward, which reduces the upward velocity until the ball stops and falls.
items.skill: Critique a free-body diagram

items.prompt: Block 1 (4.0 kg) and block 2 (2.0 kg) are tied together by a string and rest on a frictionless horizontal table. A 24 N horizontal force pulls block 1 away from block 2. Taking the two blocks and the string as one system, list the external forces and find the net external force. Why does the string tension not appear?
items.answer: External forces: total weight 58.8 N down, total normal force 58.8 N up, and the 24 N pull; net external force 24 N in the direction of the pull. The tension is internal, so its pulls on the two blocks cancel within the system.
steps: Total weight = (6.0)(9.8) = 58.8 N, balanced by the normal forces.
The string pulls block 1 back and block 2 forward; both act inside the system, so they cancel in the sum, leaving 24 N.
items.skill: Choose a system to simplify the net force

weeks.title: Newton's third law and equilibrium
weeks.objective: Identify Newton's third-law force pairs by the two interacting objects, and use Newton's first law to find unknown forces on objects at rest or moving at constant velocity, including forces at angles.

connection.before: Week 4's systems and free-body diagrams, with forces resolved into components along chosen axes.
connection.after: Week 6 applies Newton's second law when the net force is not zero, for single objects, connected objects and inclines.

days: Interactions: every force has a partner of equal magnitude and opposite direction, of the same type, exerted on the other object.
Separate third-law pairs from balanced forces on a single object; trace contact forces through stacked and touching objects.
Newton's first law: inertia, constant velocity with zero net force, and inertial reference frames.
Equilibrium with forces at angles: hanging objects, ramps and ropes solved with ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.
Mixed practice: equilibrium problems with stated sign conventions and a short check.
explanation: Forces come from interactions. If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force on A that has the same magnitude, the opposite direction and the same type (contact or gravitational), at the same time. The two forces of a pair act on different objects, so they never appear on the same free-body diagram and never cancel each other. A falling apple pulls up on Earth exactly as hard as Earth pulls down on the apple; Earth's acceleration is negligible only because its mass is enormous. The figure shows a person pushing a wall: the push of the person on the wall, F_{PW}, and the push of the wall on the person, F_{WP}, form a pair.

To find a force's partner, name the force as 'the force of X on Y'; its partner is 'the force of Y on X'. For a book resting on a table, the weight (Earth on book) and the normal force (table on book) are equal in size here, but that equality comes from the first law, because the book is not accelerating, not from the third law. The partner of the weight is the book's gravitational pull on Earth, and the partner of the normal force is the book's push down on the table.

Newton's first law says that an object's velocity stays constant, including staying at rest, unless the net external force on it is not zero. A moving object needs no force to keep moving; forces change velocity. This holds in inertial reference frames, frames that are not accelerating. Equilibrium means zero net force, which in components is ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0. For an object hanging from two cables at angles θ_1 and θ_2 above the horizontal, the horizontal components of the tensions cancel and their vertical components together support the weight.

Method: draw the free-body diagram, choose axes (often along and perpendicular to a ramp), write the two component sums equal to zero and solve them together. Common errors are calling the weight and the normal force a third-law pair, believing that a heavier or faster object exerts a larger force in a collision, adding a forward force to keep an object moving at constant velocity, and forgetting that a tension at an angle has both components.

figures.alt: A sign hangs below a knot from a short vertical cord. Cable 1 runs from the knot up to the left to the ceiling at 30° above the horizontal; cable 2 runs up to the right to the ceiling at 60° above the horizontal.

Key: free-body diagram of the knot with dashed horizontal and vertical axes: T_1 up and to the left at 30° above horizontal, a longer T_2 up and to the right at 60° above horizontal, and T_3 straight down.
figures.caption: Key: forces on the knot

figures.alt: Block A rests on top of a wider block B, which rests on the floor.
A person P stands on the floor and pushes a wall with one arm. One arrow labeled F_{PW} acts on the wall, pointing into it; an arrow labeled F_{WP} acts on the person, pointing away from the wall.
figures.caption: A third-law pair: person and wall

examples.prompt: The 12 kg sign in the figure hangs at rest. Find the tension in each cable.
examples.answer: Cable 1: about 59 N (58.8 N); cable 2: about 102 N
steps: The knot is in equilibrium; the vertical cord pulls down on it with the sign's weight, (12)(9.8) = 117.6 N.
Horizontal: T_1 cos 30° = T_2 cos 60°, so T_2 = 1.732T_1. Vertical: T_1 sin 30° + T_2 sin 60° = 117.6 N.

examples.prompt: A loaded truck and a small car collide head-on. During the collision, how does the force the truck exerts on the car compare with the force the car exerts on the truck?
choices: The truck's force is larger because the truck has more mass
The forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
The car's force is larger because the car slows down more
The forces are equal only if the vehicles have equal speeds
examples.answer: (B) The forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
steps: The two forces are an interaction pair: the truck on the car and the car on the truck.
Newton's third law makes their magnitudes equal at every instant, whatever the masses or speeds.
The effects differ: the same force gives the lighter car a much larger acceleration.

examples.prompt: A 70 kg skier glides straight down a slope inclined at 15° at constant velocity. Find the total resistive force (friction plus air drag) along the slope and the normal force from the snow.
examples.answer: Resistive force about 178 N up the slope; normal force about 663 N
steps: Constant velocity means equilibrium. Use axes along the slope (down positive) and perpendicular to it.
Along the slope: mg sin 15° − F_resist = 0, so F_resist = (70)(9.8) sin 15° ≈ 178 N.
Perpendicular: F_N − mg cos 15° = 0, so F_N ≈ 686 cos 15° ≈ 663 N.

worksheets.title: Interaction pairs
worksheets.directions: Name each force as the force of one object on another. Give numerical answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A book rests on a table. What is the third-law partner of the gravitational force Earth exerts on the book?
choices: The normal force the table exerts on the book
The force the book exerts on the table
The gravitational force the book exerts on Earth
The normal force the floor exerts on the table
items.answer: (C) The gravitational force the book exerts on Earth
steps: The partner of 'Earth on book' is 'book on Earth', of the same type.
The table's normal force acts on the same object, the book, so it is not the partner.
items.skill: Name a third-law partner

items.prompt: Block A (2.0 kg) rests on block B (5.0 kg), which rests on the floor, as shown. Find the magnitude and direction of (a) the force of A on B, (b) the force of the floor on B and (c) the force of B on the floor.
items.answer: (a) 19.6 N down; (b) 68.6 N up; (c) 68.6 N down
steps: A is at rest, so B pushes up on A with 19.6 N; by the third law A pushes down on B with 19.6 N.
B is at rest: F_floor on B = (5.0)(9.8) + 19.6 = 68.6 N up; its partner, B on floor, is 68.6 N down.
items.skill: Trace forces through stacked objects

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg apple falls from a tree. Find the magnitude of the gravitational force the apple exerts on Earth, and Earth's resulting acceleration. Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10^24 kg.
items.answer: 4.9 N toward the apple; about 8.2 × 10^−25 m/s^2
steps: Earth pulls the apple with (0.50)(9.8) = 4.9 N, so the apple pulls Earth with 4.9 N.
items.skill: Apply the third law to unequal masses

items.prompt: A horse pulls a cart forward, and the cart pulls back on the horse with a force of equal magnitude. Which statement explains how the cart can speed up?
choices: The two forces act on different objects; the cart speeds up when the horse's pull exceeds the friction on the cart
The forces cancel, so the cart cannot speed up
The horse's pull is slightly larger than the cart's pull
The cart's pull on the horse acts only after the cart starts moving
items.answer: (A) The two forces act on different objects; the cart speeds up when the horse's pull exceeds the friction on the cart
steps: The pair acts on two different objects, so it cannot cancel on either one.
Only the forces on the cart decide its acceleration: the forward pull and the backward friction.
items.skill: Explain why pair forces do not cancel

items.prompt: A student on a skateboard pushes on a wall with a horizontal 150 N force and rolls backward. Identify the force that makes the student roll backward: the object that exerts it, its magnitude and direction, and its third-law partner.

rubric.criterion: States that the wall exerts the force on the student.
Gives its magnitude, 150 N, pointing away from the wall.
Names the partner: the student's 150 N push on the wall, toward the wall.

items.answer: The wall pushes the student with 150 N directed away from the wall; its partner is the student's 150 N push on the wall.
steps: The student's hands interact with the wall, so the force on the student comes from the wall.
Third law: equal magnitude, opposite direction, acting on the other object.
items.skill: Identify the source of a force

items.prompt: Two teams pull on the ends of a rope, each exerting 600 N, and the rope does not move. Then one team lets go and its end is tied to a tree, while the other team still pulls with 600 N. What is the tension in the rope in each case?
items.answer: 600 N in both cases
steps: In each case the rope is in equilibrium with 600 N pulling on each end.
The tree exerts the same 600 N as the absent team did, so the tension is 600 N, not 1200 N.
items.skill: Find tension in an equilibrium rope

worksheets.title: Equilibrium by components
worksheets.directions: Draw a free-body diagram, choose axes, and write ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A 50 N sign hangs from two cables that each make 25° with the horizontal, symmetric about the sign. Find the tension in each cable.
items.answer: About 59 N each
steps: By symmetry the tensions are equal and their horizontal components cancel.
items.skill: Solve symmetric equilibrium

items.prompt: A 20 kg box is held at rest on a frictionless ramp inclined at 35° by a horizontal push. Find the magnitude of the push and the normal force.
items.answer: Push ≈ 137 N; normal force ≈ 239 N
steps: Axes horizontal and vertical: F_N sin 35° = F_push and F_N cos 35° = mg = 196 N.
items.skill: Choose axes for a horizontal push on a ramp

items.prompt: A lamp hangs from the middle of a cord whose two halves make an angle θ with the horizontal. As the cord is pulled tighter so that θ approaches zero, the tension in the cord
items.answer: (C) becomes very large
steps: Vertical balance: 2T sin θ = mg, so T = mg/(2 sin θ).
As θ approaches 0, sin θ approaches 0 and T grows without limit; a cord can never be pulled perfectly straight under a load.
items.skill: Reason about limiting cases

items.prompt: A 40 kg crate is pulled across a level floor at constant velocity by a rope at 20° above the horizontal with a tension of 90 N. Find the friction force and the normal force on the crate.
items.answer: Friction ≈ 85 N opposite the motion; normal force ≈ 361 N
steps: Constant velocity: horizontal forces balance, so f = 90 cos 20° ≈ 84.6 N.
Vertical: F_N = mg − 90 sin 20° = 392 − 30.8 ≈ 361 N.
items.skill: Apply equilibrium to constant velocity

items.prompt: A 4.0 kg bird feeder hangs from the middle of a wire stretched between two posts 6.0 m apart. The middle of the wire sags 0.40 m below the tops of the posts. Find the tension in the wire.

rubric.criterion: Free-body diagram of the attachment point with two equal tensions and the weight.
Finds the angle from the geometry: tan θ = 0.40/3.0, θ ≈ 7.6°.
Writes 2T sin θ = mg.

items.answer: About 148 N (about 1.5 × 10^2 N)
steps: Each half of the wire spans 3.0 m horizontally and drops 0.40 m, so tan θ = 0.40/3.0 and θ ≈ 7.6°.
items.skill: Combine geometry with equilibrium

items.prompt: An object moves east at a constant velocity of 3.0 m/s. Which statement must be true?
choices: The net force on the object is zero
A net force acts toward the east
No forces act on the object
