examples.prompt: A 0.15 kg ball on a frictionless, level table is tied to a 0.80 m string whose other end is fixed to a peg, and it moves in a circle at 2.0 revolutions per second. Find the ball's speed, its centripetal acceleration and the tension in the string.
examples.answer: Speed ≈ 10 m/s (10.1 m/s); acceleration ≈ 126 m/s^2; tension ≈ 19 N
steps: a_c = v^2/r = (10.1)^2/0.80 ≈ 126 m/s^2 toward the peg.
The tension is the only horizontal force: T = ma_c = 0.15 × 126 ≈ 19 N.

examples.prompt: A 1200 kg car rounds a flat, circular curve of radius 45 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tires and the road is 0.60. Find the greatest speed at which the car can take the curve without sliding.
examples.answer: About 16 m/s
steps: Static friction supplies the inward net force: mv^2/r ≤ μ_s mg.
The mass cancels: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.60 × 9.8 × 45).
v_max = √(264.6) ≈ 16 m/s, for any mass of car.

examples.prompt: A roller-coaster car passes through the bottom of a dip whose radius of curvature is 12 m at 15 m/s. Find the normal force the seat exerts on a 55 kg rider.
examples.answer: About 1.57 × 10^3 N upward, nearly three times her weight
steps: At the bottom the center is above; take up as positive: F_N − mg = mv^2/r.
F_N ≈ 1570 N, compared with her weight of 539 N.

passages.title: Investigation data: a puck on an air table
passages.text:
A puck glides with negligible friction on a level air table. A light string tied to the puck passes through a small hole at the center of the table and supports a hanging mass M beneath it. A student sets the puck moving in a circle of radius 0.50 m so that the hanging mass stays at rest, then times 10 revolutions. She repeats this for several hanging masses.
| M (kg) | 0.050 | 0.100 | 0.150 | 0.200 | 0.250 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| time for 10 revolutions (s) | 28.6 | 19.9 | 16.5 | 14.1 | 12.8 |
passages.attribution: Original data set written for Liminal.

worksheets.title: Centripetal acceleration and force
worksheets.directions: Take the direction toward the center as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: The tip of a fan blade moves in a circle of radius 0.30 m and completes 20 revolutions in 4.0 s. Find the tip's speed and centripetal acceleration.
items.answer: Speed ≈ 9.4 m/s; acceleration ≈ 296 m/s^2 (about 3.0 × 10^2 m/s^2)
items.skill: Compute speed and centripetal acceleration from a period

items.prompt: Seen from above, a car moves counterclockwise around a circular track at constant speed. When the car is at the easternmost point of the track, in which direction does its acceleration point?
items.answer: (D) West
steps: Uniform circular motion has acceleration toward the center.
From the easternmost point, the center lies to the west. (The velocity there points north.)
items.skill: Locate the direction of centripetal acceleration

items.prompt: Earth moves around the Sun in a nearly circular orbit of radius 1.50 × 10^11 m with a period of 365 days. Find Earth's orbital speed and centripetal acceleration.
items.answer: Speed ≈ 2.99 × 10^4 m/s; acceleration ≈ 5.96 × 10^−3 m/s^2
items.skill: Apply circular kinematics at large scale

items.prompt: An object moves in a circle of fixed radius. If its speed doubles, the net force needed to keep it on the circle is
items.answer: (B) four times as large
steps: F_net = mv^2/r.
Doubling v multiplies v^2, and so the force, by 4.
items.skill: Reason proportionally about centripetal force

items.prompt: A 1.5 kg ball on a frictionless, level table is whirled in a circle of radius 0.60 m by a string that breaks if its tension exceeds 120 N. Find the greatest speed the ball can have.
items.answer: About 6.9 m/s
steps: Tension supplies the inward force: T = mv^2/r.
items.skill: Find a limiting speed from a maximum force

items.prompt: A student says that when a car turns left, a passenger slides toward the right door because a centrifugal force pushes her outward. Explain what actually happens, in terms of forces and inertia, from the viewpoint of someone standing on the road.

rubric.criterion: States that no object pushes the passenger outward; in the road's frame there is no outward force on her.
Explains that by inertia her body tends to continue in a straight line while the car turns left beneath her.
Explains that when she reaches the door, the door pushes her inward (to the left), supplying the net inward force that makes her turn with the car.

items.answer: Nothing pushes her outward. Her body tends to keep moving in a straight line while the car turns, so the car's right side moves toward her; the door then pushes her toward the center of the turn, which is the net inward force on her.
steps: Every force needs an interacting object; nothing outside her is pushing her to the right.
The inward push of the door (or seat friction) changes her velocity so that she follows the curve.
items.skill: Correct the centrifugal-force misconception

worksheets.title: What supplies the inward force?
worksheets.directions: Draw a free-body diagram and take the direction toward the center as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A coin rides on a turntable that turns at a constant rate, without sliding. Which force gives the coin its centripetal acceleration?
choices: The normal force from the turntable
items.answer: (B) Static friction from the turntable
steps: The coin does not slide on the surface, so the friction is static.
The normal force and the weight are vertical and cancel; only friction is horizontal, toward the center.
items.skill: Identify the force supplying circular motion

items.prompt: A coin sits 0.12 m from the center of a turntable that turns at 45 revolutions per minute. Find the smallest coefficient of static friction that keeps the coin from sliding.
items.skill: Find a minimum friction coefficient

items.prompt: A 900 kg car drives over the top of the hill shown at 12 m/s. The radius of curvature of the hilltop is 30 m. Find the normal force on the car at the top, and the greatest speed at which the car can pass over the top without leaving the road.
items.answer: Normal force ≈ 4.5 × 10^3 N; maximum speed ≈ 17 m/s
steps: Toward the center (down) positive: mg − F_N = mv^2/r, so F_N = 900(9.8 − 144/30) = 900(5.0) = 4500 N.
The car leaves the road when F_N = 0: v_max = √(gr) = √(9.8 × 30) ≈ 17 m/s.
items.skill: Analyze the top of a hill

items.prompt: A Ferris wheel of radius 9.0 m turns once every 24 s. Find the force the seat exerts on a 50 kg rider at the top and at the bottom of the wheel.
items.answer: Top ≈ 459 N; bottom ≈ 521 N
items.skill: Compare the top and bottom of a vertical circle

items.prompt: A 300 kg roller-coaster cart travels around the inside of a vertical loop of radius 5.0 m. (a) Draw the cart's free-body diagram at the top of the loop. (b) Find the minimum speed at the top for the cart to stay on the track. (c) Find the normal force on the cart at the top if its speed there is 9.0 m/s.

rubric.criterion: Free-body diagram with the normal force and the weight both pointing down, toward the center.
Sets F_N = 0 at the minimum speed so that mg = mv^2/r.
v_min = √(gr) = 7.0 m/s.

items.answer: (b) 7.0 m/s; (c) about 1.9 × 10^3 N (1920 N), directed down
steps: At the top both forces point toward the center: F_N + mg = mv^2/r.
Minimum speed: F_N = 0 gives v = √(9.8 × 5.0) = 7.0 m/s.
items.skill: Analyze the top of a loop

items.prompt: A 0.40 kg ball on a 0.70 m string is swung in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 5.0 m/s. Find the tension in the string there.
items.answer: About 18 N
steps: At the bottom the center is above: T − mg = mv^2/r.
items.skill: Find tension at the bottom of a vertical circle

worksheets.title: Investigation: testing F = mv^2/r
worksheets.directions: Use the air-table data set for every item. Show work on graphs and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

items.prompt: For the air-table setup, explain why the hanging weight Mg equals the net inward force on the puck, and show that a graph of Mg against v^2 should be a straight line through the origin. What does its slope represent?

rubric.criterion: The hanging mass is at rest, so the string tension equals Mg, and the tension is the only horizontal force on the puck: Mg = mv^2/r.
Mg is proportional to v^2, so the graph is a line through the origin with slope m/r.

items.answer: The hanging mass is in equilibrium, so T = Mg, and T is the only horizontal force on the puck, so Mg = mv^2/r. Plotting Mg against v^2 gives a straight line through the origin with slope m/r.
steps: Equilibrium of the hanging mass: T = Mg.
Second law for the puck along the radius: T = mv^2/r, so Mg = (m/r)v^2.
items.skill: Derive a linearized model

items.prompt: From the air-table data, compute the period T, the speed v and v^2 for each trial, and the hanging weight Mg.
steps: T = (time for 10 revolutions)/10, and v = 2πr/T with r = 0.50 m.
items.skill: Process raw timing data

items.prompt: Using your processed air-table data, plot Mg against v^2 on the grid with labeled axes and scales, and draw a single best-fit line.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled Mg (N) and v^2 (m^2/s^2) with scales that use most of the grid.
All five points plotted correctly from the processed data.
One straight best-fit line passing close to the origin.

items.answer: The five points lie close to a straight line through the origin.
steps: Plot the computed v^2 on the horizontal axis and Mg on the vertical axis.
Draw one line that balances the points; the key's fitted line passes through the origin.
items.skill: Plot linearized data

items.prompt: Using your best-fit line for the air-table data, find the slope with units and use it to find the mass of the puck.
items.answer: Slope ≈ 0.40 kg/m (accept 0.38–0.42 kg/m); puck mass ≈ 0.20 kg (accept 0.19–0.21 kg)
steps: Read two points on the line, such as (0, 0) and (6.0 m^2/s^2, 2.41 N): slope ≈ 2.41/6.0 ≈ 0.40 N·s^2/m^2, which is kg/m.
Slope = m/r, so m = slope × r = 0.40 × 0.50 ≈ 0.20 kg.
items.skill: Extract a physical quantity from a slope

items.prompt: Suppose the string slipped so that the puck actually moved in a circle somewhat larger than 0.50 m, but the student still used r = 0.50 m in every calculation. How would the puck mass she calculates compare with the true mass?
choices: It would be larger than the true mass
It would be smaller than the true mass
It would equal the true mass
It cannot be determined from the information given
items.answer: (A) It would be larger than the true mass
steps: With the true radius r_t, the true speed is 2πr_t/T, larger than the computed 2π(0.50)/T, so each computed v^2 is too small by the factor (0.50/r_t)^2.
Then Mg = m(true v^2)/r_t makes the fitted slope m r_t/0.25 instead of m/0.50, and the computed mass (slope × 0.50) is m r_t/0.50, larger than m.
items.skill: Trace a systematic error through an analysis

items.prompt: For the air-table investigation, explain why the student timed 10 revolutions rather than one. Then identify one other source of error and describe how to reduce it.

rubric.criterion: Timing 10 revolutions spreads the reaction-time error of starting and stopping the clock over 10 periods, reducing the uncertainty in T by about a factor of 10.
Names another plausible source: friction where the string passes through the hole, the radius changing during a trial, or the hanging mass moving up and down.
Describes a matching improvement, such as a smooth tube at the hole, a marker to hold the radius at 0.50 m, or video timing.

items.answer: The start and stop errors (a few tenths of a second) are the same for one or ten revolutions, so timing ten makes their effect on each period about ten times smaller. Another source: friction at the hole means the tension on the puck is less than Mg; a smooth plastic sleeve in the hole reduces it.
steps: Fractional timing uncertainty = (reaction error)/(measured time), which falls as the measured time grows.
Friction at the hole would make the true inward force smaller than Mg, giving a calculated mass that is too large.
items.skill: Reduce uncertainty in timing measurements

items.prompt: Using the same air table and puck, design a procedure to test how the hanging weight needed depends on the radius of the circle when the puck's speed is kept the same. Say what you would measure and control, and what graph should be a straight line if F = mv^2/r is correct.

rubric.criterion: Independent variable: radius r (several values); dependent variable: the hanging weight Mg needed for a steady circle.
Keeps the speed fixed by adjusting the period so that 2πr/T is constant (for example, T proportional to r), measured by timing 10 revolutions; same puck throughout.
Plots Mg against 1/r, which should be a straight line through the origin with slope mv^2.

items.answer: Vary r, adjust the hanging mass until the circle is steady at the chosen speed (setting the period T = 2πr/v for each radius and checking it by timing 10 revolutions), record Mg, and plot Mg against 1/r; a straight line through the origin with slope mv^2 supports the model.
steps: At fixed speed the model gives Mg = mv^2(1/r).
Linearizing with 1/r on the horizontal axis gives a slope that should equal mv^2, which can be checked using the known puck mass.
items.skill: Design an experiment that linearizes a model

weeks.title: Kinetic energy and work
weeks.objective: Compute translational kinetic energy and the work done by constant and position-dependent forces, and use the work–energy theorem to connect net work to changes in speed.

connection.before: Week 8's circular motion and Unit 2's free-body diagrams and Newton's second law.
connection.after: Week 10 stores work as potential energy in gravitational and spring systems.

days: Kinetic energy K = (1/2)mv^2: a scalar that depends on the square of speed; compare objects by ratio reasoning.
Work by a constant force, W = Fd cos θ: positive, negative and zero work, and the net work done by several forces.
Work as the signed area under a force–position graph, including forces that change with position.
The work–energy theorem, W_net = ΔK: stopping distances, speeds after a push and kinetic-energy graphs.
Mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving: K = (1/2)mv^2. It is a scalar, measured in joules (1 J = 1 kg·m^2/s^2), and it is never negative, because the speed is squared. Direction does not matter: a cart moving east at 4 m/s and an identical cart moving west at 4 m/s have the same kinetic energy. Because K depends on v^2, doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by 4, while doubling the mass only doubles it.

A force does work on an object when the object moves while the force acts and the force has a component along the displacement. For a constant force, W = Fd cos θ, where d is the size of the displacement and θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Equivalently, W = F_∥d, using only the component of the force along the motion. Work is positive when that component points with the motion, negative when it points against the motion, and zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion. The figure shows a rope pulling at an angle: only the horizontal component of the pull does work as the object moves along the floor. The normal force on a sliding box and the inward force on an object in uniform circular motion do no work.

When a force changes with position, plot F (the component along the motion) against x. The work is the signed area between the graph and the x-axis: area above the axis is positive work, area below is negative work. The net work is the sum of the work done by every force, which also equals the work done by the net force. By Newton's second law and the constant-acceleration relation v^2 = v_0^2 + 2aΔx, multiplying F_net = ma by Δx gives the work–energy theorem: W_net = ΔK = (1/2)mv_f^2 − (1/2)mv_i^2. On a graph of K against x, the slope is the net force.

Common errors: using cos θ when θ is measured from the vertical rather than from the displacement; claiming that the normal force or gravity does work on an object moving horizontally; forgetting that work by friction on a sliding object is negative; treating kinetic energy as a vector and subtracting energies of objects moving in opposite directions; and using the change in speed, (v_f − v_i)^2, instead of the change in the squares, v_f^2 − v_i^2.

figures.alt: A suitcase on a level floor is pulled to the right by a strap angled 40° above the horizontal; the pulling force F lies along the strap, and an arrow below the suitcase shows its displacement d to the right.
figures.caption: Only the component of F along the displacement does work

figures.alt: Graph of force F in newtons against position x in meters from 0 to 8 m: F rises in a straight line from 0 at x = 0 to 30 N at x = 2.0 m, stays at 30 N until x = 5.0 m, then falls in a straight line to 0 at x = 7.0 m.
Graph of horizontal force F in newtons against position x in meters: F is +20 N from x = 0 to x = 3.0 m and −10 N from x = 3.0 m to x = 6.0 m.
Velocity–time graph of a car: v rises in a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 12 m/s at t = 4 s, stays at 12 m/s until t = 8 s, then falls in a straight line to 4 m/s at t = 12 s.

Graph of a block's kinetic energy K in joules against position x in meters from 0 to 10 m: K rises in a straight line from 0 at x = 0 to 24 J at x = 4.0 m, stays at 24 J until x = 6.0 m, then falls in a straight line to 6 J at x = 10 m.
Key: graph of net force against position: +6.0 N from 0 to 4.0 m, 0 from 4.0 to 6.0 m and −4.5 N from 6.0 to 10 m.
figures.caption: Key: net force from the slope of K against x

examples.prompt: A 0.145 kg baseball moves at 40 m/s, and a 6.0 kg bowling ball rolls at 7.0 m/s. Which has more kinetic energy, and how much does each have?
examples.answer: The bowling ball: about 147 J, against 116 J for the baseball.
steps: K = (1/2)mv^2 for each object; direction does not matter.
Bowling ball: (1/2)(6.0 kg)(7.0 m/s)^2 = 3.0 × 49 = 147 J, so the slower, heavier ball has more kinetic energy.

examples.prompt: A traveler pulls the suitcase shown 15 m across a level floor with a 60 N force along a strap at 40° above the horizontal. Kinetic friction on the suitcase is 35 N. Find the work done by the pull, by friction, by the normal force and by gravity, and the net work.
examples.answer: Pull ≈ 689 J; friction −525 J; normal force 0; gravity 0; net work ≈ 164 J.
steps: Friction points opposite the displacement: W_f = (35 N)(15 m)cos 180° = −525 J.
The normal force and gravity are perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so each does zero work; W_net = 689 J − 525 J ≈ 164 J.

examples.prompt: The graph shows the net horizontal force on a 4.0 kg cart that starts from rest at x = 0. Find the work done on the cart from x = 0 to x = 7.0 m and the cart's speed at x = 7.0 m.
examples.answer: Work 150 J; speed ≈ 8.7 m/s
steps: Work is the area under the F–x graph: triangle (1/2)(2.0 m)(30 N) = 30 J, rectangle (3.0 m)(30 N) = 90 J, triangle (1/2)(2.0 m)(30 N) = 30 J.

worksheets.title: Kinetic energy and work by a constant force
worksheets.directions: State the direction you take as positive where it matters. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: If the speed of a cart triples while its mass stays the same, its kinetic energy becomes
items.answer: (C) 9 times as large
steps: K = (1/2)mv^2 depends on the square of the speed.
Tripling v multiplies v^2, and so K, by 3^2 = 9.
items.skill: Reason proportionally about kinetic energy

items.prompt: A 1500 kg car travels at 25 m/s on a highway. Find its kinetic energy.
items.skill: Compute kinetic energy

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg toy truck has 36 J of kinetic energy. How fast is it moving?
steps: Solve K = (1/2)mv^2 for v: v = √(2K/m).
items.skill: Find speed from kinetic energy

items.prompt: A gardener pushes a lawn mower 12 m across a level lawn with an 80 N force directed along the handle, which points 50° below the horizontal. How much work does the push do on the mower?
steps: Only the horizontal component of the push is along the displacement: W = Fd cos 50°.
items.skill: Compute work by a force at an angle

items.prompt: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. How much work does Earth's gravitational force do on the satellite during one quarter of an orbit?
choices: It depends on the satellite's mass
items.answer: (C) Zero
steps: In a circular orbit the gravitational force points toward the center, perpendicular to the velocity at every instant.
A force perpendicular to the motion has no component along the displacement, so it does no work; the speed and kinetic energy stay constant.
items.skill: Recognize zero work by a perpendicular force

items.prompt: A worker uses a rope to lower a 20 kg box straight down 1.5 m at constant velocity. Find the work done on the box by the rope, by gravity, and by the net force.
items.answer: Rope −294 J (about −2.9 × 10^2 J); gravity +294 J; net work 0
steps: Constant velocity means the rope's tension equals the weight, mg = (20 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 196 N, pointing up while the box moves down.
W_rope = (196 N)(1.5 m)cos 180° = −294 J; W_g = (196 N)(1.5 m)cos 0° = +294 J; the net work is 0, consistent with no change in kinetic energy.
items.skill: Compute positive and negative work

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg hockey puck slides 15 m across rough ice, slowing from 9.0 m/s to 6.0 m/s. Find the work done by friction and the average friction force on the puck.

rubric.criterion: Uses the work–energy theorem with friction as the only force doing work: W_f = ΔK.
f = |W_f|/d = 11.25 J / 15 m = 0.75 N (accept 0.74–0.76 N), directed opposite the motion.

items.answer: W_f ≈ −11 J (−11.25 J); friction force 0.75 N opposite the motion.
steps: Gravity and the normal force are vertical and do no work, so W_net = W_f = ΔK = (1/2)(0.50 kg)[(6.0 m/s)^2 − (9.0 m/s)^2] = 0.25(36 − 81) = −11.25 J.
items.skill: Apply the work–energy theorem with friction

worksheets.title: Force–position graphs and the work–energy theorem
worksheets.directions: Take +x as positive. Find work as signed area where a graph is given. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: The graph shows the horizontal force on a cart as it moves along a level track. Find the work done by this force from x = 0 to x = 6.0 m.
steps: Area from 0 to 3.0 m: (20 N)(3.0 m) = +60 J; area from 3.0 to 6.0 m: (−10 N)(3.0 m) = −30 J.
items.skill: Find work as signed area

items.prompt: The force in the graph is the only horizontal force on a 2.5 kg cart that starts from rest at x = 0 on a frictionless track. Find the cart's speed at x = 3.0 m and at x = 6.0 m.
items.answer: About 6.9 m/s at 3.0 m and 4.9 m/s at 6.0 m
steps: At 6.0 m, W = 30 J, so v = √(2 × 30/2.5) = √(24) ≈ 4.9 m/s; the cart slows but keeps moving forward.
items.skill: Use work–energy with a graph

items.prompt: The graph shows the velocity of a car moving in a straight line. During which interval is the net work done on the car negative?
items.answer: (C) 8 to 12 s
steps: Net work equals the change in kinetic energy, so it is negative when the speed decreases.
The speed drops from 12 m/s to 4 m/s only between 8 s and 12 s.
items.skill: Connect net work to a velocity graph

items.prompt: The car whose velocity is graphed has a mass of 1200 kg. Find the net work done on it from t = 0 to t = 4 s and from t = 8 s to t = 12 s.
items.answer: 0 to 4 s: about +8.6 × 10^4 J; 8 to 12 s: about −7.7 × 10^4 J
items.skill: Compute net work from speeds

items.prompt: With its brakes applied hard, a car moving at 15 m/s skids to a stop in 18 m. Assuming the same constant friction force, how far would it skid from 30 m/s? Explain using work and kinetic energy.
items.answer: 72 m. The friction force times the stopping distance equals the initial kinetic energy, which is 4 times as large at twice the speed, so the distance is 4 times as long.
steps: −fd = 0 − (1/2)mv^2, so d = mv^2/(2f) is proportional to v^2.
Doubling v multiplies d by 4: 4 × 18 m = 72 m.
items.skill: Reason about stopping distance with energy

items.prompt: Block P has mass m and block Q has mass 2m. They have the same kinetic energy. Which statement is correct?
choices: P is faster, by a factor of √(2)
P is faster, by a factor of 2
Q is faster, by a factor of √(2)
items.answer: (A) P is faster, by a factor of √(2)
steps: So v_P = √(2) v_Q.
items.skill: Compare speeds at equal kinetic energy

items.prompt: A rubber bumper at the end of a track pushes back on a cart with a force that grows in proportion to how far the bumper is squeezed, from 0 to 900 N over 0.15 m of compression. A 12 kg cart moving at 3.0 m/s runs into the bumper. Does the bumper stop the cart before it is fully squeezed? If so, how far is it squeezed when the cart stops?

rubric.criterion: Finds the cart's kinetic energy: (1/2)(12)(3.0)^2 = 54 J.
Finds the most work the bumper can do as the triangular area (1/2)(900 N)(0.15 m) = 67.5 J and concludes that the cart stops in time, because 54 J < 67.5 J.
Writes the bumper force as F = (900/0.15)x = 6000x (N, with x in m) and the work over a compression x as (1/2)(6000)x^2.
Solves 3000x^2 = 54 J for x ≈ 0.13 m (accept 0.13–0.14 m).

items.answer: Yes. The cart has 54 J, and the bumper can absorb up to 67.5 J, so the cart stops after about 0.13 m of compression.
steps: The bumper force is F = 6000x newtons, and the work it does over a compression x is the triangle area (1/2)(6000x)(x) = 3000x^2.
Setting 3000x^2 = 54 J gives x = √(0.018) ≈ 0.134 m, less than 0.15 m.
items.skill: Use a linear force graph to find a stopping distance

worksheets.title: Work in context
worksheets.directions: Draw a free-body diagram before computing work. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A box slides down a rough ramp. Which force acting on the box does positive work on it?
items.answer: (D) Gravity
steps: Gravity has a component down the slope, along the displacement, so its work is positive.
The normal force is perpendicular to the motion (zero work), and kinetic friction points up the slope, against the motion (negative work).
items.skill: Determine the sign of work by each force

items.prompt: A rope parallel to a snowy slope pulls a 30 kg sled 25 m up the slope at constant speed. The slope makes 20° with the horizontal and μ_k = 0.10. Find the work done on the sled by the rope, by gravity and by friction.
steps: W_g = −mg sin 20° × 25 m ≈ −2.51 × 10^3 J; W_f = −μ_k mg cos 20° × 25 m ≈ −691 J; the three add to zero, as they must at constant speed.
items.skill: Compute work on an incline

items.prompt: A student says, "A weightlifter holding a barbell motionless over her head is doing a lot of work on the barbell, because she gets tired." Evaluate the claim using the physics definition of work.

rubric.criterion: States that work requires a displacement with a force component along it, and the barbell does not move, so the lifter does zero work on it.
Explains that her fatigue comes from energy used inside her muscles (internal energy changes), not from work done on the barbell.

items.answer: The claim is incorrect. The barbell does not move, so the lifter's upward force does no work on it. She tires because her muscles convert chemical energy to thermal energy internally while holding the weight.
steps: W = Fd cos θ is zero when d = 0, whatever the size of the force.
Energy used by the body is not the same as work done on the object being held.
items.skill: Apply the definition of work

items.prompt: A 0.060 kg ball hits a wall at 25 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 20 m/s. Find the change in the ball's kinetic energy and the net work done on the ball by the wall.
items.answer: ΔK ≈ −6.8 J, so the wall does about −6.8 J of net work on the ball
steps: By the work–energy theorem the net work equals ΔK; kinetic energy depends on speed only, so the reversal of direction does not matter.
items.skill: Apply work–energy to a rebound

items.prompt: Two carts start from rest on a frictionless track. Equal constant forces push each cart through the same distance. Cart B has 4 times the mass of cart A. Compare their final kinetic energies and their final speeds.
items.answer: Their kinetic energies are equal; cart A's speed is 2 times cart B's.
steps: Equal forces over equal distances do equal work, so ΔK is the same for both.
items.skill: Reason about work and speed

items.prompt: A rope pulls a 50 kg crate 8.0 m across level ground with a constant force at 30° above the horizontal. The crate speeds up from 1.0 m/s to 3.0 m/s, and kinetic friction does −400 J of work on it. Find the tension in the rope.
items.answer: About 87 N
items.skill: Work backward from the work–energy theorem

items.prompt: The graph shows the kinetic energy of a 3.0 kg block moving along a straight, level track as a function of its position. Take the direction of motion (+x) as positive. (a) Find the net force on the block in each of the three intervals. (b) Sketch a graph of the net force against position from 0 to 10 m. (c) Find the block's speed at x = 10 m.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the slope of K against x equals the net force, because ΔK = F_net Δx.
Net forces +6.0 N, 0 and −4.5 N for the three intervals.
Graph of three horizontal segments at those values over 0–4.0 m, 4.0–6.0 m and 6.0–10 m.

items.answer: (a) +6.0 N, 0 and −4.5 N; (b) three horizontal segments; (c) 2.0 m/s
items.skill: Translate between energy and force graphs

weeks.title: Potential energy
weeks.objective: Describe potential energy as energy stored in the configuration of a system, compute gravitational and spring potential energy, and relate the work done by a conservative force to the change in potential energy.

connection.before: Week 9's definition of work, the area under a force–position graph and the work–energy theorem.
connection.after: Week 11 adds kinetic and potential energy to apply conservation of energy and energy bar charts.

days: Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface: ΔU_g = mgΔy, the choice of a zero level, and why potential energy belongs to a system.
Spring potential energy U_s = (1/2)kx^2 as the area under the spring-force graph; stretch and compression.
Conservative forces: path-independent work, W_c = −ΔU, and why friction has no potential energy.
Gravitational potential energy far from Earth, U_G = −Gm_1m_2/r, and reading potential-energy graphs (force from the slope).
Mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: Potential energy is energy stored in the arrangement of a system of objects that exert conservative forces on each other. It belongs to the system, not to one object: a raised book has gravitational potential energy only as part of the book–Earth system. Near Earth's surface the change is ΔU_g = mgΔy, where Δy is the change in height. The zero level is a free choice; it changes the value of U_g at a point but never the change ΔU_g between two points, and only changes have physical meaning.

A force is conservative when the work it does on an object moving between two points does not depend on the path taken. Gravity and ideal spring forces are conservative, and for them W_c = −ΔU: when gravity does positive work on a falling ball, the potential energy of the ball–Earth system decreases by the same amount. The figure shows two routes between the same two levels; gravity does the same work along either one. Kinetic friction is not conservative: its work depends on the length of the path, so there is no friction potential energy.

An ideal spring exerts a force of magnitude kx, where x is the stretch or compression measured from the spring's natural length. The work needed to deform it is the triangular area under the force–deformation graph, so the stored energy is U_s = (1/2)kx^2, the same for a stretch or a compression of equal size. Far from Earth, g is not constant, and the gravitational potential energy of two masses separated by r is U_G = −Gm_1m_2/r, taking U_G = 0 when they are infinitely far apart. U_G is negative and rises toward zero as r increases. On any graph of potential energy against position, the conservative force is the negative of the slope: it points toward lower potential energy.

Common errors: assigning potential energy to a single object; measuring heights from different zero levels within one problem; using the total length of a spring instead of its stretch from the natural length; forgetting to square x in (1/2)kx^2; writing a positive U_G or using mgΔy across distances comparable to Earth's radius; and expecting friction to have a potential energy.

figures.alt: Side view of two routes between a lower level A and an upper level B separated vertically by Δy: path 1 is a straight ramp and path 2 is a longer route of steps and landings.
figures.caption: Two paths between the same two levels

figures.alt: Graph of spring force magnitude F against stretch x: a straight line through the origin with slope k; the triangle under the line from 0 to a stretch x is shaded and labeled U_s = (1/2)kx^2.
figures.caption: Spring potential energy as the area under F = kx

figures.alt: Graph of the gravitational potential energy U_G of a satellite–Earth system against the distance r from Earth's center, starting at r = R (Earth's radius) and marked at R, 2R, 3R and 4R. The curve is negative everywhere and rises toward zero as r increases.
Graph of potential energy U in joules against position x in meters for a cart on a track: straight segments join (0, 40), (2, 10), (4, 10), (6, 30) and (8, 20).
Graph of spring potential energy U_s in joules against position x in meters from −0.20 m to 0.20 m: a U-shaped curve with its minimum of 0 at x = 0 and reaching 2.0 J at x = ±0.20 m.
Graph of the force F in newtons needed to stretch a spring against the stretch x in meters: a straight line from the origin to (0.30 m, 36 N).

examples.prompt: A 55 kg student climbs from the ground floor of a school to a classroom 7.5 m higher, either by the stairs or by a long wheelchair ramp. Find the change in gravitational potential energy of the student–Earth system for each route, and the student's potential energy at ground level if the classroom floor is chosen as the zero level.
examples.answer: ΔU_g ≈ +4.0 × 10^3 J (4042 J) by either route; with the classroom as zero, U_g at ground level ≈ −4.0 × 10^3 J.
steps: Gravity is conservative, so ΔU_g depends only on the change in height, not on the route.
With the zero at the classroom, ground level is at y = −7.5 m, so U_g = mgy ≈ −4042 J; the change from ground to classroom is still +4042 J.

examples.prompt: A spring with k = 400 N/m is compressed 0.12 m from its natural length. How much energy does it store? How much additional work is needed to compress it to 0.24 m?
examples.answer: 2.9 J (2.88 J) stored; about 8.6 J more is needed.
steps: At 0.24 m: U_s = (1/2)(400)(0.24)^2 = 11.52 J, 4 times as much because x doubled.
Additional work = 11.52 J − 2.88 J = 8.64 J ≈ 8.6 J.

examples.prompt: A 500 kg satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10^6 m to one of radius 1.4 × 10^7 m, measured from Earth's center. Find the change in the gravitational potential energy of the satellite–Earth system, and compare it with the value mgΔr would give. (Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10^24 kg; G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2.)
examples.answer: ΔU_G ≈ +1.42 × 10^10 J; mgΔr would give 3.43 × 10^10 J, more than twice too large.
steps: mgΔr = (500)(9.8)(7.0 × 10^6) ≈ 3.43 × 10^10 J is too large because g weakens with distance from Earth.

worksheets.title: Gravitational and spring potential energy
worksheets.directions: State your zero level for gravitational potential energy. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Which of these can have gravitational potential energy?
choices: The system of a ball and Earth
items.answer: (D) The system of a ball and Earth
steps: Potential energy is stored in the configuration of interacting objects.
Gravitational potential energy needs both the ball and Earth in the system.
items.skill: Identify the system that stores potential energy

items.prompt: A 0.80 kg book is moved from a table 0.75 m high to a shelf 2.10 m above the floor. Find the change in gravitational potential energy of the book–Earth system.
items.answer: About +10.6 J
items.skill: Compute a change in gravitational potential energy

items.prompt: A 62 kg diver stands on a platform 10 m above the water. Find the gravitational potential energy of the diver–Earth system with the water surface as the zero level, and again with the platform as the zero level, at the moment the diver reaches the water.
items.answer: Water as zero: 6.1 × 10^3 J on the platform and 0 at the water. Platform as zero: 0 on the platform and −6.1 × 10^3 J at the water. The change is −6.1 × 10^3 J either way.
steps: U_g = mgy = (62 kg)(9.8 m/s^2)(10 m) ≈ 6076 J at the platform measured from the water.
Shifting the zero subtracts the same constant from every value, so the change stays −6076 J.
items.skill: Show that only changes in potential energy matter

items.prompt: A spring with k = 250 N/m is stretched 0.20 m from its natural length. How much potential energy does it store?
items.skill: Compute spring potential energy

items.prompt: A spring stretched by a distance x from its natural length stores energy U. If it is instead stretched by x/2, it stores
steps: U_s = (1/2)kx^2 is proportional to x^2.
Halving x multiplies U_s by (1/2)^2 = 1/4.
items.skill: Reason proportionally about spring energy

items.prompt: A spring stores 6.0 J when it is compressed 0.20 m. Find its spring constant.
steps: Solve U_s = (1/2)kx^2 for k: k = 2U_s/x^2.
items.skill: Find a spring constant from stored energy

items.prompt: The graph shows the force needed to stretch a spring. (a) Find the spring constant. (b) Find the energy stored when the spring is stretched 0.30 m. (c) Find the work needed to stretch it from 0.10 m to 0.30 m.

rubric.criterion: k = slope = 36 N / 0.30 m = 120 N/m.
Work from 0.10 to 0.30 m = 5.4 J − 0.60 J = 4.8 J, the area between those stretches.

steps: The slope of F against x is k = 36/0.30 = 120 N/m.
items.skill: Read spring energy from a force graph

worksheets.title: Conservative forces and potential-energy graphs
worksheets.directions: Take +x as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2.

items.prompt: A 70 kg hiker reaches a lookout 120 m above the trailhead, either by a gentle 2.4 km trail or by a steep 300 m path, like the two routes in the figure. Find the change in gravitational potential energy of the hiker–Earth system for each route.
items.answer: About +8.2 × 10^4 J for both routes
steps: The change depends only on the change in height, so the route length does not matter.
items.skill: Apply path independence

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball is thrown up, rises 3.0 m, and then falls to a point 5.0 m below its highest point. How much work does gravity do on the ball over the whole trip?
steps: Gravity's work depends only on the net change in height: the ball ends 5.0 m − 3.0 m = 2.0 m below its start.
items.skill: Use W = −ΔU for gravity

items.prompt: The graph shows the potential energy of a cart–track system as the cart moves along the track. In which interval or intervals does the conservative force on the cart point in the +x direction, and how large is it there?
items.answer: From 0 to 2 m, with magnitude 15 N, and from 6 to 8 m, with magnitude 5.0 N
steps: The force is the negative of the slope of U against x, so it points in +x where U decreases.
U decreases from 0 to 2 m (slope −30 J / 2 m = −15 N, so F = +15 N) and from 6 to 8 m (slope −5.0 N, so F = +5.0 N).
items.skill: Find force from a potential-energy graph

items.prompt: For the same potential-energy graph, in which interval is the conservative force on the cart zero?
items.answer: (B) 2 to 4 m
steps: The force is zero where the slope of U against x is zero.
U stays at 10 J from 2 m to 4 m.
items.skill: Interpret a flat region of a potential-energy graph

items.prompt: Points A and B on a level floor are 4.0 m apart. A 5.0 kg box is slid from A to B either along the straight line or by a detour of 3.0 m to point C and then 5.0 m from C to B. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.30. Find the work done by friction for each route, and explain what the result shows about friction.
items.answer: Straight: about −59 J; detour: about −118 J. Friction's work depends on the path, so friction is not conservative and has no potential energy.
steps: f_k = μ_k mg = 0.30(5.0 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 14.7 N, always opposite the motion.
items.skill: Distinguish conservative and nonconservative forces

items.prompt: A 1200 kg space probe moves away from Earth from 1.0 × 10^7 m to 4.0 × 10^7 m from Earth's center. Find the change in the gravitational potential energy of the probe–Earth system. (Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10^24 kg.)
items.skill: Compute gravitational potential energy far from Earth

items.prompt: The graph shows the gravitational potential energy of a satellite–Earth system. (a) Explain why U_G is negative at every distance shown. (b) Explain what it means that U_G approaches zero as r grows very large. (c) Without calculating values, find the ratio of the energy needed to move the satellite from R to 2R to the energy needed to move it from 2R to 3R.

rubric.criterion: Zero is chosen at infinite separation; the attractive force does positive work as the objects come together, so U_G decreases below zero.
U_G near zero means the satellite is nearly free of Earth's gravitational interaction; raising it to infinity requires adding energy until U_G = 0.

items.answer: (a) U_G = 0 is defined at infinite separation, and the attraction lowers U as the objects approach. (b) At very large r the interaction becomes negligible. (c) The first step needs 3 times as much energy.
steps: From R to 2R: GMm/(2R); from 2R to 3R: GMm/(6R); the ratio is 3.
items.skill: Interpret a gravitational potential-energy graph

worksheets.title: Potential energy in context
worksheets.directions: State the system and zero level you use. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A 900 kg elevator car rises from a parking level 4.0 m below the ground floor to a floor 30 m above the ground floor. Find the change in gravitational potential energy of the car–Earth system.
items.answer: About +3.0 × 10^5 J
items.skill: Handle heights on both sides of a zero level

items.prompt: How far must a spring with k = 180 N/m be stretched to store the same energy as is gained by raising a 0.50 kg ball 1.2 m?
items.answer: About 0.26 m
items.skill: Compare gravitational and spring energy

items.prompt: A spring is first stretched 5 cm from its natural length and then compressed 5 cm from its natural length. How do the stored energies compare?
choices: The compressed spring stores negative energy
items.answer: (C) They store equal energy
steps: U_s = (1/2)kx^2 depends on x^2, so the sign of the deformation does not matter.
Equal deformations store equal energy.
items.skill: Apply U_s to stretch and compression

items.prompt: A 25 kg child stands still on a pogo stick whose spring has k = 8000 N/m. How much is the spring compressed, and how much energy does it store? (Ignore the mass of the pogo stick.)
items.answer: About 0.031 m (3.1 cm); about 3.8 J
items.skill: Combine equilibrium with spring energy

items.prompt: The graph shows the potential energy stored in a spring as a block attached to it moves along a horizontal line, with x measured from the spring's natural length. (a) Find the spring constant. (b) Find the magnitude and direction of the spring force on the block at x = 0.10 m. (c) Find the stored energy at x = −0.15 m.

rubric.criterion: Uses a point on the curve, (0.20 m, 2.0 J), with U_s = (1/2)kx^2 to get k = 100 N/m.
F = kx = 10 N at x = 0.10 m, directed toward x = 0 (the −x direction), consistent with the negative of the slope of U.

items.answer: (a) 100 N/m; (b) 10 N in the −x direction; (c) about 1.1 J
steps: At 0.10 m the slope of U is positive, so the force points in −x with magnitude kx = 10 N; at −0.15 m, U_s = 50(0.0225) = 1.125 J.
items.skill: Read a spring potential-energy graph

items.prompt: Which statement about the zero level of gravitational potential energy is correct?
choices: It must be at the ground
It must be at the lowest point of the motion
It changes ΔU_g but not U_g
It changes the value of U_g but not the change ΔU_g
items.answer: (D) It changes the value of U_g but not the change ΔU_g
steps: Moving the zero adds the same constant to U_g everywhere.
Differences cancel that constant, and only differences affect motion.
items.skill: Interpret the zero of potential energy

items.prompt: A 300 kg satellite on an elliptical orbit moves from 8.0 × 10^6 m to 6.5 × 10^6 m from Earth's center. Find the work done on it by Earth's gravity during this motion. (Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10^24 kg; G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2.)
items.answer: About +3.4 × 10^9 J
steps: GMm ≈ 1.19 × 10^17 J·m and (1/6.5 × 10^6 − 1/8.0 × 10^6) ≈ 2.88 × 10^−8 m^−1, so W_g ≈ +3.4 × 10^9 J: gravity does positive work as the satellite moves closer.
items.skill: Relate work by gravity to potential energy

weeks.title: Conservation of energy and energy bar charts
weeks.objective: Choose a system, decide whether its mechanical energy is conserved, represent energy changes with bar charts, and solve for speeds, heights and compressions with conservation of energy.

connection.before: Week 9's work–energy theorem and week 10's gravitational and spring potential energy.
connection.after: Week 12 adds friction and other nonconservative work, multistep systems and a paper investigation.

days: Systems and energy: what counts as internal or external, and when the total mechanical energy of a system stays constant.
Energy bar charts: initial energies, external work and final energies drawn to a consistent scale.
Conservation with gravity: falling and thrown objects, frictionless tracks and pendulums.
Conservation with springs: launchers, bumpers and a spring combined with gravity.
Mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: The energy of a system changes only when something outside the system transfers energy in or out, for example by doing work. If no external force does work on a system and no friction or other nonconservative force acts inside it, its mechanical energy, the sum of kinetic and potential energies, stays constant: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f. Conservation does not mean nothing changes; it means kinetic and potential energy trade with each other while their sum stays fixed.

The choice of system decides how gravity appears. With the ball alone as the system, Earth is outside, gravity is an external force, and its work changes the ball's kinetic energy: W_g = ΔK. With the ball and Earth together, gravity is an internal interaction, and its effect is the change in gravitational potential energy: ΔK + ΔU_g = 0. Use one description or the other, never both, or gravity is counted twice. A spring belongs in the system when you want to use its potential energy.

An energy bar chart shows the accounting: bars for the kinetic, gravitational and spring energies at the start, a bar for work done by external forces, and bars for the same energies at the end. The bars must balance: K_i + U_gi + U_si + W_ext = K_f + U_gf + U_sf. The figure shows a dropped ball, with the ball and Earth as the system and the ground as the zero level: potential energy turns into kinetic energy and the total stays the same. Sketching the bars before writing equations shows which terms are zero and which way energy flows.

Common errors: counting gravity both as work and as potential energy; using the length along a slope instead of the vertical height in mgΔy; expecting the speed at the bottom of a frictionless track to depend on the shape of the track or on the mass (it depends only on the drop and the initial speed, though the time does depend on the shape); and measuring spring compression from the wrong point.

figures.alt: Energy bar chart for a dropped ball, system ball and Earth. Initial: gravitational potential energy 4 units, kinetic and spring energy zero. Work column empty. Final (partway down): kinetic energy 3 units and gravitational potential energy 1 unit.
figures.caption: Energy bar chart for a falling ball

figures.alt: A pendulum: a small bob on a string of length 1.6 m hangs from a fixed support and is pulled aside so that the string makes 40° with the vertical.

Side profile of a roller-coaster track: point A on a hilltop 25 m above the ground, point B at the bottom of a valley at ground level, point C on a second hilltop 15 m high and point D on a rise 8.0 m high.
figures.caption: Track heights

figures.alt: A vertical spring launcher: a small ball rests on top of a spring that is compressed in a tube standing on the floor.
Blank energy bar chart with columns K, U_g and U_s under the heading Initial, a column W under External work, and columns K, U_g and U_s under Final, all on a common zero line.
Key: energy bar chart with spring energy 4 units in the initial group, no external work and kinetic energy 4 units in the final group.
figures.caption: Key: spring launches a cart

figures.alt: Key: energy bar chart, system ball and Earth, ground as the zero level. Initial: kinetic energy 3 units and gravitational potential energy 2 units. Work zero. Final at the top: kinetic energy zero and gravitational potential energy 5 units.
figures.caption: Key: ball thrown up from a balcony

examples.prompt: A 2.0 kg rock is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s from the top of a 12 m cliff. Use energy to find its speed just before it hits the ground below, first with the rock alone as the system and then with the rock and Earth as the system.
examples.answer: About 17 m/s (17.3 m/s) either way
steps: Rock alone: gravity is external and does W_g = mgΔh = (2.0)(9.8)(12) = 235 J, so (1/2)mv_f^2 = (1/2)(2.0)(8.0)^2 + 235 J = 64 J + 235 J = 299 J.
Rock and Earth: no external work, so K_i + U_gi = K_f + U_gf, and ΔU_g = −235 J becomes kinetic energy, giving the same 299 J.
v_f = √(2 × 299 J / 2.0 kg) ≈ 17.3 m/s; the direction of the throw does not affect the speed.

examples.prompt: A roller-coaster car rolls over hilltop A of the track shown at 4.0 m/s. Treat the track as frictionless. Find the car's speed at the bottom of the valley, point B.
examples.answer: About 22 m/s (22.5 m/s)
steps: System: car, track and Earth, with no external work, so (1/2)mv_A^2 + mgy_A = (1/2)mv_B^2 + mgy_B.
v_B = √(506) ≈ 22.5 m/s, for any mass of car.

examples.prompt: A spring with k = 800 N/m is compressed 0.10 m and launches a 0.50 kg block across a frictionless floor and up a frictionless ramp inclined at 30°. How high does the block rise, and how far along the ramp does it travel?
examples.answer: Height ≈ 0.82 m; distance along the ramp ≈ 1.6 m
steps: Bar chart: initial U_s, final U_g, all other bars zero.
Along the ramp: d = h / sin 30° ≈ 1.6 m.

worksheets.title: Energy bar charts and system choice
worksheets.directions: Name your system and zero level. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2, neglect friction and air resistance, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A ball falls freely. A student chooses the ball alone, not Earth, as the system. Why does the system's energy increase as the ball falls?
choices: Gravitational potential energy of the system decreases
Gravity, an external force, does positive work on the system
Energy is not conserved for falling objects
items.answer: (B) Gravity, an external force, does positive work on the system
steps: Without Earth in the system there is no gravitational potential energy to track.
Earth's pull is then an external force, and its positive work increases the ball's kinetic energy.
items.skill: Describe energy changes for a chosen system

items.prompt: A cart is held at rest against a compressed spring on a level, frictionless track and then released. It moves away from the spring. Using the blank bar chart, show the energies of the cart–spring system before release and after the cart leaves the spring.

rubric.criterion: Initial: only a spring-energy bar (no kinetic energy, and no change in U_g on a level track).
External work bar zero, because nothing outside the cart–spring system does work.
Final: only a kinetic-energy bar, equal in height to the initial spring-energy bar.

items.answer: Initial U_s only; W = 0; final K equal to the initial U_s.
steps: The track is level, so U_g does not change; the cart starts at rest, so K_i = 0.
With no external work, all the spring energy becomes kinetic energy once the spring is relaxed.
items.skill: Draw an energy bar chart

items.prompt: A 0.25 kg apple falls from a branch 3.5 m above the ground. Using energy, find its speed and its kinetic energy just before it lands.
items.answer: About 8.3 m/s; about 8.6 J
items.skill: Apply conservation to free fall

items.prompt: The pendulum shown is released from rest. Find the speed of the bob at the lowest point of its swing.
items.answer: About 2.7 m/s
steps: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.374) ≈ 2.7 m/s; the string's tension is perpendicular to the motion and does no work.
items.skill: Apply conservation to a pendulum

items.prompt: Two identical balls leave the same balcony with the same speed, one thrown straight up and one thrown horizontally. Neglecting air resistance, how do their speeds compare just before they reach the ground?
choices: The ball thrown up is faster
The ball thrown horizontally is faster
It depends on the balcony's height
items.answer: (C) Their speeds are equal
steps: Both start with the same kinetic energy and fall through the same height.
Energy is a scalar, so (1/2)mv_f^2 = (1/2)mv_0^2 + mgh gives the same v_f for both, whatever the launch direction.
items.skill: Use the scalar nature of energy

items.prompt: For the roller-coaster track shown, a car rolls over hilltop A at 4.0 m/s. Treating the track as frictionless, find the car's speed at the top of the second hill, point C.
items.answer: About 15 m/s (14.6 m/s)
items.skill: Apply conservation between two heights

items.prompt: In the vertical launcher shown, the spring has k = 500 N/m and is compressed 0.080 m below its natural length. It launches a 0.050 kg ball straight up. How high does the ball rise above its launch position? (Treat the launch position as the ball's position when the spring is compressed.)
items.answer: About 3.3 m
steps: All of it becomes U_g at the top: h = 1.6 J / (0.050 kg × 9.8 m/s^2) ≈ 3.3 m.
items.skill: Convert spring energy to height

worksheets.title: Conservation with springs and gravity
worksheets.directions: Draw a quick bar chart before writing equations. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2, neglect friction, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 0.20 kg block slides at 3.0 m/s across a frictionless floor into a horizontal spring with k = 180 N/m. Find the spring's maximum compression.
steps: (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2)kx^2 at maximum compression, so x = v √(m/k).
items.skill: Find a maximum compression

items.prompt: For the same block and spring, find the block's speed when the spring is compressed 0.050 m.
items.answer: About 2.6 m/s
items.skill: Split energy between kinetic and spring forms

items.prompt: On the frictionless track shown, a second car with half the mass rolls over hilltop A at the same speed as the first. Compared with the first car, its speed at point C is
items.answer: (B) the same
steps: Every energy term is proportional to m, so the mass cancels from the conservation equation.
v_C depends only on v_A, g and the drop in height.
items.skill: Recognize when mass cancels

items.prompt: For the track shown, the car rolls over hilltop A at 4.0 m/s with negligible friction. Find its speed at point D. Could the car pass over a 26 m hill built after D? Explain.
items.answer: About 19 m/s (18.7 m/s) at D. No: the highest it could rise is 25 m + (4.0 m/s)^2/(2g) ≈ 25.8 m, less than 26 m.
steps: The total energy per kilogram is fixed, so the car can reach at most y = y_A + v_A^2/(2g) ≈ 25.8 m before stopping.
items.skill: Use total energy to find a highest point

items.prompt: A 1.5 kg block is dropped from rest 0.40 m above the top of a vertical spring with k = 600 N/m. Find the maximum compression of the spring.
items.answer: About 0.17 m
steps: Take the lowest point as the zero of U_g: mg(0.40 + x) = (1/2)kx^2, so 300x^2 − 14.7x − 5.88 = 0.
x = [14.7 + √(14.7^2 + 4(300)(5.88))]/600 ≈ 0.17 m (the negative root has no meaning here).
items.skill: Combine spring and gravitational energy

items.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from a balcony and rises to its highest point. Take the ground below as the zero level. (a) Draw energy bar charts from release to the highest point with the ball and Earth as the system. (b) Describe how the bar chart changes if the system is the ball alone, and explain why both descriptions agree.

rubric.criterion: Ball–Earth chart: initial K and U_g both positive (the balcony is above the zero level).
Final: K = 0 at the top and U_g larger by the amount of the initial K; external work zero.
Ball-only chart: no U_g bars; K decreases to zero and the external-work bar is negative (gravity does negative work).
Explains agreement: the negative work by gravity on the ball equals −ΔU_g of the ball–Earth system, so each description accounts for the same energy once.

items.answer: (a) Initially K and U_g; finally all U_g, with W = 0. (b) With the ball alone, only K appears; it falls to zero because gravity does negative work. Both give the same loss of kinetic energy.
steps: Ball and Earth: K turns into U_g with no external work.
Ball alone: W_g = −mgΔy = ΔK, which matches −ΔU_g in the other description.
items.skill: Compare system choices on bar charts

items.prompt: Two identical blocks are released from rest at the same height on two frictionless ramps, one steep and one gentle. Which statement about the blocks at the bottom is correct?
choices: They have the same speed, and the block on the steep ramp arrives sooner
The block on the steep ramp is faster
They have the same speed and arrive at the same time
The block on the gentle ramp is faster
items.answer: (A) They have the same speed, and the block on the steep ramp arrives sooner
steps: Energy conservation gives v = √(2gh) for both.
The steep ramp is shorter and its acceleration g sin θ is larger, so that block takes less time.
items.skill: Separate speed from time in energy problems

worksheets.title: Multistage motion and system choice
worksheets.directions: Break each motion into stages and name the system for each. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2, neglect friction and air resistance, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 65 kg ski jumper starts from rest and leaves the takeoff 30 m lower. She lands on the slope a further 12 m below the takeoff. Treating friction and air resistance as negligible, find her speed at takeoff and on landing.
items.answer: Takeoff ≈ 24 m/s; landing ≈ 29 m/s
steps: Landing, 42 m below the start: v = √(2g × 42 m) ≈ 28.7 m/s; the mass does not matter.
items.skill: Apply conservation over several stages

items.prompt: A student analyzes a falling ball with the ball–Earth system and writes ΔK + ΔU_g = W_gravity. What is wrong with this equation?
choices: Kinetic energy is not part of the ball–Earth system
It should include the ball's spring energy
It counts gravity twice: as potential energy and as external work
items.answer: (D) It counts gravity twice: as potential energy and as external work
steps: Inside the ball–Earth system, gravity is internal and is represented by ΔU_g.
The correct statement is ΔK + ΔU_g = 0 (no external work).
items.skill: Avoid double counting gravity

items.prompt: A toy dart gun has a spring with k = 1200 N/m compressed 0.050 m. It fires a 0.010 kg dart horizontally from the edge of a 1.2 m high table. Find the dart's speed as it leaves the gun and just before it hits the floor.
items.answer: About 17 m/s (17.3 m/s) leaving; about 18.0 m/s at the floor
items.skill: Chain spring and gravitational energy

items.prompt: A cart is released from rest at height H on a frictionless track that leads into a vertical loop of radius 4.0 m. Find the smallest H for which the cart stays on the track at the top of the loop.
items.answer: H = 10 m (2.5 times the radius)
steps: At the top with the least speed, gravity alone supplies the inward force: mg = mv^2/R, so v^2 = gR.
Energy from release to the top (height 2R): mgH = mg(2R) + (1/2)m(gR), so H = 2.5R = 10 m.
items.skill: Combine energy with circular motion

items.prompt: A 0.30 kg ball on a 1.2 m string is held with the string horizontal and released. (a) Find the ball's speed at the lowest point. (b) Find the tension in the string there. (c) Explain why the tension does no work on the ball during the swing.

rubric.criterion: Uses mgL = (1/2)mv^2 to get v = √(2gL) ≈ 4.8 m/s (accept 4.8–4.9 m/s).
At the bottom, T − mg = mv^2/L.
T = mg + 2mg = 3mg ≈ 8.8 N (accept 8.7–8.9 N).
The tension is always along the string, perpendicular to the ball's velocity on the circle, so it has no component along the displacement.

items.answer: (a) About 4.8 m/s; (b) about 8.8 N; (c) the tension is perpendicular to the motion at every instant.
items.skill: Use energy to find a force at the bottom of a swing

items.prompt: A person lifts a 4.0 kg box straight up 2.0 m at constant speed. With the box and Earth as the system, find the work done by the person and the changes in kinetic and gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: Work by the person ≈ +78 J; ΔK = 0; ΔU_g ≈ +78 J
steps: The person is external to the box–Earth system; at constant speed the lifting force is mg = 39.2 N, so W = (39.2 N)(2.0 m) ≈ 78 J.
ΔK = 0, so the external work all appears as ΔU_g = mgΔy ≈ 78 J.
items.skill: Account for external work on a system

weeks.title: Nonconservative work and multistep systems
weeks.objective: Account for energy transferred to internal energy by friction and for work done by outside agents, solve multistep energy problems, and analyze supplied release-height data with a linearized graph.

connection.before: Week 11's conservation of mechanical energy, system choice and energy bar charts.
connection.after: Week 13 measures how fast energy is transferred (power) and reviews Unit 3 for the unit test.

days: Friction and internal energy: ΔE_int = f_k d for the system of the sliding object and the surface, and bar charts with an internal-energy column.
Work by outside agents (people, motors, winches) on a system: W_ext = ΔK + ΔU + ΔE_int.
Multistep problems: a curved ramp, a rough patch and a spring; track the energy at each boundary.
Paper investigation: linearize supplied release-height and speed data and find the fraction of energy kept.
Mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: When a block slides across a rough floor, kinetic friction does negative work on the block, and the block and floor warm up. If the system includes both surfaces, friction is internal, and the mechanical energy lost becomes internal (thermal) energy: ΔE_int = f_k d, where d is the total length of the sliding path, not the displacement. A block that slides back and forth across a rough patch converts energy on every pass. The figure adds a column for this internal energy to the bar chart.

The full energy statement for a system is W_ext = ΔK + ΔU_g + ΔU_s + ΔE_int, where W_ext is the work done by forces from outside the system, such as a person's push or a motor's cable. A winch dragging a crate up a rough ramp at constant speed does work that goes partly into gravitational potential energy and partly into internal energy; the kinetic energy does not change.

Multistep problems become manageable when the motion is split at the points where the physics changes: the bottom of a frictionless curve, the ends of a rough patch, the moment a spring is reached. Write one energy statement for each stage and use the result of one stage as the start of the next. Check that each stage's answer is possible: a block cannot have negative kinetic energy, so if the energy runs out partway across a rough patch, the block stops there.

Common errors: using the straight-line displacement instead of the path length for friction; using mg instead of the normal force mg cos θ for friction on an incline; treating friction's work as negative internal energy; and ignoring friction during the part of the motion where a spring is still pushing.

College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.
