examples.prompt: A sled and rider (40 kg in total) pass the top of a 6.0 m high snowy hill at 2.0 m/s and reach the bottom at 9.5 m/s. (a) How much mechanical energy was converted to internal energy on the way down? (b) On the level snow at the bottom, μ_k = 0.15. How far does the sled slide before stopping?
examples.answer: (a) About 6.3 × 10^2 J (627 J); (b) about 31 m
steps: System: sled, snow and Earth. Initial energy: mgh + (1/2)mv_i^2 = (40)(9.8)(6.0) + (1/2)(40)(2.0)^2 = 2352 J + 80 J = 2432 J.
Final kinetic energy: (1/2)(40)(9.5)^2 = 1805 J, so ΔE_int = 2432 J − 1805 J ≈ 627 J.

examples.prompt: A 2.0 kg block is released from rest at the top of the curved ramp shown. The ramp is frictionless, the rough patch has μ_k = 0.25, and the spring has k = 1500 N/m. Find the block's speed as it leaves the rough patch the first time and the spring's maximum compression. (The floor under the spring is frictionless.)
examples.answer: Speed ≈ 4.8 m/s; maximum compression ≈ 0.18 m
steps: Stage 1 (ramp): K = mgh = (2.0)(9.8)(1.8) = 35.28 J at the bottom.

examples.prompt: The winch shown pulls a 150 kg crate 8.0 m up the 25° ramp at constant speed. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. How much work does the winch do, and where does that energy go?
examples.answer: About 7.1 × 10^3 J: about 4.97 × 10^3 J to gravitational potential energy and 2.13 × 10^3 J to internal energy
steps: System: crate, ramp and Earth; the winch cable is external. Constant speed, so ΔK = 0 and W_winch = ΔU_g + ΔE_int.

passages.title: Investigation data: release height and speed
passages.text:
A 0.50 kg cart is released from rest on a straight ramp. A photogate at the bottom of the ramp measures the cart's speed v. The student varies the release height h, measured vertically from the photogate's level, and records one averaged speed for each height.
| h (m) | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.40 | 0.50 | 0.60 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v (m/s) | 1.25 | 1.81 | 2.18 | 2.56 | 2.82 | 3.12 |
passages.attribution: Original data set written for Liminal.

worksheets.title: Friction and internal energy
worksheets.directions: Include the sliding surfaces in your system. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 5.0 kg box slides across a floor with μ_k = 0.40 and stops after 2.5 m. Find its initial speed and the increase in internal energy of the box and floor.
items.answer: About 4.4 m/s; 49 J
steps: ΔE_int = μ_k mg d = 0.40(5.0)(9.8)(2.5) = 49 J, all of the initial kinetic energy.
items.skill: Relate friction to internal energy

items.prompt: A book slides across a table and comes to rest. For the system of the book and the table, which statement is correct?
choices: Total energy stays the same while mechanical energy decreases
items.answer: (C) Total energy stays the same while mechanical energy decreases
steps: Friction is internal to the book–table system, so no energy leaves it.
The book's kinetic energy becomes internal energy of the surfaces.
items.skill: Track energy forms in a closed system

items.prompt: A 50 kg skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a 4.0 m high ramp and reaches the bottom at 8.0 m/s. How much mechanical energy was converted to internal energy?
items.skill: Find energy dissipated from speeds and heights

items.prompt: A car with locked brakes leaves skid marks 28 m long on a level road where μ_k = 0.70. Estimate the car's speed when the brakes locked.
items.answer: About 19.6 m/s (about 20 m/s)
steps: (1/2)mv^2 = μ_k mg d; the mass cancels.
items.skill: Reconstruct a speed from a skid

items.prompt: A block slides down a rough incline at constant speed. For the system of the block, the incline and Earth, which describes the energy changes?
choices: K decreases; U_g is constant; E_int increases
K is constant; U_g decreases; E_int is constant
K increases; U_g decreases; E_int is constant
K is constant; U_g decreases; E_int increases by the same amount
items.answer: (D) K is constant; U_g decreases; E_int increases by the same amount
steps: Constant speed means ΔK = 0.
The block loses height, and with no external work the lost U_g must appear as internal energy.
items.skill: Interpret constant-speed motion with friction

items.prompt: A box is given a quick push and slides up a rough ramp, coming to rest partway up. Using the blank bar chart, show the energies of the box–ramp–Earth system from just after the push to the moment the box stops.

rubric.criterion: Initial: a kinetic-energy bar only (take the starting point as the zero of U_g).
External work zero once the push has ended; final kinetic energy zero.
Final U_g and ΔE_int bars that are both positive and add up to the initial K.

items.answer: Initial K only; W = 0; final U_g plus ΔE_int equal to the initial K.
steps: After the push nothing outside the system does work on it.
Some of the kinetic energy becomes U_g and the rest becomes internal energy through friction.
items.skill: Draw a bar chart with internal energy

worksheets.title: Multistep energy problems
worksheets.directions: Split each motion into stages and write an energy statement for each. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: For the 2.0 kg block on the track shown (frictionless ramp starting 1.8 m up, rough patch 2.5 m long with μ_k = 0.25, frictionless floor under the spring), the block keeps sliding back and forth. Where does it finally come to rest?
items.answer: On its third crossing of the rough patch, 2.2 m from the patch's left end (0.3 m short of the right end)
steps: The block starts with 35.28 J, and each full crossing converts 12.25 J; 35.28/12.25 ≈ 2.88 crossings.
After two crossings 10.78 J remains; on the third it slides d = 10.78 J / (0.25 × 2.0 × 9.8 N) = 2.2 m before stopping.
items.skill: Track energy over repeated passes

items.prompt: A 500 kg roller-coaster car passes a point 20 m above the ground at 6.0 m/s and later passes a point at ground level at 18 m/s. How much mechanical energy was converted to internal energy between the two points?
items.answer: About 2.6 × 10^4 J
items.skill: Find energy dissipated between two points

items.prompt: The crate on the 25° ramp shown is at rest 8.0 m up the ramp when the winch cable breaks. The coefficients of friction are μ_s = 0.35 and μ_k = 0.20. Does the crate slide down? If so, find its speed when it reaches the bottom of the ramp.
items.answer: Yes, because tan 25° ≈ 0.47 exceeds μ_s = 0.35; it reaches the bottom at about 6.2 m/s.
steps: The crate slides if mg sin θ > μ_s mg cos θ, that is, if tan θ > μ_s.
items.skill: Decide whether motion starts, then use energy

items.prompt: A ball dropped from 2.0 m bounces back up to 1.5 m. What fraction of the ball–Earth system's mechanical energy was converted to other forms in the bounce?
steps: At the tops of the motion all mechanical energy is U_g, proportional to height.
The ball keeps 1.5/2.0 = 75% of its energy, so 25% was converted.
items.skill: Compare energies at turning points

items.prompt: A 0.80 kg block is pushed against a spring (k = 320 N/m), compressing it 0.15 m on a floor with μ_k = 0.30, and released. How far from its release point does the block stop?
items.answer: About 1.5 m
steps: Stored energy: (1/2)(320)(0.15)^2 = 3.6 J. Friction acts from the moment of release, so 3.6 J = μ_k mg d.
d = 3.6 J / (0.30 × 0.80 × 9.8 N) ≈ 1.5 m (the block leaves the spring after 0.15 m with energy to spare).
items.skill: Combine a spring with friction

items.prompt: A shopper pushes a 25 kg cart from rest 12 m across a level parking lot with a horizontal 40 N force while rolling resistance on the cart is 15 N. Find the cart's final speed and the energy converted to internal energy.
items.answer: About 4.9 m/s; 180 J converted
items.skill: Include external work and friction

items.prompt: A 60 kg skier starts from rest at the top of a straight slope that drops 30 m vertically over a length of 120 m. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.080 on the slope and on the level snow at the bottom. Ignore air resistance. (a) Find the skier's speed at the bottom of the slope. (b) Find how far she glides on the level snow before stopping.

rubric.criterion: Finds the slope angle from sin θ = 30/120 (θ ≈ 14.5°) and the friction force μ_k mg cos θ ≈ 45.5 N.
Energy on the slope: mgh − μ_k mg cos θ (120 m) = (1/2)mv^2, with 17 640 J − 5.47 × 10^3 J ≈ 1.22 × 10^4 J.
On the level, μ_k mg d = kinetic energy at the bottom, giving d ≈ 2.6 × 10^2 m (accept 255–262 m).

items.skill: Solve a two-stage problem with friction

worksheets.title: Investigation: release height and speed
worksheets.directions: Use the release-height data set for every item. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2, show work on graphs, and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

items.prompt: For the ramp investigation, show that if no mechanical energy were converted to internal energy, v^2 = 2gh. What graph of the data should then be a straight line through the origin, and what would its slope be?

rubric.criterion: With no loss, mgh = (1/2)mv^2, so v^2 = 2gh (the mass cancels).
Graph v^2 against h: a straight line through the origin with slope 2g = 19.6 m/s^2.

items.answer: mgh = (1/2)mv^2 gives v^2 = 2gh, so v^2 against h is a straight line through the origin with slope 2g ≈ 19.6 m/s^2.
steps: The cart starts from rest, so all of the lost U_g would become K.
If a fixed fraction of the energy is kept, the graph is still a straight line, but its slope is smaller than 2g.
items.skill: Derive a linearized energy model

items.prompt: Compute v^2 for each trial in the release-height data.
steps: Square each measured speed, keeping three significant figures.
items.skill: Process data for a linear graph

items.prompt: Plot v^2 against h on the grid, with labeled axes and scales, and draw a single best-fit line.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled v^2 (m^2/s^2) and h (m), with scales that use most of the grid.
All six points plotted correctly.
One straight best-fit line passing close to the origin.

items.answer: The six points lie close to a straight line through the origin.
steps: Put h on the horizontal axis and v^2 on the vertical axis.
Draw one line that balances the points; the key's line passes through the origin.
items.skill: Plot linearized data

items.prompt: Find the slope of your best-fit line, with units. What fraction of the cart's lost gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy at the photogate?
items.answer: Slope ≈ 16 m/s^2 (accept 15.5–16.7 m/s^2); fraction ≈ 0.82 (accept 0.79–0.85)
steps: Using points on the line such as (0, 0) and (0.60 m, 9.68 m^2/s^2), the slope ≈ 16.1 m/s^2.
(1/2)mv^2 = f mgh gives v^2 = 2fgh, so f = slope/(2g) ≈ 16.1/19.6 ≈ 0.82.
items.skill: Interpret a slope as an energy fraction

items.prompt: For the 0.60 m trial with the 0.50 kg cart, how much mechanical energy was converted to internal energy (and rotational energy of the wheels) on the way down?
items.answer: About 0.51 J
steps: Converted: 2.94 J − 2.43 J ≈ 0.51 J, about 17% of the lost U_g.
items.skill: Compute energy converted in one trial

items.prompt: Suppose the student had measured each height h as the distance along the ramp's surface instead of vertically. Compared with the correct analysis, the slope of the v^2 against h graph would be
items.answer: (A) smaller
steps: The distance along the ramp is h/sin θ, larger than the vertical height by the same factor for every trial.
Every point moves right by that factor while v^2 is unchanged, so the slope shrinks by sin θ.
items.skill: Trace a measurement error through a graph

items.prompt: Design an experiment with the same ramp and photogate to test whether the fraction of energy kept depends on the cart's mass. Say what you would vary, what you would keep the same, what you would measure, and how you would use graphs to reach a conclusion.

rubric.criterion: Varies the cart's mass by adding known masses; keeps the ramp, its angle and surface, and the photogate position the same.
For each mass, measures v at several heights h (several trials each) with the photogate.
Plots v^2 against h for each mass and compares the slopes (or the fractions slope/2g); equal slopes within uncertainty mean the fraction does not depend on mass.

items.answer: Add known masses to the cart; for each total mass, release it from several measured heights and record the photogate speed. Plot v^2 against h for each mass and compare slope/2g. If the fractions agree within uncertainty, the fraction kept does not depend on mass.
steps: The mass cancels in the ideal model, so any trend in slope with mass shows how friction or rolling losses scale with mass.
Repeated trials at each height reduce random uncertainty in v.
items.skill: Design a controlled experiment

weeks.title: Power and Unit 3 synthesis
weeks.objective: Define power as the rate of energy transfer, compute average and instantaneous power (including P = Fv), read power and energy graphs, and choose between energy and force methods in multistep problems.

connection.before: Weeks 9–12: work, potential energy, conservation of energy and energy converted by friction.
connection.after: Unit 4 turns to momentum and impulse in week 14, for interactions that energy alone cannot describe.

days: Power as a rate: P = ΔE/Δt = W/Δt, the watt and the kilowatt-hour, and the area under a power–time graph.
Instantaneous power P = Fv cos θ for a force on a moving object; constant speed against resistance; efficiency.
Power in lifting, pumping and climbing; slopes of energy–time graphs.
Unit 3 synthesis: choosing energy or force methods, and moving among words, equations, bar charts and graphs.
Unit 3 review and the Unit 3 test.
explanation: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or converted: P = ΔE/Δt, or P = W/Δt when the transfer is by work. It is a scalar measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Two students who carry identical boxes up the same stairs do the same work, but the one who climbs faster has the greater power. A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power: 1 kWh = (1000 J/s)(3600 s) = 3.6 × 10^6 J.

On a graph of power against time, the area under the curve is the energy transferred. The figure shows a motor's power output as it starts, runs steadily and stops. On a graph of energy against time, the slope is the power. Average power over an interval is the total energy divided by the elapsed time, which is not the same as the average of the starting and ending power unless the power changes linearly.

When a constant force F acts on an object moving with velocity v, the work done in a short time Δt is FvΔt cos θ, so the instantaneous power is P = Fv cos θ. A car cruising at constant speed needs an engine power equal to the total resistive force times the speed. At a fixed power, a larger speed means a smaller driving force, which is why a car accelerates more slowly as it speeds up. Efficiency compares useful output with input energy or power; the rest is converted to internal energy.

Synthesis: use energy methods when a problem asks about speeds, heights, compressions or distances and does not need time; use Newton's second law and kinematics when it asks for an acceleration or a time. Common errors: calling the kilowatt-hour a unit of power; dividing by the wrong time; using P = Fv with the average speed when the force changes; and forgetting that an engine at constant speed still supplies power to make up for friction and drag.

figures.alt: Graph of a motor's power output P in watts against time t in seconds from 0 to 20 s: P rises in a straight line from 0 to 600 W at t = 5 s, stays at 600 W until t = 15 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 at t = 20 s.
figures.caption: Power output of a motor

figures.alt: Graph of total energy E in joules transferred by an electric hoist against time t in seconds: straight segments join (0, 0), (4, 2000), (10, 2000) and (14, 5200).

Key: graph of energy in joules against height y in meters from 0 to 7.35 m: U_g rises in a straight line from 0 to 36 J, K falls in a straight line from 36 J to 0, and the total E is a horizontal line at 36 J. The K and U_g lines cross at y ≈ 3.7 m, 18 J.
figures.caption: Key: energies of a ball launched upward

examples.prompt: A 72 kg climber climbs a stairwell that rises 15 m in 20 s. Find the average power she delivers to raise her body. If her body converts chemical energy to this work with 25% efficiency, at what rate does she use chemical energy?
examples.answer: About 529 W (0.53 kW); about 2.1 kW of chemical power
steps: The useful work is the gain in gravitational potential energy: mgΔy = (72)(9.8)(15) = 10 584 J.
Efficiency = useful output/input, so input = 529 W / 0.25 ≈ 2.1 × 10^3 W.

examples.prompt: At 27 m/s on a level highway, the total resistive force (drag plus rolling resistance) on a car is 650 N. Find the power the engine must deliver to the wheels to keep that speed. If the engine is 20% efficient, how much fuel energy does it use in one hour?
examples.answer: About 1.8 × 10^4 W (17.6 kW); about 3.2 × 10^8 J per hour
steps: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, 650 N.

examples.prompt: Use the graph of the motor's power output to find the energy it delivers from t = 0 to t = 20 s and its average power over that time.
steps: Energy is the area under the P–t graph.
Average power = 9000 J / 20 s = 450 W, less than the 600 W peak.

worksheets.title: Power as a rate
worksheets.directions: Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A 1200 W electric kettle runs for 3.5 min. How much energy does it use?
items.answer: About 2.5 × 10^5 J
steps: E = PΔt with Δt = 3.5 × 60 = 210 s.
items.skill: Compute energy from power and time

items.prompt: Which quantity does the kilowatt-hour measure?
items.answer: (B) Energy
steps: A kilowatt-hour is a power multiplied by a time.
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^6 J, an amount of energy.
items.skill: Distinguish power from energy

items.prompt: A crane lifts an 800 kg steel beam 24 m at constant speed in 40 s. Find the power the crane delivers to the beam.
items.answer: About 4.7 × 10^3 W
items.skill: Compute lifting power

items.prompt: Two students carry identical boxes up the same flight of stairs. Student A takes 10 s and student B takes 20 s. Which statement is correct?
choices: A does twice as much work as B
A and B have the same power
A and B do the same work, and B's power is twice A's
A and B do the same work, and A's power is twice B's
items.answer: (D) A and B do the same work, and A's power is twice B's
steps: Work depends on the weight and the height, which are the same for both.
Power = work/time, so half the time means twice the power.
items.skill: Compare power for equal work

items.prompt: The graph shows the total energy an electric hoist has transferred to its load. Find the hoist's power output during each of the three time intervals.
steps: Power is the slope of the energy–time graph.
items.skill: Find power as the slope of an energy graph

items.prompt: A 60 W incandescent bulb is replaced by a 9.0 W LED bulb that gives the same light. Both are on for 5.0 h each day. How much energy does the change save in 30 days? Give the answer in kilowatt-hours and in joules.
items.answer: About 7.7 kWh, or about 2.8 × 10^7 J
steps: The power saved is 60 W − 9.0 W = 51 W, for 5.0 h × 30 = 150 h.
items.skill: Convert between kilowatt-hours and joules

worksheets.title: Power, force and velocity
worksheets.directions: Use P = Fv for a force along the motion. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A boat's propeller pushes it forward with a constant 2.4 × 10^3 N force while the boat moves at a constant 8.0 m/s. Find the power delivered by the propeller force.
items.answer: About 1.9 × 10^4 W
steps: P = Fv for a force along the velocity.
items.skill: Use P = Fv

items.prompt: A cyclist can sustain a power output of 300 W to the pedals. At racing speed the total resistive force on her and the bicycle is 25 N. What steady speed can she maintain on level ground?
items.answer: 12 m/s
steps: At steady speed the propulsive force equals the resistive force: P = F_r v.
items.skill: Find a top speed from power

items.prompt: A 1100 kg car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 8.0 s on a level road. Ignoring friction and drag, find the average power delivered to the car and the instantaneous power at the end of the 8.0 s.
steps: F = ma = 1100 × (20/8.0) = 2750 N, so at 20 m/s, P = Fv = 55 000 W, twice the average because the speed grows steadily.
items.skill: Compare average and instantaneous power

items.prompt: A car's engine delivers constant power to the wheels as the car speeds up on a level road. As the speed increases, the forward force on the car
items.answer: (B) decreases
steps: P = Fv with P constant.
A larger v requires a smaller F.
items.skill: Reason with P = Fv at constant power

items.prompt: An elevator car (1000 kg) carrying 400 kg of passengers rises at a constant 2.5 m/s. Ignore friction and any counterweight. Find the power the cable delivers, and the electrical power the motor draws if it is 75% efficient.
items.answer: Cable ≈ 3.4 × 10^4 W; electrical input ≈ 4.6 × 10^4 W
steps: At constant velocity the cable tension equals the total weight: (1400 kg)(9.8 m/s^2) = 13 720 N.
items.skill: Include efficiency in a power problem

items.prompt: A rope pulls a 40 kg sled across level snow at a constant 1.5 m/s. The rope makes 25° with the horizontal, and μ_k = 0.12. Find the tension in the rope and the power the rope delivers to the sled.

rubric.criterion: Equilibrium with the normal force reduced by the rope: T cos 25° = μ_k(mg − T sin 25°).
T ≈ 49 N (accept 48–50 N).
P = Tv cos 25° ≈ 67 W (accept 65–68 W).

items.answer: Tension ≈ 49 N; power ≈ 67 W
steps: Only the horizontal component of T is along the motion: P = (49 N)(1.5 m/s)(0.906) ≈ 67 W, the rate at which friction converts energy to internal energy.
items.skill: Compute power from a force at an angle

items.prompt: A runner doubles her speed on level ground. If the air drag on her is proportional to the square of her speed and dominates the other resistive forces, the power she must supply against drag changes by a factor of
steps: P = F_drag v with F_drag proportional to v^2, so P is proportional to v^3.
Doubling v multiplies P by 2^3 = 8.
items.skill: Combine proportional reasoning with P = Fv

worksheets.title: Unit 3 synthesis
worksheets.directions: Decide first whether energy or force methods fit the question. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg block slides from rest down a frictionless incline 4.0 m long that makes 35° with the horizontal. Find its speed at the bottom and the time it takes to get there.
items.answer: About 6.7 m/s; about 1.2 s
steps: Energy: h = (4.0 m)sin 35° ≈ 2.29 m, so v = √(2gh) ≈ 6.7 m/s.
Time needs kinematics: a = g sin 35° ≈ 5.62 m/s^2, so t = v/a ≈ 1.2 s.
items.skill: Choose energy for speed and kinematics for time

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball is launched straight up from the ground at 12 m/s. Neglect air resistance, and take the ball and Earth as the system with the ground as the zero level. (a) On one set of axes, sketch the kinetic energy, the gravitational potential energy and the total energy against the height y, from the ground to the highest point. (b) Find the highest point. (c) Find the height at which K = U_g.

rubric.criterion: Total energy drawn as a horizontal line at (1/2)(0.50)(12)^2 = 36 J.
U_g a straight line rising from 0 and K a straight line falling to 0, both linear in y, with K + U_g = 36 J everywhere.
Highest point y = v^2/(2g) ≈ 7.3 m (accept 7.3–7.4 m).
K = U_g where U_g = 18 J: y ≈ 3.7 m (accept 3.6–3.7 m).

items.answer: (a) U_g rises linearly, K falls linearly, E is constant at 36 J; (b) about 7.3 m; (c) about 3.7 m
steps: E = 36 J and U_g = mgy = 4.9y (J), so K = 36 − 4.9y.
Top: 4.9y = 36 gives y ≈ 7.35 m; K = U_g when 4.9y = 18, y ≈ 3.67 m.
items.skill: Represent energy as a function of height

items.prompt: A pump lifts water from a well 18 m deep at 50 kg per minute and discharges it at ground level with a speed of 4.0 m/s. Find the pump's minimum power output.
items.answer: About 154 W
steps: Each second the pump moves 50/60 ≈ 0.833 kg of water.
items.skill: Compute power as an energy rate

items.prompt: A 70 kg cyclist coasts down a 5.0° slope at a constant 12 m/s. At what rate is the mechanical energy of the cyclist–Earth system converted to internal energy by drag and friction?
steps: At constant speed K is constant, so the rate of loss of U_g equals the conversion rate.
items.skill: Relate constant-speed motion to dissipation rate

items.prompt: An 80 kg skydiver falls at a constant terminal speed of 55 m/s. At what rate does air drag convert mechanical energy into internal energy of the skydiver and the air?
items.answer: About 4.3 × 10^4 W
steps: At terminal speed the drag force equals the weight, 784 N.
P = Fv = (784 N)(55 m/s) ≈ 4.3 × 10^4 W, equal to the rate of loss of U_g.
items.skill: Find a dissipation rate at terminal speed

items.prompt: A student says, "Lift A has a motor twice as powerful as lift B, so lift A can raise twice as much mass to the top of the building." Evaluate the claim.

rubric.criterion: Power is the rate of energy transfer, so the claim compares energies only if the times are the same; given equal time, A can do twice the work and lift twice the mass.
Notes that given enough time, B can lift any mass that A can (each trip's energy is mgh), so the claim is true only for equal lift times.

items.answer: Only partly. With equal time, A transfers twice the energy and can lift twice the mass the same height. But power limits how fast energy is delivered, not the total, so B can lift the same mass if it takes twice as long.
steps: Energy needed = mgh; time needed = mgh/P.
Doubling P halves the time for the same load or doubles the load for the same time.
items.skill: Evaluate a claim about power

items.prompt: An 800 kg roller-coaster car is pulled at a constant 1.2 m/s up a lift hill that rises 35 m along a track inclined at 30°. (a) Ignoring friction, find the power of the lift motor. (b) The car passes over the top at 1.2 m/s, and 15% of its mechanical energy (measured from ground level) is converted to internal energy on the way down. Find its speed at ground level.
items.answer: (a) About 4.7 × 10^3 W; (b) about 24 m/s
items.skill: Combine power with energy accounting

weeks.title: Momentum and impulse
weeks.objective: Compute momentum as a vector, relate impulse to change in momentum, find impulse as the area under a force–time graph, and explain how stretching a collision's duration reduces the average force.

connection.before: Unit 2's Newton's second law and Unit 3's kinetic energy, which momentum complements.
connection.after: Week 15 uses momentum conservation for systems whose objects push on each other.

days: Momentum p = mv: a vector with a sign in one dimension; momentum of a system; comparing momentum with kinetic energy.
Change in momentum and impulse, J = F_avg Δt = Δp, including rebounds where the velocity reverses.
Force–time graphs: impulse as signed area, average force, and momentum–time graphs whose slope is the net force.
Stretching the stopping time: airbags, padding, catching; F_net = Δp/Δt as the general form of Newton's second law.
Mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: An object's momentum is p = mv, its mass times its velocity. Momentum is a vector with the direction of the velocity, measured in kg·m/s. In one dimension, choose a positive direction and give each momentum a sign. The momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of its parts, and it equals the total mass times the velocity of the center of mass, p_sys = Mv_cm. Two objects moving toward each other with equal and opposite momenta have zero total momentum but plenty of kinetic energy, so momentum and kinetic energy describe different things.

A net force acting for a time changes momentum. The impulse of a force is J = F_avg Δt (in N·s, the same unit as kg·m/s), and the impulse–momentum theorem says J_net = Δp = mv_f − mv_i. Rewritten as F_net = Δp/Δt, this is the general form of Newton's second law. In a rebound, the velocity reverses, so the change in momentum is larger than for a stop: a ball arriving at +6 m/s and leaving at −4 m/s has Δv = −10 m/s.

Collision forces are rarely constant. On a graph of force against time, the impulse is the signed area under the curve, and the average force is that area divided by the contact time. The figure shows a bat's force on a ball during a few milliseconds of contact. For a fixed change in momentum, a longer contact time means a smaller average force: an airbag, a gym mat or bending your knees on landing spreads the same impulse over more time. On a graph of momentum against time, the slope is the net force.

Common errors: dropping the signs, so that a rebound looks like a smaller change than a stop; confusing momentum with kinetic energy (an object with more momentum need not have more kinetic energy); using speed instead of velocity in Δp; and thinking that a softer landing reduces the impulse, when it only reduces the average force.

figures.alt: Graph of the force F in newtons exerted by a bat on a ball against time t in milliseconds: F rises in a straight line from 0 to 3000 N at t = 1.0 ms, stays at 3000 N until t = 3.0 ms, then falls in a straight line to 0 at t = 5.0 ms.
figures.caption: Force of a bat on a ball

figures.alt: Graph of the net horizontal force F in newtons on a puck against time t in seconds: a triangle rising from 0 at t = 0 to 24 N at t = 0.30 s and back to 0 at t = 0.60 s, then a downward triangle reaching −12 N at t = 0.80 s and returning to 0 at t = 1.0 s.
Graph of a cart's momentum p in kg·m/s against time t in seconds: p is 6 kg·m/s from t = 0 to 2 s, falls in a straight line to −3 kg·m/s at t = 5 s, and stays at −3 kg·m/s until t = 8 s.

Key: two force–time curves on the same axes for an egg stopped by a pillow and by a hard floor; the floor curve is tall and narrow, the pillow curve is low and wide, and the areas under them are equal.
figures.caption: Key: same impulse, different contact times

figures.alt: Key: vector diagram. The initial momentum p_i points east, 1.36 units long; the final momentum p_f points north, 1.02 units long; the impulse J = p_f − p_i is drawn from the tip of p_i to the tip of p_f, pointing up and to the left.
figures.caption: Key: impulse as a change in momentum

examples.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball rolls east at 6.0 m/s and a 3.0 kg ball rolls west at 4.0 m/s. Take east as positive. Find each ball's momentum, the total momentum of the two-ball system and the total kinetic energy.
examples.answer: +12 kg·m/s and −12 kg·m/s; total momentum 0; total kinetic energy 60 J
steps: Momentum adds as vectors: +12 + (−12) = 0.
Kinetic energy is a scalar and never negative: (1/2)(2.0)(36) + (1/2)(3.0)(16) = 36 J + 24 J = 60 J.

examples.prompt: A 0.45 kg soccer ball arrives at a player's head at 12 m/s and leaves along the same line in the opposite direction at 9.0 m/s. The contact lasts 0.020 s. Find the impulse on the ball and the average force of the head on the ball.
examples.answer: Impulse ≈ 9.5 N·s (9.45 N·s) and average force ≈ 4.7 × 10^2 N, both directed away from the player
steps: Take the outgoing direction as positive: v_i = −12 m/s and v_f = +9.0 m/s.

examples.prompt: A 0.145 kg baseball moving at 38 m/s toward the batter is struck by the bat; the graph shows the bat's force on the ball, directed away from the batter. Find the impulse, the ball's velocity after contact and the average force during contact. (Ignore other forces during the contact.)
examples.answer: Impulse 10.5 N·s; final velocity about 34 m/s away from the batter; average force 2.1 × 10^3 N
steps: Take away from the batter as positive: v_f = v_i + J/m = −38 m/s + 10.5/0.145 ≈ −38 + 72.4 ≈ +34 m/s.

worksheets.title: Momentum and impulse
worksheets.directions: State your positive direction. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: Which object has the greatest magnitude of momentum?
choices: A 5.0 kg bowling ball at 8.0 m/s
items.answer: (B) A 70 kg runner at 7.0 m/s
steps: The runner's 490 kg·m/s is greatest.
items.skill: Compare momenta

items.prompt: A 65 kg skater glides west at 4.0 m/s. Taking east as positive, what is the skater's momentum?
items.answer: −260 kg·m/s (260 kg·m/s west)
steps: p = mv with the sign of the velocity.
items.skill: Give momentum a sign

items.prompt: A 1.2 kg cart's velocity changes from +3.0 m/s to −1.5 m/s. Find the change in its momentum.
items.answer: −5.4 kg·m/s
steps: Δp = 1.2 × (−4.5) = −5.4 kg·m/s; using speeds would wrongly give −1.8 kg·m/s.
items.skill: Compute a change in momentum through a reversal

items.prompt: A constant 15 N net force acts on a 4.0 kg object, initially at rest, for 2.0 s. Find the impulse and the object's final speed.
items.answer: Impulse 30 N·s; final speed 7.5 m/s
steps: Δp = J, so v = 30 N·s / 4.0 kg = 7.5 m/s.
items.skill: Apply the impulse–momentum theorem

items.prompt: Two objects have the same magnitude of momentum. The object with the greater mass has
items.answer: (B) less kinetic energy
steps: With equal p, a larger m gives a smaller K (and a smaller speed).
items.skill: Relate momentum and kinetic energy

items.prompt: The graph shows the momentum of a cart moving along a straight track. Find the net force on the cart during each of the three intervals.
steps: Net force is the slope of the momentum–time graph, F_net = Δp/Δt.
From 2 to 5 s: (−3 − 6) kg·m/s / 3 s = −3.0 N; the flat intervals have zero net force.
items.skill: Find net force as the slope of p against t

items.prompt: An egg dropped onto a pillow survives, while an identical egg dropped from the same height onto a hard floor breaks. (a) Compare the impulses on the two eggs as they are stopped. (b) Sketch force–time graphs for both on the same axes. (c) Explain why only one egg breaks.

rubric.criterion: Both eggs arrive with the same velocity and stop, so Δp and the impulse are the same.
Sketch: the floor curve is tall and narrow, the pillow curve low and wide, with equal areas.
The pillow stretches the stopping time, so F_avg = Δp/Δt is smaller; the floor's large force breaks the shell.

items.answer: (a) Equal impulses. (b) Floor: tall, narrow pulse; pillow: low, wide pulse; equal areas. (c) The pillow's longer contact time gives a smaller average force.
steps: Same drop height means the same speed on arrival and the same change in momentum to zero.
F_avg = Δp/Δt: a longer Δt means a smaller force.
items.skill: Explain impulse and contact time

worksheets.title: Force–time graphs and average force
worksheets.directions: Take the direction of the first push as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: The graph shows the net horizontal force on a 2.0 kg puck that is at rest at t = 0 on frictionless ice. Find the total impulse from t = 0 to t = 1.0 s and the puck's velocity at t = 1.0 s.
items.answer: Impulse +4.8 N·s; velocity +2.4 m/s
steps: v = J/m = 4.8 N·s / 2.0 kg = 2.4 m/s in the positive direction.
items.skill: Find impulse as signed area

items.prompt: For the same puck and force graph, at what time is the puck's speed greatest, and what is that speed?
steps: The speed increases while the net force is positive, until t = 0.60 s, and decreases after that.
items.skill: Locate a maximum from a force graph

items.prompt: In a crash, a 70 kg driver moving at 15 m/s is brought to rest. Find the average force on the driver if an airbag stops him in 0.12 s, and if instead the steering wheel stops him in 0.010 s.
items.answer: Airbag: about 8.8 × 10^3 N; steering wheel: about 1.1 × 10^5 N
steps: Δp = 0 − (70)(15) = −1050 kg·m/s in either case.
items.skill: Compare average forces for different stopping times

items.prompt: A ball of mass m moving at speed v strikes a wall head-on and bounces straight back with the same speed v. What is the magnitude of the impulse the wall exerts on the ball?
items.answer: (D) 2mv
steps: Taking the rebound direction as positive, Δp = mv − (−mv) = 2mv.
Zero would be the change in kinetic energy, not in momentum.
items.skill: Compute impulse in a rebound

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from 1.8 m onto a floor and rebounds to a height of 1.25 m. The contact lasts 0.015 s. Find the impulse from the floor and the average force the floor exerts on the ball during contact.
items.answer: Impulse ≈ 5.4 N·s upward; average floor force ≈ 3.7 × 10^2 N upward
steps: During contact the net force is F_floor − mg, so F_floor = Δp/Δt + mg ≈ 363 N + 4.9 N ≈ 368 N.
items.skill: Find a contact force including gravity

items.prompt: Two carts at rest on a frictionless track, of masses m and 2m, each receive a push described by the same force–time graph. Which quantity is the same for both carts after the push?
items.answer: (A) Final momentum
steps: The same force–time graph gives the same impulse, so the same Δp.
The heavier cart ends with half the speed, so its kinetic energy p^2/(2m) is half as large.
items.skill: Identify what equal impulses imply

items.prompt: A 0.42 kg ball arrives at a catcher's hands at 18 m/s. (a) If the catcher lets her hands move back 0.30 m while stopping the ball with a uniform deceleration, find the stopping time and the average force on the ball. (b) Repeat for stiff hands that move back only 0.050 m. (c) Explain the difference in terms of impulse.

rubric.criterion: Uses the average speed (9.0 m/s) to find Δt = d/v_avg: 0.033 s and 0.0056 s.
F ≈ 1.4 × 10^3 N for the stiff hands (accept 1300–1400 N).
Explains that the impulse (7.56 N·s) is the same in both cases, so a longer stopping time means a smaller average force.

items.answer: (a) About 0.033 s and 2.3 × 10^2 N (227 N); (b) about 0.0056 s and 1.4 × 10^3 N; (c) the impulse is the same, so the longer stop needs less force.
steps: Uniform deceleration: v_avg = 9.0 m/s, so Δt = 0.30/9.0 ≈ 0.0333 s or 0.050/9.0 ≈ 0.00556 s.
items.skill: Relate stopping distance, time and force

worksheets.title: Momentum of systems and vectors
worksheets.directions: State your positive directions. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: Cart A (2.0 kg) moves at +3.0 m/s and cart B (1.0 kg) moves at −1.5 m/s on the same track. Find the total momentum of the two-cart system and the velocity of its center of mass.
items.skill: Compute system momentum and center-of-mass velocity

items.prompt: Two pucks on frictionless ice are joined by a compressed spring and released. While the spring pushes them apart, the velocity of the two-puck system's center of mass
items.answer: (C) stays the same
steps: The spring forces are internal to the system, and the vertical forces balance, so the net external force is zero.
With zero net external force, p_sys = Mv_cm is constant.
items.skill: Connect external force to center-of-mass motion

items.prompt: A 0.17 kg puck sliding east at 8.0 m/s is struck by a stick and afterward moves north at 6.0 m/s. Find the magnitude and direction of the impulse the stick gives the puck.
items.answer: About 1.7 N·s, directed about 37° north of west
steps: Components (east and north positive): p_i = (1.36, 0) and p_f = (0, 1.02) kg·m/s, so J = p_f − p_i = (−1.36, +1.02) N·s.
items.skill: Find impulse as a vector change

items.prompt: A loaded truck and a small car collide head-on. During the collision, which statement is correct?
choices: The truck exerts a larger force on the car than the car exerts on the truck
The car's momentum changes more than the truck's
The forces are equal in size, and both velocities change by the same amount
The forces are equal in size, and the car's velocity changes more
items.answer: (D) The forces are equal in size, and the car's velocity changes more
steps: The forces are a third-law pair, equal in size and acting for the same time, so the impulses and the changes in momentum are equal in size.
Δv = Δp/m, so the smaller mass has the larger change in velocity.
items.skill: Combine the third law with impulse

items.prompt: During a storm, 300 hailstones, each of mass 0.0040 kg and falling at 15 m/s, hit a flat skylight every second and stop without bouncing. Find the average force the hail exerts on the skylight.
items.answer: 18 N, directed downward
steps: Each second the hail delivers momentum 300 × 0.0040 kg × 15 m/s = 18 kg·m/s.
F_avg = Δp/Δt = 18 kg·m/s per 1 s = 18 N.
items.skill: Find force as a rate of momentum transfer

items.prompt: The momentum of a 0.80 kg cart on a level track increases at a steady rate from 0 to 2.4 kg·m/s in 1.5 s. Find the net force on the cart and its final speed.
items.skill: Use F_net = Δp/Δt

items.prompt: A student claims, "If a 1500 kg car and a 0.20 kg baseball have the same momentum, the car must have more kinetic energy because it is so much heavier." Evaluate the claim, and support your answer with a numerical example.

rubric.criterion: Uses K = p^2/(2m) (or computes each speed and K) to compare objects with equal momentum.
Shows with numbers, such as p = 6.0 kg·m/s: baseball 30 m/s and 90 J; car 0.0040 m/s and 0.012 J.
Concludes the claim is wrong: with equal momentum, the lighter object has more kinetic energy.

items.answer: The claim is wrong. K = p^2/(2m), so for equal momentum the lighter object has more kinetic energy. With p = 6.0 kg·m/s, the baseball moves at 30 m/s with 90 J, while the car moves at 0.0040 m/s with only 0.012 J.
items.skill: Evaluate a claim comparing momentum and energy

weeks.title: Conservation of linear momentum
weeks.objective: Decide when a system's momentum is conserved, and apply conservation of momentum to recoil, sticking collisions and two-dimensional interactions using before-and-after diagrams, momentum bar charts and graphs.

connection.before: Week 14's momentum, impulse and the third-law pairs of Unit 2.
connection.after: Week 16 classifies collisions by what happens to kinetic energy and closes Unit 4 with an investigation and the unit test.

days: Why momentum is conserved: internal forces come in third-law pairs, so only an external impulse can change a system's momentum.
Recoil and explosions from rest: total momentum stays zero; before-and-after diagrams.
Objects that stick together; momentum bar charts; reading a collision from velocity–time graphs.
Momentum in two dimensions: conserve each component separately; intersections and glancing hits.
Mixed practice and a short check.
explanation: When two objects interact, Newton's third law makes their forces on each other equal in size and opposite in direction, and the forces act for the same time. Their impulses therefore cancel, and the total momentum of the two-object system does not change. In general, the momentum of a system changes only when a net external impulse acts on it: if ΣF_ext = 0, then p_sys,i = p_sys,f. This is true however complicated the internal forces are, which is why momentum conservation works for collisions and explosions whose details are unknown.

Choose the system so that the interaction is internal. A rifle and its bullet, or two colliding carts, make good systems. Gravity and the normal force on carts on a level track cancel, so they give no net external impulse. During a brief collision, external forces such as friction are usually much smaller than the collision forces and act for only a short time, so momentum just before equals momentum just after, to a good approximation. For a ball bouncing off the ground, Earth's push is external to the ball, so the ball's momentum alone is not conserved.

Draw a before-and-after diagram with a stated positive direction, list each object's mass and velocity, and write m_A v_A,i + m_B v_B,i = m_A v_A,f + m_B v_B,f. A momentum bar chart shows the same accounting with signed bars, as in the figure: the bars before and after must add to the same total. In two dimensions, momentum is conserved separately in the x and y directions, so write one equation for each component and combine the results with the Pythagorean theorem.

Common errors: dropping the sign of a velocity in the opposite direction; using only one object's momentum; forgetting the combined mass when objects stick together; adding speeds instead of components in two dimensions; and applying conservation when an external force, such as the ground's push on a bouncing ball, delivers a large impulse.

examples.prompt: A 55 kg skater standing at rest on smooth ice throws a 4.0 kg medicine ball east at 6.0 m/s. Find the skater's velocity just after the throw.
examples.answer: About 0.44 m/s west (−0.44 m/s with east positive)
steps: System: skater and ball. Friction is negligible and vertical forces cancel, so momentum is conserved; it starts at zero.
v_s = −24/55 ≈ −0.44 m/s, so she moves west.

examples.prompt: An 1800 kg truck moving at 12 m/s rear-ends a 1200 kg car moving at 5.0 m/s in the same direction, and the two lock bumpers. Find their common velocity just after the collision.
examples.answer: 9.2 m/s in the original direction
steps: During the brief collision, external forces are small compared with the collision forces, so momentum is conserved.
After: (3000 kg)v = 27 600 kg·m/s, so v = 9.2 m/s.

examples.prompt: At the intersection shown, the car and the SUV collide and stick together. Find the speed and direction of the wreck just after the collision.
examples.answer: About 8.3 m/s at 44° north of east
steps: x (east): p_x = (1500)(14) = 21 000 kg·m/s; y (north): p_y = (2000)(10) = 20 000 kg·m/s; each component is conserved.
Direction: tan^−1(20 000/21 000) ≈ 43.6°, about 44° north of east.

worksheets.title: Recoil and sticking collisions
worksheets.directions: Draw a before-and-after diagram and state your positive direction. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: The total momentum of a system stays constant when
choices: no forces act inside the system
the net external force on the system is zero
the objects move at constant speed
items.answer: (B) the net external force on the system is zero
steps: Internal forces cancel in pairs and cannot change the total momentum.
Only a net external impulse changes p_sys.
items.skill: State the condition for momentum conservation

items.prompt: A 4.5 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet horizontally at 750 m/s. Find the rifle's recoil speed if it is free to move.
items.answer: About 1.7 m/s, opposite the bullet
steps: Momentum is zero before firing: 0 = (0.010)(750) + (4.5)v_r.
items.skill: Apply momentum conservation to recoil

items.prompt: A 15 000 kg railroad car rolling at 3.0 m/s couples with a 10 000 kg car at rest. Find their common speed.
items.skill: Solve a coupling collision

items.prompt: A 0.20 kg lump of clay moving horizontally at 8.0 m/s hits and sticks to a 1.4 kg cart at rest on a level track. Find the cart's speed afterward.
items.skill: Include the combined mass

items.prompt: A person standing at rest on frictionless ice throws a ball forward. Just after the throw, the total momentum of the person–ball system is
items.answer: (C) zero
steps: The system's momentum was zero, and no net external impulse acted.
The person's backward momentum cancels the ball's forward momentum.
items.skill: Apply conservation to an explosion from rest

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg cart moving at +2.0 m/s and a 0.30 kg cart moving at −4.0 m/s collide head-on and stick together. Find their velocity just after the collision.
steps: v = −0.20 / 0.80 = −0.25 m/s, in the direction the lighter cart was moving.
items.skill: Handle opposite directions with signs

items.prompt: Two carts of masses 1.0 kg and 3.0 kg are held at rest with a compressed spring between them and then released. The 1.0 kg cart moves left at 1.8 m/s. Find the velocity of the 3.0 kg cart.
items.answer: 0.60 m/s to the right
steps: Total momentum stays zero: (1.0)(−1.8) + (3.0)v = 0, taking right as positive.
items.skill: Analyze a spring-driven separation

worksheets.title: Before-and-after reasoning
worksheets.directions: Take right as positive unless told otherwise. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: The diagram shows two carts before and after they collide on a level, frictionless track. Find cart B's velocity after the collision.
items.answer: 4.0 m/s to the right
items.skill: Use a before-and-after diagram

items.prompt: For the collision in the diagram, draw a momentum bar chart on the blank chart showing each cart's momentum before and after, and explain how the chart shows that momentum is conserved.

rubric.criterion: Before bars: p_A = +6.0 kg·m/s and p_B = −1.0 kg·m/s (below the zero line).
After bars: p_A = +1.0 kg·m/s and p_B = +4.0 kg·m/s.
Explains that both totals are +5.0 kg·m/s: momentum moved from A to B, and the total did not change.

items.answer: Before: +6.0 and −1.0; after: +1.0 and +4.0 (kg·m/s). Both totals are +5.0 kg·m/s.
steps: p = mv for each cart with signs.
A loses 5.0 kg·m/s and B gains 5.0 kg·m/s, so the sum is unchanged.
items.skill: Draw a momentum bar chart

items.prompt: The graph shows the velocities of carts A and B as they collide on a level track. Find the ratio m_B/m_A. If cart A has a mass of 0.40 kg, what is cart B's mass?
steps: Momentum conservation: m_A(4.0) = m_A(1.0) + m_B(2.0), so m_B(2.0) = m_A(3.0).
items.skill: Find a mass ratio from velocity graphs

items.prompt: A ball falls and bounces off the ground. Why is the ball's momentum not conserved during the bounce?
choices: The ground exerts a large external force on the ball
Momentum is never conserved in a bounce
items.answer: (A) The ground exerts a large external force on the ball
steps: With the ball alone as the system, the ground's push is an external force that delivers a large impulse.
For the ball–Earth system that push is internal, and the system's momentum is conserved; Earth's change in velocity is too small to notice.
items.skill: Choose a system in which momentum is conserved

items.prompt: An 80 kg astronaut, initially at rest beside a 1200 kg satellite, pushes off it and moves away at 0.90 m/s. Find the satellite's speed, and the time until they are 10 m apart.
items.answer: Satellite 0.060 m/s; about 10 s (10.4 s)
steps: They separate at 0.90 + 0.060 = 0.96 m/s, so t = 10 m / 0.96 m/s ≈ 10.4 s.
items.skill: Combine momentum with relative motion

items.prompt: A 0.050 kg dart moving horizontally sticks in a 0.45 kg block resting on a frictionless air track. The block and dart move off at 1.6 m/s. Find the dart's speed before impact.
items.answer: 16 m/s
steps: m_d v_d = (m_d + m_b)(1.6 m/s).
items.skill: Work backward from a sticking collision

items.prompt: Carts X and Y rest on a level, frictionless track with a compressed spring between them. Cart X has twice the mass of cart Y. When the spring is released, which statement is correct?
choices: X has twice Y's kinetic energy
Y has twice X's speed and four times X's kinetic energy
Y has twice X's speed and twice X's kinetic energy
items.answer: (D) Y has twice X's speed and twice X's kinetic energy
steps: Equal and opposite momenta: (2m)v_X = mv_Y, so v_Y = 2v_X.
K = p^2/(2m) with equal p: the lighter cart Y has twice the kinetic energy.
items.skill: Compare speeds and energies after a push-apart

worksheets.title: Momentum in two dimensions and multi-object systems
worksheets.directions: Conserve each component separately. Take east and north as positive. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures; give directions as angles from a compass direction.

items.prompt: A 3.0 kg object at rest explodes into three 1.0 kg pieces. One moves east at 12 m/s and another moves north at 9.0 m/s. Find the velocity of the third piece.
items.answer: 15 m/s at about 37° south of west
steps: Total momentum stays zero: p_3 = −(12, 0) − (0, 9.0) = (−12, −9.0) kg·m/s.
items.skill: Apply component conservation to an explosion

items.prompt: Puck A (0.20 kg) slides east at 5.0 m/s and strikes puck B (0.20 kg), which is at rest. Afterward, A moves at 3.0 m/s at 53° north of east. Find B's speed and direction.
items.answer: 4.0 m/s at about 37° south of east
steps: A after: (3.0 cos 53°, 3.0 sin 53°) ≈ (1.8, 2.4) m/s; with equal masses, velocities add like momenta.
items.skill: Solve a glancing collision

items.prompt: A 60 kg student runs at 4.0 m/s and jumps onto a 40 kg cart at rest. (a) Find the speed of the student and cart together. (b) The student then steps off the back of the cart so that her horizontal velocity relative to the ground is zero. Find the cart's speed afterward.
steps: (b) The system's momentum stays 240 kg·m/s; with the student at rest, (40)v_c = 240, so v_c = 6.0 m/s.
items.skill: Apply conservation in two stages

items.prompt: A cart rolls along a level, frictionless track while sand pours straight down into it from a hopper above. What happens to the cart's speed, and why?
choices: It decreases, because the horizontal momentum is shared with more mass
It stays the same, because the sand falls vertically
It increases, because the sand's weight pushes the cart
It decreases, because friction acts on the sand
items.answer: (A) It decreases, because the horizontal momentum is shared with more mass
steps: The falling sand has no horizontal momentum, and no horizontal external force acts, so the horizontal momentum of cart plus sand is constant.
As the total mass grows, the shared velocity must shrink.
items.skill: Apply horizontal momentum conservation with added mass

items.prompt: Skaters A (50 kg) and B (75 kg) stand together at rest on smooth ice and push apart. A moves away at 1.5 m/s. (a) Find B's velocity. (b) How far apart are they 2.0 s later? (c) Explain what happens to the center of mass of the two skaters.

rubric.criterion: 0 = (50)(1.5) + (75)v_B gives v_B = −1.0 m/s (1.0 m/s in the opposite direction).
Separation after 2.0 s: (1.5 + 1.0)(2.0) = 5.0 m.
The center of mass stays at rest where it started, because the pushes are internal and the net external force is zero; B, the heavier skater, stays closer to it.

items.answer: (a) 1.0 m/s opposite to A; (b) 5.0 m; (c) the center of mass stays at rest at the starting point.
steps: Internal pushes cannot change the system's momentum, which stays zero.
Positions after 2.0 s: A at +3.0 m and B at −2.0 m, and (50)(3.0) + (75)(−2.0) = 0, so the center of mass is still at the origin.
items.skill: Connect momentum conservation to center of mass

items.prompt: A 0.012 kg bullet moving at 450 m/s passes straight through a 2.0 kg block resting on a frictionless surface and leaves at 150 m/s. Find the block's speed afterward.
items.skill: Solve a pass-through collision

items.prompt: Two carts on a level, frictionless track collide. Which describes a graph of the total momentum of the two-cart system against time, from before the collision until after it?
choices: A line that drops during the collision and then levels off
A line that rises during the collision and then levels off
A curve that dips to zero at the moment of impact
items.answer: (A) A horizontal line
steps: The net external force is zero throughout, so the total momentum never changes.
Each cart's own momentum changes during the collision, but the changes cancel.
items.skill: Represent conservation on a graph

weeks.title: Elastic and inelastic collisions
weeks.objective: Classify collisions by comparing kinetic energy before and after, solve elastic and perfectly inelastic collisions, chain momentum and energy in two-stage problems, and analyze supplied collision data with a linearized graph.

connection.before: Week 15's conservation of momentum and Unit 3's kinetic energy and internal energy.
connection.after: Unit 5 begins rotational motion in week 17, where torque and angular quantities parallel force and momentum.

days: Classify collisions: momentum is conserved in every isolated collision, while kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones; perfectly inelastic collisions stick.
Elastic collisions in one dimension: equal masses exchange velocities, and the relative velocity reverses.
Two-stage problems: momentum through the collision, then energy afterward (ballistic pendulum, skidding wreck, spring bumper).
Paper investigation: supplied air-track collision data, kinetic-energy fractions and a linearized graph.
Unit 4 review and the Unit 4 test.
explanation: In any collision between objects isolated from outside forces, total momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy is a different matter. In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy after equals the total before; hard steel balls and magnetic bumpers come close. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy becomes internal energy, sound or permanent deformation. When the objects stick together, the collision is perfectly inelastic, and the loss of kinetic energy is as large as momentum conservation allows. To classify a collision, compute the total kinetic energy before and after.

For an elastic collision in one dimension, the two conservation laws together show that the relative velocity reverses: v_B,f − v_A,f = −(v_B,i − v_A,i). Using this with the momentum equation avoids squaring velocities. When equal masses collide elastically head-on and one is at rest, they exchange velocities: the moving object stops and the target moves off with the original velocity. A light object bouncing off a much heavier one at rest rebounds with nearly its original speed.

Many problems have two stages. In a ballistic pendulum, a projectile embeds in a hanging block (a perfectly inelastic collision, so use momentum), and then the block swings up (no collision, so use energy). Energy conservation cannot be used through the collision itself, because kinetic energy is lost there. The figure shows such a setup. The same chaining applies to cars that lock together and then skid to a stop, or carts that compress a spring bumper.

Common errors: conserving kinetic energy in a collision that is not elastic; using energy conservation across the instant of a perfectly inelastic collision; thinking that 'elastic' means the objects bounce apart (objects can separate and still lose kinetic energy); and forgetting that kinetic energy can never increase in a collision unless stored energy, such as a compressed spring or an explosive, is released.

College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

examples.prompt: A 0.30 kg cart moving at 2.0 m/s strikes a 0.20 kg cart at rest. Afterward the 0.30 kg cart moves at 0.40 m/s and the 0.20 kg cart at 2.4 m/s, both in the original direction. Check that momentum is conserved and classify the collision.
examples.answer: Momentum 0.60 kg·m/s before and after; kinetic energy 0.60 J before and after, so the collision is elastic.
steps: Kinetic energy is unchanged, so the collision is elastic (check: the relative speed is 2.0 m/s before and 2.4 − 0.40 = 2.0 m/s after).

examples.prompt: A 0.010 kg bullet is fired horizontally into a 1.5 kg block hanging as a ballistic pendulum, like the one shown, and stays in it. The block rises 0.12 m. Find the speed of the block just after impact, the speed of the bullet, and the fraction of the bullet's kinetic energy that remains as kinetic energy just after impact.
examples.answer: Block about 1.5 m/s (1.53 m/s); bullet about 2.3 × 10^2 m/s; only about 0.66% of the kinetic energy remains (over 99% is converted).
steps: Stage 2 (swing, energy conserved): (1/2)(m + M)V^2 = (m + M)gh, so V = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.12) ≈ 1.53 m/s.
Stage 1 (collision, momentum conserved): mv = (m + M)V, so v = (1.51 kg)(1.53 m/s)/(0.010 kg) ≈ 232 m/s.
K_after/K_before = m/(m + M) = 0.010/1.51 ≈ 0.0066, so about 99.3% becomes internal energy.

examples.prompt: A 0.20 kg glider moving at 0.90 m/s collides elastically and head-on with a 0.40 kg glider at rest. Taking the 0.20 kg glider's initial direction as positive, find both velocities after the collision.
examples.answer: 0.20 kg glider: −0.30 m/s (it rebounds); 0.40 kg glider: +0.60 m/s
steps: Elastic, so the relative velocity reverses: v_B − v_A = 0.90 m/s.
Substituting v_B = v_A + 0.90: 0.18 = 0.60v_A + 0.36, so v_A = −0.30 m/s and v_B = 0.60 m/s (kinetic energy 0.081 J before and 0.009 + 0.072 = 0.081 J after).

passages.title: Investigation data: gliders on an air track
passages.text:
Glider A (0.250 kg) is launched by a spring launcher at the same setting every time, so it reaches glider B at 0.80 m/s. Glider B is at rest before each collision. Photogates measure each glider's velocity just after the collision; velocities to the right (away from the launcher) are positive.
Table 1: glider B also has a mass of 0.250 kg; the bumpers between the gliders are changed.
| bumpers | v_A after (m/s) | v_B after (m/s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| magnets | 0.01 | 0.79 |
| rubber band | 0.12 | 0.68 |
| hook and loop (they stick) | 0.40 | 0.40 |
Table 2: hook-and-loop bumpers, so the gliders stick; glider B is loaded so that its total mass is M; v_f is the common speed after the collision.
| M (kg) | 0.25 | 0.50 | 0.75 | 1.00 | 1.25 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| v_f (m/s) | 0.405 | 0.268 | 0.198 | 0.161 | 0.134 |
