examples.prompt:
A spring launcher on a table 0.80 m high fires a 0.020 kg ball horizontally. The landing distance R for each compression x is:
| x (m) | 0.020 | 0.040 | 0.060 | 0.080 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R (m) | 0.42 | 0.85 | 1.24 | 1.66 |
What graph tests the model (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)mv^2, and what spring constant do the data give?
examples.answer: Plot R against x; the model predicts a line through the origin. The slope is about 20.5, giving v/x = √(k/m) ≈ 51 s^−1 and k ≈ 52 N/m
steps: The model gives v = x√(k/m); the fall time t = √(2(0.80)/9.8) ≈ 0.404 s is the same for every launch, so R = vt = [t√(k/m)]x.
R against x is a straight line through the origin with best-fit slope about 20.5, so √(k/m) = 20.5/0.404 ≈ 51 s^−1.

examples.prompt: A block of mass m hangs from a vertical spring of constant k. Derive the period of its vertical oscillations, and explain whether it differs from the period of the same block on the same spring on a level, frictionless surface.
examples.answer: T = 2π√(m/k) in both cases: gravity only shifts the equilibrium position down by mg/k.
steps: At equilibrium the spring is stretched Δx_0 = mg/k.
If the block is a further y below equilibrium, the net force is mg − k(Δx_0 + y) = −ky, a Hooke's-law restoring force.
The motion is simple harmonic with T = 2π√(m/k), the same as on a level surface; only the center of the oscillation moves.

examples.prompt: A student times a cart rolling from rest over several distances with a hand stopwatch. She always starts the watch about 0.10 s late, and her reaction time also varies by about 0.05 s from trial to trial. Classify each error and describe how each would show up on a graph of distance against time squared.
examples.answer: The late start is systematic: every time is too short by the same amount, so the points are shifted and the line does not pass through the origin. The trial-to-trial variation is random: points scatter on both sides of the best-fit line, and averaging repeated trials reduces it.
steps: An error that pushes every reading the same way is systematic; one that varies unpredictably is random.
A constant shortfall in t distorts every t^2 value in the same direction, which shows up as a shifted line or a nonzero intercept.
Random scatter averages out over repeated trials, but the systematic error needs a better technique, such as starting and stopping with a sensor.

passages.title: Investigation data: a floating test tube
passages.text:
A flat-bottomed test tube with outside cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10^−4 m^2, length 0.16 m and mass 12 g floats upright in an unknown liquid, as in the figure. The student adds lead shot of mass m and measures the submerged depth d with a ruler held against the tube.
| m (g) | 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 16 | 20 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| d (cm) | 5.5 | 7.2 | 9.1 | 10.8 | 12.8 | 14.5 |
passages.attribution: Original data set written for Liminal.

passages.title: Investigation data: springs joined end to end
passages.text:
A 0.50 kg cart on a level, low-friction track is pulled by a chain of n identical springs hooked end to end, the other end of the chain fixed to a wall, as in the figure. For each n the student pulls the cart aside, releases it, and times 10 full oscillations.
| n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time for 10 oscillations (s) | 7.0 | 9.9 | 12.2 | 14.1 | 15.7 |
passages.attribution: Original data set written for Liminal.

worksheets.title: Investigation: a floating test tube
worksheets.directions: Use the test-tube data and figure. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. This is a paper investigation with supplied data; it does not replace hands-on lab work.

items.prompt: Before you look at the data, design a procedure that uses a flat-bottomed test tube, lead shot, a balance and a ruler to determine the density of a liquid by floating the tube in it. Name the quantities you would measure, the graph you would make, and how you would get the density from it.

rubric.criterion: Measures the tube's outside cross-sectional area (diameter) and the total floating mass with the balance for at least five loads of shot.
Measures the submerged depth for each load with the tube floating upright and still, reading at eye level and repeating.
Plots d against total mass M and uses ρ = 1/(slope × A).

items.answer: Measure the tube's outside diameter to get A. For at least five loads of shot, find the total mass M with the balance, float the tube upright, and read the submerged depth d at eye level (repeating each reading). Plot d against M; since d = M/(ρA), the slope is 1/(ρA), so ρ = 1/(slope × A).
steps: Floating means the buoyant force ρ(Ad)g equals the weight Mg.
So d is proportional to M, and the slope of d against M contains the density.
items.skill: Design a procedure for a fluid measurement

items.prompt: Show that for the floating tube, the submerged depth should be d = M/(ρA), where M is the total mass of the tube and shot, ρ is the liquid's density and A is the tube's cross-sectional area. What graph of the test-tube data should be a straight line through the origin?

rubric.criterion: Sets the buoyant force equal to the weight: ρ(Ad)g = Mg.
Concludes d = M/(ρA), so d against total mass M (tube plus shot) is a line through the origin with slope 1/(ρA).

items.answer: Floating: ρ(Ad)g = Mg, so d = M/(ρA). A graph of d against M = 0.012 kg + m is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/(ρA).
steps: The displaced volume is Ad, so F_b = ρAdg.
For equilibrium F_b = Mg; g cancels.
items.skill: Derive a linear model

items.prompt: Using the test-tube data, compute the total mass M = 12 g + m (in kilograms) for each trial and convert d to meters. Plot d against M on the grid, with labeled axes and scales, and draw a single best-fit line.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled d (m) and M (kg) with uniform scales; all six points plotted correctly.
One straight best-fit line passing close to the origin.

items.answer: The six points lie on a straight line through (very nearly) the origin, with slope about 4.5 m/kg.
steps: Add 0.012 kg to each shot mass, and divide each depth by 100.
The line through the points passes close to the origin, as the model predicts.
items.skill: Plot data and draw a best-fit line

items.prompt: Find the slope of your best-fit line with units, and use it to calculate the density of the liquid.
items.answer: Slope about 4.5 m/kg; density about 1.1 × 10^3 kg/m^3 (accept 1.05–1.15 × 10^3 kg/m^3)
steps: Two well-separated points on the best-fit line, for example (0.012 kg, 0.0545 m) and (0.032 kg, 0.145 m): slope ≈ (0.145 − 0.0545) m / (0.032 − 0.012) kg ≈ 4.5 m/kg.
items.skill: Extract a physical constant from a slope

items.prompt: The student repeats the investigation in the same liquid with a wider tube whose cross-sectional area is twice as large. How does the slope of d against M change?
choices: It stays the same, because the liquid is the same
items.answer: (B) It halves
steps: The slope is 1/(ρA).
Doubling A halves the slope: each added gram sinks the wider tube only half as far.
items.skill: Predict a change in slope

items.prompt: Which change to the test-tube procedure would most reduce random uncertainty in the measured density?
choices: Using more loads of shot spread over the tube's full range and repeating each depth reading
Using a liquid of greater density
Measuring d from the top of the tube instead of its bottom
Recording each depth to more decimal places than the ruler can show
items.answer: (A) Using more loads of shot spread over the tube's full range and repeating each depth reading
steps: More, well-spread data points and repeated readings reduce the effect of scatter on the slope.
Extra decimal places add no real precision, and measuring from the top does not give the submerged depth.
items.skill: Reduce random uncertainty

items.prompt: Use your result for the test tube to find the largest mass of shot it can carry while still floating in this liquid. The tube is 0.16 m long.
items.answer: About 23 g of shot (a total floating mass of about 35 g)
steps: The tube can be submerged at most 0.16 m: M_max = ρA(0.16 m) = (1.1 × 10^3)(2.0 × 10^−4)(0.16) ≈ 0.035 kg.
Subtract the tube's 12 g: about 23 g of shot; equivalently, M_max = (0.16 m)/(slope).
items.skill: Extrapolate a linear fit to a limit

worksheets.title: Investigation: springs joined end to end
worksheets.directions: Use the spring-chain data and figure. Use 2–3 significant figures. This is a paper investigation with supplied data; it does not replace hands-on lab work.

items.prompt: Each spring in the chain has constant k. Explain why a chain of n identical springs behaves like one spring of constant k/n, then show that T^2 should be proportional to n for the 0.50 kg cart, and state what the slope of T^2 against n represents.

rubric.criterion: Each spring in the chain carries the same force F and stretches F/k, so the chain stretches nF/k and k_chain = k/n.
Uses T = 2π√(m/k_chain) to get T^2 = (4π^2m/k)n.
Slope = 4π^2m/k.

items.answer: A force F stretches each spring by F/k, so the chain stretches nF/k: k_chain = k/n. Then T = 2π√(mn/k), so T^2 = (4π^2m/k)n, a line through the origin with slope 4π^2m/k.
steps: Springs in series share the same force, and their stretches add.
Substituting k/n into the period relation and squaring gives T^2 proportional to n.
items.skill: Model springs in series

items.prompt: From the spring-chain data, compute the period T and T^2 for each n, then plot T^2 against n on the grid with labeled axes and scales and draw a single best-fit line.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled T^2 (s^2) and n with uniform scales; points plotted correctly.
One straight best-fit line passing close to the origin.

items.answer: T = 0.70, 0.99, 1.22, 1.41, 1.57 s; T^2 = 0.49, 0.98, 1.49, 1.99, 2.46 s^2. The points lie on a straight line through (nearly) the origin.
steps: T = (time for 10 oscillations)/10; square each value.
The points rise by about 0.5 s^2 per spring, as the model predicts.
items.skill: Linearize oscillation data

items.prompt: Use the slope of your T^2 against n line to find the spring constant k of one spring.
items.answer: Slope about 0.50 s^2 per spring, so k ≈ 40 N/m (accept 38–42 N/m)
items.skill: Extract a spring constant from a slope

items.prompt: Take k = 40 N/m for each spring. With a chain of three springs, the 0.50 kg cart is pulled 0.060 m from equilibrium and released. Find its maximum speed and how long it takes to first reach equilibrium.
items.answer: Maximum speed about 0.31 m/s; it first reaches equilibrium after about 0.30 s (one quarter of a 1.22 s period)
steps: T = 2π√(0.50/13.3) ≈ 1.22 s; from a turning point to equilibrium takes T/4 ≈ 0.30 s.
items.skill: Use oscillator energy and timing

items.prompt: A student claims, "Adding more springs to the chain will make the cart oscillate faster, because more springs push and pull on it." Evaluate the claim using the data and the model.

rubric.criterion: Notes from the data that the period grows with n (0.70 s for one spring to 1.57 s for five).
Explains with k_chain = k/n: a longer chain stretches more for the same force, so it is a softer spring.
Concludes the claim is wrong: T = 2π√(mn/k) increases with n, so the cart oscillates more slowly.

items.answer: The claim is wrong. Springs in series share one force, so their stretches add and the chain is softer: k_chain = k/n. Then T = 2π√(mn/k) grows with n, as the data show (0.70 s for one spring, 1.57 s for five).
steps: More springs in a chain means more total stretch for the same pull.
A smaller effective spring constant gives a longer period.
items.skill: Argue from data and a model

items.prompt: At the instant the oscillating cart passes through its equilibrium position, which quantities have their maximum magnitudes?
items.answer: (A) Speed and kinetic energy
steps: At equilibrium the net spring force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and the spring potential energy is at its minimum.
All of the oscillator's energy is kinetic there, so speed and kinetic energy are largest.
items.skill: Relate position to energy in SHM

worksheets.title: Writing qualitative/quantitative arguments
worksheets.directions: For each written item, derive or cite a relation first, then use it in your explanation. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and ρ_water = 1000 kg/m^3.

items.prompt: Block X (mass m) and block Y (mass 4m) are attached to identical springs on a level, frictionless surface. Block X is pulled out a distance A and block Y a distance 2A, and both are released at the same instant. A student claims, "Block Y reaches its equilibrium position later than X, and moving faster." Use equations to evaluate each part of the claim.

rubric.criterion: Uses v_max = A√(k/m): X has A√(k/m) and Y has 2A√(k/(4m)) = A√(k/m), so the maximum speeds are equal.
Uses T = 2π√(m/k): Y's period is twice X's, so Y takes twice as long (T/4) to reach equilibrium.
Concludes that the first part of the claim is correct and the second is wrong: Y arrives later but at the same speed.

items.answer: Half right. Y's period is twice X's (T ∝ √(m)), so Y reaches equilibrium later. But v_max = A√(k/m) is the same for both: Y has twice the amplitude and half of √(k/m).
steps: T_Y = 2π√(4m/k) = 2T_X, and each block first reaches equilibrium after a quarter period.
v_max,Y = (2A)√(k/(4m)) = A√(k/m) = v_max,X.
items.skill: Evaluate a two-part claim with equations

items.prompt: A beaker of water on a scale reads 12.0 N. A metal ball of weight 3.0 N and volume 5.0 × 10^−5 m^3 hangs from a string and is lowered into the water until it is fully submerged, without touching the beaker. Find the new scale reading and the string tension, and explain why the scale reading changes even though the ball does not touch the beaker.

rubric.criterion: Buoyant force on the ball: (1000)(5.0 × 10^−5)(9.8) ≈ 0.49 N, so the tension is about 2.5 N.
By Newton's third law, the ball pushes down on the water with 0.49 N, so the scale reads about 12.5 N.
Explains that the water pushes up on the ball and the ball pushes down on the water with an equal force, which the beaker passes to the scale.

items.answer: Buoyant force ≈ 0.49 N, so the tension is about 2.5 N and the scale reads about 12.5 N. The water pushes up on the ball, so by the third law the ball pushes down on the water with the same 0.49 N.
steps: The scale supports the beaker, the water and the ball's reaction force: 12.0 + 0.49 ≈ 12.5 N.
items.skill: Apply the third law to buoyancy

items.prompt: An ice cube floats in a glass of water filled to the brim. When the ice melts, the water level
choices: falls, because ice is less dense than water
falls, because the melted water has less mass than the ice
items.answer: (C) stays the same
steps: Floating ice displaces its own weight of water.
When it melts, it becomes exactly that weight of water, which fills the volume it was displacing.
items.skill: Apply buoyancy to a melting object

items.prompt: A pendulum 0.50 m long hangs from the ceiling of an elevator. Derive an expression for its period when the elevator accelerates upward at a, calculate it for a = 2.0 m/s^2, and compare it with the period when the elevator is at rest.

rubric.criterion: Explains that in the accelerating elevator the string must supply m(g + a) at equilibrium, so the bob behaves as if gravity were g + a.
At rest T = 2π√(L/g) ≈ 1.42 s, so the period is shorter when accelerating upward.

items.answer: T = 2π√(L/(g + a)) ≈ 1.29 s for a = 2.0 m/s^2, shorter than the 1.42 s period at rest.
steps: Relative to the elevator, the bob's equilibrium tension is m(g + a), so the effective gravity is g + a.
items.skill: Adapt a period relation to a new situation

items.prompt: Carts X (2.0 kg) and Y (8.0 kg) each have 16 J of kinetic energy. Derive an expression for momentum in terms of mass and kinetic energy, and use it to decide which cart needs the larger impulse to stop and by what factor.

rubric.criterion: Derives p = √(2mK) from K = p^2/(2m).
p_X = 8.0 kg·m/s and p_Y = 16 kg·m/s.
Concludes that Y needs twice the impulse, because the impulse to stop equals the momentum.

items.answer: p = √(2mK): p_X = 8.0 kg·m/s and p_Y = 16 kg·m/s, so cart Y needs twice the impulse.
steps: p_X = √(2 × 2.0 × 16) = 8.0 kg·m/s; p_Y = √(2 × 8.0 × 16) = 16 kg·m/s; stopping impulse = −p.
items.skill: Connect energy and momentum symbolically

items.prompt: A block slides from rest down a rough ramp of height h and length d inclined at θ, with coefficient of kinetic friction μ_k. Which expression for its speed at the bottom has consistent units and could be correct?
items.answer: (D) v = √(2g(h − μ_k d cos θ))
steps: Inside the square root every term must have units of m^2/s^2: g times a length works, a bare length does not.
Energy confirms it: mgh − μ_k mg cos θ d = (1/2)mv^2.
items.skill: Check an expression with units

weeks.title: Practice exam, self-scoring and error analysis
weeks.objective: Take the full practice exam under timed conditions, score it with the key and scoring guidelines, record raw points by section, question type and unit, and classify every lost point to plan targeted review.

connection.before: Weeks 30–32 reviewed all eight units and the four free-response question types.
connection.after: Week 34 uses the raw-point tally from this week to choose targeted review sheets.

days: Section I of the practice exam: 42 multiple-choice questions in 85 minutes, in one sitting.
Section II of the practice exam: 4 free-response questions in 95 minutes, in one sitting.
Score Section I with the key, read the rationale for every missed item, and record raw points by unit.
Score Section II with the scoring guidelines, row by row, and record raw points by question type.
Error analysis: classify each lost point, rework the items, and write a one-page review plan.
explanation: Take the practice exam as a rehearsal. Section I has 42 multiple-choice questions in 85 minutes, about 2 minutes each; Section II has four free-response questions in 95 minutes: mathematical routines (10 points), translation between representations (12 points), experimental design and analysis (10 points) and qualitative/quantitative translation (8 points). Any calculator is allowed in both sections. Use Liminal's formula reference while practicing, and before the real exam practice with College Board's own equation sheet from the AP® Physics 1 exam page, since its layout differs from Liminal's. Work in two timed sittings without notes, and mark questions to return to rather than stalling.

Score honestly with the key and the scoring guidelines. Each rubric row is worth its points only when the criterion is fully met; a correct final number reached by incorrect physics does not earn the reasoning points. Record raw points in a tally:
| Section or type | Raw points earned | Points available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section I (multiple choice) | | 42 |
| Mathematical routines | | 10 |
| Translation between representations | | 12 |
| Experimental design and analysis | | 10 |
| Qualitative/quantitative translation | | 8 |
Also record multiple-choice points by unit. These are practice tallies, not AP® scores; Liminal does not convert them to the 1–5 scale or estimate one.

Classify every lost point before reworking it. Typical categories are: concept or model (wrong physics, such as assuming the normal force equals mg on an incline); representation (misreading a graph or diagram); system or sign (wrong system, missing external force, inconsistent positive direction); algebra or arithmetic; units and significant figures; reading the question; and time. The category tells you what to practice: concept errors need explanation and new problems, while arithmetic errors need checking habits.

Turn the tally into a plan. Compare the fraction of points earned in each unit and question type, list the two or three weakest, and choose week 34's sheets accordingly. Rework each missed item on fresh paper before rereading its solution. Common mistakes in self-scoring are giving credit for an answer without the required reasoning, skipping the rationales for items answered correctly by guessing, and reviewing only the questions that felt hard rather than the ones the tally shows were missed.

examples.prompt: Scoring practice. Question (3 points): A constant net force of 3.0 N acts on a 1.5 kg cart that starts from rest. Find its speed after 2.0 s. Rubric: 1 point for a = F/m = 2.0 m/s^2; 1 point for a correct kinematics relation, v = v_0 + at; 1 point for 4.0 m/s, with units, consistent with correct work. A student wrote: "a = 3.0/1.5 = 2.0 m/s^2. v = (1/2)at^2 = (1/2)(2.0)(2.0)^2 = 4.0 m/s." How many points does the response earn?
examples.answer: 1 of 3 points: the acceleration point only. The kinematics relation is wrong, and the correct-looking 4.0 m/s comes from incorrect work, so it does not earn the answer point.
steps: Row 1: a = 2.0 m/s^2 is correct, so 1 point.
Row 2: (1/2)at^2 is a displacement, not a speed; the correct relation is v = v_0 + at, so 0 points.
Row 3: the number matches only by coincidence; the answer point requires correct work, so 0 points.

examples.prompt: Error analysis. A practice item asked for the friction force on a 5.0 kg box at rest on a ramp inclined at 20°, with μ_s = 0.60. A student chose 28 N, calculated as μ_s mg cos 20°. Find the correct answer and classify the error.
examples.answer: The friction force is about 17 N (16.8 N), equal to mg sin 20°. The error is a concept/model error: static friction is not automatically at its maximum value μ_s F_N.
steps: The box is at rest, so friction balances the component of gravity along the ramp: f = mg sin 20° = (5.0)(9.8)(0.342) ≈ 16.8 N.
μ_s mg cos 20° ≈ 27.6 N is only the largest friction can be; since 16.8 N < 27.6 N, the box stays put with f = 16.8 N.
The student's arithmetic was fine; the model of static friction was wrong.

examples.prompt: Building the tally. A student's Section I raw points by unit were: Unit 1, 4 of 5; Unit 2, 6 of 8; Unit 3, 5 of 8; Unit 4, 4 of 5; Unit 5, 2 of 5; Unit 6, 1 of 3; Unit 7, 2 of 3; Unit 8, 4 of 5. In Section II the student earned 6 of 10 (mathematical routines), 8 of 12 (translation), 7 of 10 (experimental design) and 3 of 8 (qualitative/quantitative). Find the raw totals and identify what week 34 should target first.
examples.answer: Section I: 28 of 42; Section II: 24 of 40; total 52 of 82 raw points. Target Units 5 and 6 (rotation: 2 of 5 and 1 of 3) and qualitative/quantitative writing (3 of 8).
steps: Fractions earned: Unit 5 is 0.40 and Unit 6 is 0.33, the lowest units; QQT is 0.375, the lowest question type.
Week 34's rotation sheet and written-argument practice come first; these are practice tallies only, not AP® scores.

worksheets.title: Pacing and using the formula reference
worksheets.directions: Use Liminal's formula reference. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 0.30 kg mass on a spring completes 12 oscillations in 6.0 s. Using the formula reference, choose the relations you need and find the spring constant.
steps: Period = total time / number of oscillations = 0.50 s (T = 1/f with f = 2.0 Hz).
items.skill: Select and chain reference relations

items.prompt: Which combination of SI base units is equivalent to the newton?
items.answer: (C) kg·m/s^2
steps: F = ma, so 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s^2.
kg·m/s is momentum, kg·m^2/s^2 is energy and kg/(m·s^2) is pressure.
items.skill: Check units

items.prompt: Plan your time. Section I has 42 questions in 85 minutes. Section II has 95 minutes for four questions worth 10, 12, 10 and 8 points. Find the average time per multiple-choice question, and split Section II's time in proportion to the points.
items.answer: About 2.0 minutes per multiple-choice question; Section II: about 24 min, 28–29 min, 24 min and 19 min
steps: 85 min / 42 ≈ 2.0 min per question.
Section II has 40 points, so 95 min × (10/40) ≈ 24 min, × (12/40) ≈ 28.5 min, × (10/40) ≈ 24 min and × (8/40) = 19 min.
items.skill: Budget exam time

items.prompt: Combine two relations from the reference, K = (1/2)Iω^2 and I = (1/2)MR^2 for a uniform disk, to find the angular velocity of a 3.0 kg disk of radius 0.20 m that has 12 J of rotational kinetic energy.
items.answer: 20 rad/s
items.skill: Chain reference relations

items.prompt: A question gives the depth and density of a liquid and asks for the absolute pressure. Choose the relation and find the absolute pressure 3.0 m below the surface of an open tank of oil of density 850 kg/m^3 (atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10^5 Pa).
steps: Absolute pressure includes the atmosphere: P = P_0 + ρgh.
items.skill: Distinguish absolute from gauge pressure

items.prompt: Two carts on a level, frictionless track collide and stick together. Which quantity of the two-cart system is not conserved?
items.answer: (A) Kinetic energy
steps: No net external force acts, so momentum is conserved; total energy and mass are always conserved.
In a perfectly inelastic collision some kinetic energy becomes internal energy.
items.skill: Recall conservation conditions

worksheets.title: Error analysis
worksheets.directions: Each item shows a student's work. Identify the error, name its category (concept or model, representation, system or sign, algebra or arithmetic, units, reading), and give a corrected answer. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Question: 6.0 J of net work is done on a 2.0 kg cart that starts from rest. Find its speed. Student's work: "v = W/m = 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 m/s." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Concept/model error: work changes kinetic energy, (1/2)mv^2, not mv. Correct speed: v = √(2W/m) ≈ 2.4 m/s (2.45 m/s).
steps: v = √(2 × 6.0 / 2.0) = √(6.0) ≈ 2.45 m/s; the units of W/m are J/kg = m^2/s^2, not m/s, which also flags the error.
items.skill: Diagnose a work–energy error

items.prompt: Question: a 3.0 kg ball on a rope moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.80 m and passes the top at 4.0 m/s. Find the tension at the top. Student's work: "T = mv^2/r + mg = 60 + 29.4 = 89 N." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Sign/system error: at the top, tension and gravity both point down toward the center, so T + mg = mv^2/r. Correct tension: T = 60 − 29.4 ≈ 31 N (30.6 N).
steps: At the top the center is below the ball; both T and mg point toward it.
items.skill: Diagnose a circular-motion sign error

items.prompt: Question: a 20 N force acts at the end of a rod 0.50 m from the pivot, at 30° to the rod. Find the torque about the pivot. Student's work: "τ = rF cos 30° = (0.50)(20)(0.866) = 8.7 N·m." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Representation/trigonometry error: torque uses the component of F perpendicular to the rod, F sin 30°. Correct torque: τ = (0.50)(20)(0.50) = 5.0 N·m.
steps: τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between the rod and the force.
The cosine gives the component along the rod, which produces no torque; τ = 5.0 N·m.
items.skill: Diagnose a torque error

items.prompt: Question: a block slides from rest down a frictionless ramp of height h; find its speed at the bottom. Student's work: "System: the block alone. The block's potential energy mgh turns into kinetic energy, so v = √(2gh)." The answer is right, but the reasoning is inconsistent. Identify the inconsistency and rewrite the energy statement correctly for the system the student chose.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that a single object has no gravitational potential energy; potential energy belongs to the block–Earth system.
Rewrites the statement for the block alone: gravity does external work W = mgh = ΔK (or switches to the block–Earth system with ΔK + ΔU_g = 0).

items.answer: With the block alone as the system there is no potential energy; gravity is an external force whose work mgh equals the block's ΔK, giving the same v = √(2gh). Alternatively choose the block–Earth system and write ΔK + ΔU_g = 0.
steps: Gravitational potential energy is a property of the block–Earth system.
For the block alone: W_gravity = mgh = (1/2)mv^2, so v = √(2gh).
items.skill: Diagnose a system-choice error

items.prompt: Question: find the absolute pressure 4.0 m below the surface of a freshwater lake. Student's work: "P = ρgh = (1000)(9.8)(4.0) = 3.9 × 10^4 Pa." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Reading/model error: ρgh is the gauge pressure. The absolute pressure adds the atmosphere: P = 1.01 × 10^5 + 3.9 × 10^4 ≈ 1.40 × 10^5 Pa.
steps: Absolute pressure is P = P_0 + ρgh, where P_0 is the pressure at the surface.
P = 1.01 × 10^5 Pa + 3.92 × 10^4 Pa ≈ 1.40 × 10^5 Pa; the student's value is the gauge pressure.
items.skill: Diagnose a gauge/absolute pressure error

items.prompt: Question: a ball is thrown straight up at 12 m/s. Taking up as positive, find its velocity 2.0 s later. Student's work: "v = v_0 + at = 12 + (9.8)(2.0) = 31.6 m/s." Identify the error and correct it.
items.answer: Sign error: with up positive, a = −9.8 m/s^2. v = 12 − 19.6 = −7.6 m/s, so the ball is moving downward at 7.6 m/s.
steps: Gravity points down, so a = −9.8 m/s^2 in this coordinate choice.
v = 12 + (−9.8)(2.0) = −7.6 m/s; a speed above 12 m/s for a rising ball should have looked wrong.
items.skill: Diagnose a sign error in kinematics

worksheets.title: Scoring practice with rubrics
worksheets.directions: Each item gives a short question, its rubric and a student response. Award points row by row, and explain each decision. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.

items.prompt: Question (3 points): A 0.50 kg cart on a frictionless track is pushed against a spring (k = 200 N/m), compressing it 0.10 m, and released. Find its speed after it leaves the spring. Rubric: 1 point for an energy statement (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)mv^2; 1 point for correct substitution; 1 point for 2.0 m/s with units. Student response: "(1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)mv^2, so v = √(kx^2/m) = √((200)(0.01)/0.50) = 2." How many points does it earn?
items.answer: 2 of 3 points: the energy statement and the substitution are correct, but the final answer has no units, so the last point is not earned. The correct answer is 2.0 m/s.
steps: Rows 1 and 2: the statement and the substitution √(200 × 0.010 / 0.50) are correct.
Row 3: the value 2 is right, but the answer row requires units, so 0 points; correct answer 2.0 m/s.
items.skill: Apply a calculation rubric

items.prompt: Question (3 points): Explain why the period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass of its bob. Rubric: 1 point for noting that the restoring force (or gravitational force) is proportional to the mass, so the acceleration does not depend on it; 1 point for citing a correct relation, T = 2π√(L/g); 1 point for a conclusion consistent with the relation. Student response: "Heavier and lighter objects fall at the same rate, so the bob's mass doesn't matter. T = 2π√(m/k)." How many points does it earn?
items.answer: 1 of 3 points: the first row is earned (equal free-fall acceleration). The relation cited is the spring relation and contains m, so the relation point is lost, and the conclusion contradicts the student's own equation, so the conclusion point is lost.
steps: Row 1: equal acceleration regardless of mass expresses the cancellation, so 1 point.
Row 2: T = 2π√(m/k) is for a mass on a spring; 0 points.
Row 3: the cited equation says T depends on m, contradicting the claim; 0 points.
items.skill: Apply a reasoning rubric

items.prompt: Question (3 points): Sketch the velocity–time graph of a ball thrown straight up and caught at the same height, taking up as positive. Rubric: 1 point for a single straight line with negative slope; 1 point for starting at +v_0 and ending at −v_0; 1 point for v = 0 halfway through the flight. Student response: a V-shaped graph that falls in a straight line from +v_0 to 0 at the midpoint and then rises in a straight line back to +v_0. How many points does it earn, and what did the student graph instead?
items.answer: 1 of 3 points: only the zero at the midpoint is correct. The student graphed speed, not velocity: the graph should keep falling below zero to −v_0 in one straight line.
steps: Row 1: the slope changes sign at the midpoint, so it is not one straight line with negative slope; 0 points.
Row 2: it ends at +v_0 instead of −v_0; 0 points.
Row 3: v = 0 at the midpoint, so 1 point.
items.skill: Score a graph sketch

items.prompt: Question (3 points): Design a procedure to find the spring constant of a spring using hanging masses. Rubric: 1 point for measuring the stretch for several (at least five) different masses; 1 point for controlling variables or repeating measurements, such as measuring every stretch from the same reference mark; 1 point for plotting mg against stretch and using the slope as k. Student response: "Hang a 200 g mass and measure how far the spring stretches with a ruler. Then k = mg/x. Repeat three times and average." How many points does it earn?
items.answer: 1 of 3 points: the repeated, averaged measurement earns the second row. Using one mass loses the first row, and computing k from one point instead of a graph's slope loses the third.
steps: Row 1: only one mass is used; 0 points.
Row 2: repeating and averaging is a valid way to reduce uncertainty; 1 point.
Row 3: no graph or slope; 0 points.
items.skill: Score an experimental-design answer

items.prompt: On a practice item about a block on a frictionless incline, a student wrote "normal force = mg" and got the wrong acceleration. Which category best describes this error?
items.answer: (D) Concept or model error
steps: On an incline the normal force is mg cos θ, because it balances only the perpendicular component of gravity.
The mistake is in the physics model, not in the algebra, units or reading.
items.skill: Classify an error

items.prompt: A student's practice-exam raw points are: Section I, 29 of 42; mathematical routines, 7 of 10; translation between representations, 9 of 12; experimental design and analysis, 5 of 10; qualitative/quantitative translation, 6 of 8. Find the total raw points and the fraction earned for each free-response type, and name the type to practice first.
items.answer: Total 56 of 82 raw points. Fractions: 0.70 (MR), 0.75 (TBR), 0.50 (EDA), 0.75 (QQT); practice experimental design and analysis first.
steps: 7/10 = 0.70, 9/12 = 0.75, 5/10 = 0.50, 6/8 = 0.75; the lowest is EDA. The tally is a practice record, not an AP® score.
items.skill: Use a raw-point tally to plan review

weeks.title: Targeted review from practice-exam results
weeks.objective: Use the practice-exam tally to choose review, then strengthen rotation and rotating systems, oscillations and fluids, and problems that link several units in one situation.

connection.before: Week 33's practice exam, scoring and error analysis, which produced a raw-point tally by unit and question type.
connection.after: After the exam, weeks 35 and 36 use synthesis investigations to connect the course's ideas.

days: Read your week 33 tally and error categories; choose the sheet and the two or three ideas to work on first.
Rotation and rotating systems: equilibrium, the rotational second law, rolling, angular impulse and orbits.
Oscillations and fluids: energy in simple harmonic motion, periods, pressure, buoyancy and flow.
Linked problems: collisions that start rotation or oscillation, and energy that ends in flow or oscillation.
Final mixed check, then rest: pack an approved calculator and review your one-page plan, not new material.
explanation: Targeted review works best when it is specific. Use the week 33 tally to find the units and question types with the lowest fraction of points earned, and use the error categories to decide how to practice: concept errors call for rereading an explanation and then doing fresh problems, while arithmetic and sign errors call for slower checking on mixed problems. Interleave topics rather than doing ten problems of one kind in a row, because the exam does not label its questions by unit.

Sheets A–C cover Units 5–8 and problems that link units; for a weakness in Units 1–4, use the sheets of weeks 30–31 you have not yet done. Sheet A covers Units 5 and 6: torque balance with every force on the diagram, Στ = Iα, rolling with v = ωR, angular impulse τΔt = ΔL, and circular orbits, where gravity supplies the inward force. Sheet B covers Units 7 and 8: x = A cos(2πft), (1/2)kA^2 = (1/2)mv_max^2, T = 2π√(m/k) and T = 2π√(L/g); P = P_0 + ρgh, F_b = ρ_fluid V_disp g, A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 and Bernoulli's equation.

Sheet C links units. A collision can set an object rotating (angular momentum about the pivot is conserved, but linear momentum is not, because the pivot pushes) or change an oscillator's amplitude (momentum is conserved during the brief collision, and then the oscillator's energy determines the new amplitude). Energy stored by height can end up as fluid flow. In each, identify the stages, the conserved quantity in each stage, and the quantity carried from one stage to the next.

Common errors in these areas: leaving the pivot or hinge force off a torque diagram, then using it anyway; using v = ωR for an object that slips; computing a buoyant force from the object's density instead of the fluid's; using gauge pressure where absolute pressure is needed (or the reverse); and assuming the amplitude of an oscillator is unchanged after a collision.

A dot marks the center of mass; dimension lines show 0.90 m from the feet to the center of mass and 1.50 m from the feet to the hands, measured horizontally.

figures.caption: Dart striking the rim of a disk (top view)

figures.caption: Key: kinetic energy against position

examples.prompt: A small solid ball (I = (2/5)mr^2, with r much smaller than the loop) rolls without slipping from rest down a track into a vertical loop of radius 0.40 m. What is the minimum starting height above the bottom of the loop for the ball to stay on the track at the top?
steps: At the top, with the track force at its minimum (zero), gravity alone supplies the inward force: mg = mv^2/R, so v^2 = gR.
Energy, including rotation: mgh = mg(2R) + (1/2)mv^2 + (1/2)(2/5)mr^2(v/r)^2 = mg(2R) + (7/10)mv^2.

examples.prompt: A foam board 0.50 m × 0.40 m × 0.050 m, with density 250 kg/m^3, floats flat in a pool. What is the largest mass a child can rest on it before the board is completely submerged?
examples.answer: 7.5 kg
steps: Fully submerged, the buoyant force supports ρ_water V = 1000 × 0.010 = 10 kg of total mass.
Extra mass = 10 kg − 2.5 kg = 7.5 kg.

examples.prompt: A block on a spring oscillates with amplitude 0.10 m and period 1.2 s, starting from x = +A at t = 0. When does it first reach x = A/2, and how fast is it moving then?
examples.answer: At t = T/6 = 0.20 s, moving at about 0.45 m/s (0.453 m/s) toward equilibrium
steps: x = A cos(2πt/T) = A/2 when cos(2πt/T) = 1/2, so 2πt/T = π/3 and t = T/6 = 0.20 s.
v_max = A(2π/T) = 0.10 × 5.24 ≈ 0.524 m/s; at that instant v = v_max sin(π/3) = (√(3)/2)v_max ≈ 0.453 m/s.

worksheets.title: Rotation and rotating systems
worksheets.directions: Take counterclockwise as positive. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2, G = 6.67 × 10^−11 N·m^2/kg^2 and Earth's mass 5.97 × 10^24 kg. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 70 kg person holds a push-up position, as shown. Her center of mass is 0.90 m (horizontally) from her feet, and her hands are 1.50 m from her feet. Find the upward force of the floor on her hands and on her feet.
items.answer: Hands: about 4.1 × 10^2 N (412 N); feet: about 2.7 × 10^2 N (274 N)
steps: Torques about the feet: F_hands(1.50 m) = mg(0.90 m), so F_hands = (686 N)(0.90)/1.50 ≈ 412 N.
Vertical forces: F_feet = 686 − 412 ≈ 274 N.
Check with torques about the hands: F_feet(1.50) = 686(0.60) ≈ 412 N·m, giving 274 N.
items.skill: Solve a static-equilibrium problem

items.prompt: A wheel with rotational inertia 0.50 kg·m^2 speeds up uniformly from 2.0 rad/s to 10 rad/s in 4.0 s. What net torque acts on it?
items.skill: Apply Στ = Iα

items.prompt: A wind turbine's rotor has rotational inertia 2.0 × 10^6 kg·m^2 and turns at 2.0 rad/s when the wind stops. Friction and the generator together exert a constant 4.0 × 10^4 N·m torque against the rotation. Use angular impulse to find how long the rotor takes to stop, and find how many revolutions it makes while stopping.
items.answer: 100 s; about 16 revolutions (100 rad)
steps: With constant deceleration the average angular velocity is 1.0 rad/s, so θ = (1.0)(100) = 100 rad ≈ 16 revolutions.
items.skill: Use angular impulse

items.prompt: A 1200 kg satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius 9.0 × 10^6 m to one of radius 2.7 × 10^7 m around Earth (mass 5.97 × 10^24 kg). In a circular orbit, K = GMm/(2r) and U_G = −GMm/r. Find the changes in kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy, and the work the rocket engines must do.
items.answer: ΔK ≈ −1.77 × 10^10 J; ΔU ≈ +3.54 × 10^10 J; ΔE ≈ +1.77 × 10^10 J, which is the work the engines must do
steps: ΔE = ΔK + ΔU ≈ +1.77 × 10^10 J: the satellite ends up slower but with more total energy.
items.skill: Track energy changes between orbits

items.prompt: A solid cylinder and a thin hoop, each rolling without slipping at 3.0 m/s on level ground, roll up the same incline. How high (vertically) does each rise before stopping, and what is the ratio of the heights?
items.answer: Cylinder about 0.69 m; hoop about 0.92 m; the hoop rises 4/3 as high
steps: Total kinetic energy: cylinder (1/2)mv^2 + (1/4)mv^2 = (3/4)mv^2; hoop (1/2)mv^2 + (1/2)mv^2 = mv^2.
Ratio (v^2/g)/(3v^2/(4g)) = 4/3: the hoop stores more energy in rotation at the same speed.
items.skill: Compare rolling objects with energy

items.prompt: A ball rolls without slipping down an incline. A student claims, "Friction acts on the ball, so friction does negative work and the ball's mechanical energy decreases." Evaluate the claim, explaining what static friction does to the ball's energy.

rubric.criterion: Notes that for rolling without slipping the contact point is momentarily at rest, so the static friction force does no work on the ball.
Concludes that mechanical energy (translational plus rotational kinetic energy plus gravitational energy) is conserved, so the claim is wrong.
Explains friction's role: it exerts a torque that spins the ball up, shifting energy from translation into rotation, so the ball moves more slowly than a sliding block.

items.answer: The claim is wrong. The point of contact is instantaneously at rest, so static friction does no work and mechanical energy is conserved. Friction's torque makes the ball spin, so part of the energy goes into rotation instead of translation.
steps: Work requires the point where the force acts to move along the force; the contact point of a rolling ball does not slide.
Energy: mgh = (1/2)mv^2 + (1/2)Iω^2, with no loss term.
items.skill: Explain the role of static friction in rolling

items.prompt: Which condition is required for a rigid object to be in rotational equilibrium?
choices: The net force on it is zero
Every force on it passes through the axis
The net torque on it is zero
items.answer: (D) The net torque on it is zero
steps: Rotational equilibrium means constant angular velocity, which requires zero net torque.
An object can rotate steadily in equilibrium, and forces need not pass through the axis if their torques cancel.
items.skill: State the equilibrium condition

worksheets.title: Oscillations and fluids
worksheets.directions: Use g = 9.8 m/s^2, ρ_water = 1000 kg/m^3 and atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10^5 Pa. Give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: A 0.40 kg mass on a horizontal spring oscillates with amplitude 0.10 m and total mechanical energy 0.50 J. Find the spring constant and the maximum speed.
items.skill: Use energy in SHM

items.prompt: A block oscillates on a spring with amplitude A. At what displacement from equilibrium is the magnitude of its acceleration half of its maximum value?
steps: The restoring force is −kx, so |a| = kx/m is proportional to the displacement.
|a| is largest, kA/m, at x = A, so it is half that at x = A/2.
items.skill: Relate acceleration to displacement in SHM

items.prompt: A 60 kg diver standing still at the end of a springboard pushes it down 0.15 m. Treat the board as a spring. Find the frequency at which she bounces if she rides the board without leaving it, and her maximum speed if she bounces with an amplitude of 0.10 m.
items.answer: About 1.3 Hz (1.29 Hz); about 0.81 m/s
steps: Equilibrium: k(0.15 m) = (60)(9.8), so k = 3920 N/m.
items.skill: Model a springboard as an oscillator

items.prompt: The square drain cover at the bottom of a swimming pool measures 0.20 m × 0.20 m and lies 2.5 m below the water surface. The pipe below it holds air at atmospheric pressure. Find the net force of the water and air on the cover.
items.answer: About 9.8 × 10^2 N (980 N), directed down
steps: Atmospheric pressure acts on both sides, so the net pressure is the gauge pressure ρgh = (1000)(9.8)(2.5) = 2.45 × 10^4 Pa.
items.skill: Find a force from gauge pressure

items.prompt: All the air is squeezed out from under a suction cup of radius 2.0 cm pressed against a smooth ceiling. What is the largest mass it could hold up, in the ideal case?
items.answer: About 13 kg (a force of about 127 N)
steps: With no air under the cup, the atmosphere pushes it against the ceiling with F = P_atm A = (1.01 × 10^5)(π(0.020)^2) ≈ 127 N.
Largest mass = 127 N / 9.8 m/s^2 ≈ 13 kg.
items.skill: Use atmospheric pressure

items.prompt: Water flows upward through a vertical pipe that narrows from 4.0 cm diameter at the bottom to 2.0 cm diameter at a point 1.5 m higher. The speed at the bottom is 1.0 m/s. Find the speed at the top and how much greater the pressure is at the bottom than at the top.
items.answer: 4.0 m/s at the top; the pressure at the bottom is about 2.2 × 10^4 Pa greater
steps: Continuity: half the diameter means one-quarter the area, so v_top = 4.0 m/s.
Bernoulli: P_bottom − P_top = (1/2)ρ(v_top^2 − v_bottom^2) + ρgΔy = 500(16 − 1.0) + (1000)(9.8)(1.5).
items.skill: Apply Bernoulli with both speed and height changes

items.prompt: A brick hanging from a string is fully under water. It is lowered from 0.5 m to 2.0 m below the surface. How does the buoyant force on it change?
choices: It increases, because the pressure is greater deeper
It decreases, because more water is above the brick
It becomes zero at the bottom
It stays the same, because the pressure difference between its top and bottom faces does not change
items.answer: (D) It stays the same, because the pressure difference between its top and bottom faces does not change
steps: The pressures on the top and bottom faces both increase by the same ρgΔh.
Their difference, and so F_b = ρ_water V g, is unchanged for a fully submerged object.
items.skill: Reason about buoyancy and depth

worksheets.title: Problems that link units
worksheets.directions: Name each stage and the quantity conserved in it. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and give answers with units and 2–3 significant figures.

items.prompt: In the figure, a uniform disk (1.2 kg, radius 0.15 m) can turn freely about a vertical axle through its center. A 0.020 kg dart moving at 15 m/s along a line tangent to the rim strikes the rim and sticks. (a) Which quantity is conserved during the collision, and why not the others? (b) Find the angular velocity just after. (c) Find the kinetic energy converted to other forms.

rubric.criterion: Angular momentum about the axle is conserved because the axle's force has no torque about it; linear momentum is not, because the axle pushes on the disk, and kinetic energy is not, because the dart sticks.
ω ≈ 3.2 rad/s (accept 3.1–3.3 rad/s).
K_i = 2.25 J and K_f ≈ 0.073 J, so about 2.2 J is converted.

items.answer: (a) Angular momentum about the axle. (b) About 3.2 rad/s. (c) About 2.2 J (2.25 J before, 0.07 J after).
steps: The axle exerts a force but no torque about itself, so only L about the axle is conserved.
items.skill: Analyze a collision that starts rotation

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg block slides from rest down a frictionless ramp from a height of 0.45 m onto a frictionless level floor and runs into a spring with k = 800 N/m. Find the maximum compression of the spring and how long the block stays in contact with the spring.
items.answer: Maximum compression about 0.15 m (0.149 m); contact time about 0.16 s (0.157 s)
steps: While touching the spring the block moves in simple harmonic motion and is in contact for half a period.
items.skill: Link energy to simple harmonic motion

items.prompt: A satellite is moved from one circular orbit to a circular orbit of larger radius around the same planet. Compared with the first orbit, in the new orbit its speed is
choices: greater, and its period is longer
smaller, and its period is longer
smaller, and its period is shorter
the same, and its period is longer
items.answer: (B) smaller, and its period is longer
steps: v = √(GM/r) decreases as r increases.
T = 2πr/v increases, because r grows and v shrinks.
items.skill: Compare circular orbits

items.prompt: A block of mass m on a horizontal spring oscillates on a frictionless surface with amplitude A. As the block passes through equilibrium, a lump of clay of equal mass m, with no horizontal velocity, is dropped onto it and sticks. Find the new amplitude in terms of A, and state how the period changes.

rubric.criterion: Horizontal momentum is conserved during the brief collision, so the speed at equilibrium halves: v' = v_max/2.
Uses energy after the collision: (1/2)kA'^2 = (1/2)(2m)(v_max/2)^2 = (1/2)[(1/2)kA^2], giving A' = A/√(2).
Period increases by a factor of √(2), because T = 2π√(m/k) and the mass doubles.

items.answer: A' = A/√(2) ≈ 0.71A; the period becomes √(2) times longer.
steps: Momentum: mv_max = (2m)v', so v' = v_max/2, and the kinetic energy at equilibrium halves.
That kinetic energy becomes (1/2)kA'^2, so A'^2 = A^2/2.
items.skill: Link a collision to an oscillator

items.prompt: An open rooftop tank feeds a ground-floor tap whose opening is 18 m below the tank's water surface. Ignoring friction in the pipes, find the speed at which water leaves the fully open tap and the volume flow rate through its 1.2 cm diameter opening.
steps: Bernoulli from the open surface to the open tap (both at atmospheric pressure): v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 18) ≈ 18.8 m/s.
items.skill: Link gravitational energy to flow

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg box slides across a level floor at 3.0 m/s and stops because of kinetic friction (μ_k = 0.25). Sketch graphs of the box's kinetic energy against position and against time until it stops, labeling the starting energy, the stopping distance and the stopping time. Explain why one graph is a straight line and the other is not.

rubric.criterion: K against x is a straight line from 9.0 J to zero at x ≈ 1.8 m (1.84 m).
K against t is a curve from 9.0 J to zero at t ≈ 1.2 s (1.22 s), flattening to zero slope at the end.
Explains the straight line: friction does equal work for equal distances (ΔK = −μ_k mgΔx).
Explains the curve: the speed falls linearly with time, so K ∝ v^2 is quadratic in t, and the box covers less distance per second as it slows.

items.answer: K against x: a straight line from 9.0 J to 0 at x ≈ 1.8 m. K against t: a curve from 9.0 J to 0 at t ≈ 1.2 s, steep at first and flat at the end. Friction removes equal energy per meter, but the box covers fewer meters each second as it slows, and K ∝ v^2 with v decreasing linearly in time.
steps: K_0 = (1/2)(2.0)(3.0)^2 = 9.0 J; friction force μ_k mg = 4.9 N; stopping distance 9.0/4.9 ≈ 1.84 m.
Deceleration μ_k g = 2.45 m/s^2; stopping time 3.0/2.45 ≈ 1.22 s.
K(x) = 9.0 − 4.9x is linear; K(t) = (1/2)m(3.0 − 2.45t)^2 is a parabola with zero slope at the stop.
items.skill: Translate between energy graphs in x and t

weeks.title: Synthesis investigations: an elevator ride, air drag and a fading swing
weeks.objective: Carry out three paper investigations with supplied data that combine several units: a phone accelerometer in an elevator, the fall times of a paper baking cup dropped from several heights, and a pendulum whose swings die away. Build and test models, linearize data, judge uncertainty, and plan safe household versions.

connection.before: The whole course, especially motion graphs (Unit 1), Newton's second law (Unit 2), energy (Unit 3) and oscillations (Unit 7).
connection.after: Week 36 finishes the synthesis investigations and looks ahead to further courses in physics.

days: The modeling cycle: state a model, predict a straight-line graph, test it against data and revise; compare results using uncertainty.
Investigation 1: turning a phone's acceleration readings from an elevator ride into velocity, distance and apparent weight.
Investigation 2: fall times of a paper baking cup from several heights, its terminal speed and a model of air drag (beyond the exam).
Investigation 3: how fast a pendulum's swings die away, and the energy lost per swing.
Plan a household version of one investigation with its safety notes, and present the results.
explanation: After the exam, investigations can combine units the way real problems do. Each investigation this week follows the same cycle: write a model from physics you know, decide what graph the model predicts will be a straight line, plot the supplied data, and compare the slope with the model. When the data do not fit, revise the model; when they do, use the slope or area to measure something that is hard to measure directly, such as a drag constant or the height of a building. College Board's AP® Physics 1 course framework calls for at least 25 percent of class time in hands-on laboratory work. This paper investigation uses supplied data; it does not replace that lab work and does not satisfy the AP® Course Audit or college lab-credit requirements.

Compare results using both their differences and their stated uncertainties. Half the range of repeated trials is a simple estimate of scatter; it is not a confidence interval and does not account for systematic errors. A result written as 9.62 ± 0.10 m/s^2 gives an interval from 9.52 to 9.72 m/s^2, but its interpretation depends on how the uncertainty was estimated. The relative difference from a reference, |measured − reference| / |reference| × 100%, describes their separation; it does not by itself establish agreement.

Several ideas in this week's investigations go beyond the Physics 1 exam. Air drag on a light, broad object grows roughly with the square of its speed, so a falling paper baking cup quickly reaches a terminal speed where drag balances gravity; from then on, a graph of the distance it has fallen against time is a straight line. A swinging pendulum loses a little energy to the air on every swing; when it loses the same fraction each time, its amplitude shrinks by the same factor every swing, so a graph of each amplitude against the one before it is a straight line through the origin. A phone app can provide vertical acceleration with gravity removed; use that setting and check that it reads approximately zero while stationary, so the area under its readings gives changes in velocity, just as on any acceleration–time graph.

Household versions are optional and need care. Work at floor or table height (never stand on chairs), stay clear of other people's way, hold phones securely, keep swinging objects away from faces, and never aim any object at a person or animal. Record your own data in a table before analyzing it, and note any change from the supplied procedure.

examples.prompt: Two groups measure g with pendulums. Group 1 reports 9.62 ± 0.10 m/s^2 and group 2 reports 9.95 ± 0.30 m/s^2. Compute each percent difference from 9.80 m/s^2 and decide which result agrees with 9.80 m/s^2 within its uncertainty.
examples.answer: Percent differences: about 1.8% (group 1) and 1.5% (group 2). Only group 2 agrees within its uncertainty (9.65–10.25 m/s^2 includes 9.80); group 1's range, 9.52–9.72 m/s^2, does not, which suggests a systematic error.
steps: Ranges: 9.52–9.72 m/s^2 excludes 9.80; 9.65–10.25 m/s^2 includes it.
Group 1 is more precise but probably has a systematic error, such as measuring the string length to the top of the bob instead of its center.

examples.prompt: In a drag investigation, quadrupling the mass of a falling object doubles its terminal speed. Which drag model, F_drag = bv or F_drag = cv^2, does this support? Explain with the condition for terminal speed.
examples.answer: F_drag = cv^2. At terminal speed mg = cv_t^2, so v_t = √(mg/c), which doubles when m is quadrupled. With F_drag = bv, v_t = mg/b would quadruple instead.
steps: At terminal speed the net force is zero, so drag equals weight.
Quadratic drag: v_t ∝ √(m); √(4) = 2 matches the data.
Linear drag: v_t ∝ m, which predicts a factor of 4.
